title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Accounting and auditing work is almost entirely digital and document-based: reconciling records, preparing tax returns, testing controls, drafting reports — all tasks squarely in AI's path, and already being automated via RPA, cloud platforms, and LLM-based document review. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper compliance means more small businesses and individuals get proper books, more continuous/full-population auditing replaces sampling, and advisory services expand, but statutory audit and filing requirements are fixed in volume and licensure plus regulatory sign-off caps unlimited growth. The result is a profession that persists but shifts sharply from preparation and verification toward exception handling, judgment, advisory, and AI oversight — with junior preparer roles thinning while credentialed advisors gain leverage. That combination of very high disruption with moderate demand expansion fits restructure rather than outright replacement.

title: Actors
rationale: The core of acting is embodied, in-person performance — auditions, rehearsals, live stage work, theme-park shows, on-set camera work under a director — which AI does not perform for the worker; AI instead threatens substitution in specific digital-output subfields (voiceover, narration, background extras, digital doubles and likeness replication), which is significant but not the majority of the occupation's work. That mix of largely physical/presence-based tasks with a meaningful digitally-replicable slice puts disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper production budgets do expand total content and live entertainment output, but much of the AI-driven cost reduction bypasses human performers entirely, and live venue capacity and audience attention cap growth. With disruption at 6, the occupation classifies as resilient — the theatrical, live, and star-driven core persists, though voice and background-performer niches will contract and workers will increasingly negotiate over likeness and performance-capture rights.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuarial work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — compiling and cleaning data, building statistical and stochastic models, running reserve and pricing calculations, coding in R/Python/SQL, and writing explanatory reports — all of which sit directly in the path of current AI and ML tooling. Predictive modeling is increasingly performed by data science pipelines and automated model-governance tools, and LLMs already accelerate the documentation, memo-writing, and exam-level technical reasoning that consume much of a junior actuary's time; the residual human core is professional judgment, regulatory sign-off, and stakeholder communication. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: the number of insurance products, reserve filings, pension plans, and rate submissions is structurally bounded by the number of insurers, regulators, and statutory reporting cycles, so 10x cheaper modeling mostly means more granular analysis per filing rather than 10x more filings. High disruption combined with capped, regulation-bound demand points to headcount contraction relative to output — particularly at the trainee/data-compilation tier — even though credentialing requirements will slow the adjustment and keep senior signing actuaries valuable.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
rationale: The role mixes substantial knowledge work — scheduling, vendor contracts, procurement, records and information management, compliance documentation, energy/space analytics — much of which AI and smart-building software can automate or accelerate, pushing disruption toward the high end. But the core of the job is physical-world oversight: walking facilities, supervising maintenance and janitorial staff, handling emergencies on call, negotiating with contractors, and answering to regulators, all of which requires human presence and accountability. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate: the amount of building space, staff, and records an organization has is fixed by its physical footprint, so cheaper administration does not create dramatically more facilities to manage, though span-of-control could widen. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in the resilient band — AI reshapes the administrative and records-heavy periphery (and may thin out clerical support beneath these managers) without displacing the supervisory, on-site core.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
rationale: The instructional core here — teaching reading, writing, math, and conversational English, generating leveled lesson plans, assessing progress, and drilling practical vocabulary — is exactly the language- and cognitive-work that LLMs and AI tutoring apps already do competently and at near-zero marginal cost, so disruption is high even though some in-person motivation, cultural mediation, and case-management work remains human. Elasticity is low because demand for these programs is not price-suppressed in the usual sense: enrollment is set by government funding formulas, declining numbers of adults lacking a high school credential, and learners' willingness to attend scheduled classes, and any latent demand for cheap language learning is likely captured by self-serve AI apps rather than by hiring more teachers. With high task exposure and structurally capped, funding-dependent, already-shrinking demand (BLS projects -14%), productivity gains convert into fewer instructor positions per program rather than expanded service. That combination — disruption >= 7 with elasticity <= 4 — places it in the replace category.

title: Advertising sales agents
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — prospecting, gathering client background, drafting proposals and media kits, preparing cost estimates and contracts, analyzing sales statistics, follow-up correspondence — are digital and language-based, and AI plus programmatic self-serve ad platforms already automate much of the workflow, so disruption is very high even though relationship selling retains a human element. Elasticity is low because total ad spend is bounded by advertisers' marketing budgets rather than by the cost of a salesperson; when ad buying gets cheaper and easier, spend migrates to automated auction platforms that require no agent at all rather than expanding the number of agents. The structural shift from print to programmatic digital is already driving BLS-projected declines, and AI accelerates the disintermediation. High disruption with inelastic, already-shrinking demand puts this squarely in the replace category.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language/analysis-based — campaign planning, copy and creative direction, media buying optimization, market research synthesis, pricing analysis, and performance reporting are all squarely in AI's path, and generative AI plus automated ad platforms already reshape day-to-day workflow. Elasticity is high because marketing output is highly cost-suppressed: cheaper creative and analytics unlock far more personalized campaigns, more variants, more channels, more segments, and marketing for smaller firms that previously could not afford it, while competitive dynamics mean rivals must match spending. Headcount for the managerial/strategic layer should hold or grow even as the supporting production and ad-placement roles compress, though pure advertising and promotions managers tied to legacy print/media buying face contraction. Net effect is augment: each manager orchestrates dramatically more output, with the skill mix shifting toward AI-tool fluency, data interpretation, and brand judgment.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
rationale: Core work is heavily hands-on: building and maintaining test rigs, installing instrumentation in airframes, calibrating wind tunnels and physical test equipment, and troubleshooting hardware malfunctions on site. AI meaningfully affects the digital slice — data recording and reduction, simulation setup, anomaly detection in test telemetry, documentation — but cannot replace physical presence in test cells and assembly areas, and safety/defense clearance regimes slow adoption. Elasticity is high because falling launch costs, small satellites, drones, and new electric aircraft programs mean more vehicles to test and instrument, so cheaper test-data analysis expands the number of test campaigns rather than shrinking staff. With disruption in the moderate range, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the data-handling periphery while the hands-on test and integration core endures.

title: Aerospace engineers
rationale: Aerospace engineering is predominantly computer-based knowledge work — CAD modeling, CFD and structural simulation, control-law development, trade studies, requirements documentation and certification paperwork — all of which are in the direct path of AI-assisted design, surrogate modeling, and code/document generation, driving a high disruption score. However, a meaningful share of the job involves hardware integration, physical prototype and flight testing, cleared defense work, and accountability under FAA/DoD certification regimes that resist automation, which caps disruption below the very-high band. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design iteration does unlock more programs (small satellites, drones, eVTOL, rapid defense prototyping), but total output is constrained by enormous capital costs, manufacturing capacity, airworthiness certification timelines, and government budgets rather than engineering hours. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 6, the occupation persists and grows modestly, but the skill mix shifts sharply toward AI-augmented simulation, systems integration, and verification judgment — a restructuring rather than a contraction.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on: collecting field and plant samples, operating farm and lab equipment, preparing specimens, maintaining sterile environments, and inspecting foodstuffs in processing plants — tasks that require physical presence and cannot be done by AI. AI and lab automation do meaningfully affect the data-heavy periphery (compiling and analyzing test results, generating charts and reports, image-based disease detection in crops and animals, sensor/precision-ag analytics), which is why disruption is moderate rather than low. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster testing and analysis could expand quality-control coverage, more frequent field monitoring, and more agricultural R&D, but volumes are largely anchored to physical production and regulatory sampling requirements. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes documentation and analysis workflows while the sampling, testing, and inspection core remains human.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
rationale: A substantial share of the work — experiment design, data analysis, literature review, genomic/trait modeling, grant and report writing — is cognitive and squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven crop modeling, protein/formulation design, and remote-sensing analytics are already reshaping research workflows. But the core still depends on physical lab bench work, field sampling, plant/animal trials, plant and processing facility visits, biosecurity-constrained inspections, and multi-season biological validation that cannot be compressed by software, holding disruption at moderate. Elasticity is high because agricultural R&D demand is currently suppressed by the cost and slowness of trials: cheaper discovery would unlock far more crop varieties, soil management programs, and food product formulations, especially for smaller growers and food firms. Since disruption sits at 6 with AI mainly accelerating the analytical layer rather than replacing field and lab presence, the occupation is resilient, with modest continued growth as BLS projects.

title: Agricultural engineers
rationale: A substantial share of the work is digital — CAD design, modeling of airflow/runoff, data analysis, and increasingly AI/geospatial integration — so AI tools will materially accelerate the design and analysis portions. But the core role also involves fieldwork, on-site oversight of construction and livestock facility upgrades, equipment testing, and multi-stakeholder coordination with farmers, agronomists, and regulators, which caps disruption at the moderate-high boundary. Elasticity is high because precision agriculture, automation, and sustainability engineering are cost-suppressed markets: cheaper engineering design would unlock far more farms adopting engineered solutions, and these engineers are themselves builders of AI-driven ag systems. Given disruption at 6, the occupation is classified resilient — AI reshapes tools rather than the core hybrid field/design role, and the tiny 1,700-person workforce is projected to grow.

title: Agricultural workers
rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical and outdoors — planting, pruning, hand-harvesting, feeding and herding livestock, cleaning pens, operating machinery in unpredictable terrain — none of which AI itself performs; the constraint is robotics and mechanization, not language or cognitive automation. AI contributes at the margins via precision-agriculture guidance, computer-vision crop and animal monitoring, and breeding record analytics, which shifts some work toward equipment operation but leaves the manual core intact over a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is low because food demand is roughly fixed by population and diet, and cheaper production yields lower prices rather than dramatically more output, so productivity gains show up as gradual headcount decline (as BLS projects at -3%). Since disruption is well under 7, the occupation is classified resilient — the erosion here comes from farm robotics and consolidation rather than AI reshaping the work.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: The core work is cognitive and screen-mediated — monitoring radar, sequencing aircraft, computing separations — which is nominally in AI's path, and decision-support automation (conflict detection, NextGen trajectory-based routing, digital tower/remote tower systems) is already increasing per-controller throughput. But the safety-critical, real-time, legally mandated human-in-the-loop nature of the job, plus FAA certification rules, union structures, and extreme verification burden for any autonomous system, means the core task of holding responsibility for live traffic will not transfer to AI within a decade; AI shifts controllers toward supervisory and exception-handling roles rather than replacing them. Elasticity is low because demand is a direct function of flight volume and airspace/airport capacity, not the cost of controller labor — cheaper control does not induce many more flights, and staffing is set by regulatory minimums per sector and facility. With disruption at 5 the occupation lands in the resilient category: AI reshapes the tooling and raises per-controller capacity (capping growth, as BLS already notes), but does not reshape the fundamental job.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, inspection, and component replacement in hangars and on airfields, requiring dexterity, physical presence, and FAA-certified human accountability. AI can improve predictive maintenance analytics, diagnostic support, documentation/recordkeeping, and manual/technical-reference lookup, but these are peripheral to turning wrenches and signing off airworthiness. Demand is driven by fleet size, flight hours, and regulation-mandated maintenance schedules, so cheaper diagnostics only modestly expands work (some latent deferred maintenance, growing space sector), not 10x. With low disruption to core tasks and heavy regulatory anchoring, the occupation is resilient.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
rationale: Flying is already heavily automated in cruise, but the core job — physical presence in the cockpit, hands-on takeoff/landing, preflight inspection, real-time judgment in emergencies, and legal command responsibility — is protected by deep FAA certification requirements and public/regulatory resistance to reduced-crew or autonomous passenger flight. AI over the next decade will mainly improve flight planning, weather routing, fuel optimization, and cockpit decision support rather than replace pilots, though single-pilot cargo operations are a plausible edge case late in the window. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper flight operations could expand regional, charter, and cargo air service somewhat, but demand is bounded by aircraft fleets, airport slots, and travel demand rather than by pilot labor cost alone. With disruption well below the threshold and strong regulatory insulation, this occupation is resilient over the next 10 years.

title: Animal care and service workers
rationale: The core work — feeding, bathing, grooming, exercising, restraining, and training live animals — is intensely physical, tactile, and unpredictable, making it essentially outside AI's reach; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, record-keeping, behavior-monitoring apps, and customer communication. Demand elasticity is fairly high in principle because pet-care spending is discretionary and cheaper/more convenient services (mobile grooming, sitting, training) would expand consumption, and BLS already projects 11% growth driven by pet humanization. However, since disruption is low, productivity gains from AI cannot substitute for the hands-on labor, so headcount tracks pet ownership rather than AI capability. This makes it clearly resilient: AI may modestly improve scheduling and health monitoring but does not reshape the core job.

title: Announcers and DJs
rationale: The occupation is bifurcated: broadcast announcers and radio DJs (about 61% of jobs) do work that is almost entirely voice, script-writing, research, and content curation — all directly substitutable by synthetic voice cloning, automated playlist generation, and AI-generated show prep, and BLS already flags stations opting for 'AI DJs.' Non-radio, event DJs and emcees are far less exposed because they require physical presence, live crowd reading, and client interaction, which pulls the blended disruption score down from very high to high. Elasticity is low: radio airtime is a fixed inventory (there are only 24 hours per station per day) and listener attention is not cost-suppressed, while wedding/club DJ demand is capped by the number of events, not by production cost. High substitutability of the core voice/content work combined with structurally fixed demand means productivity gains flow to headcount reduction rather than output expansion, consistent with the projected -6% for the radio segment.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
rationale: A substantial share of the work is analytical and language-based — literature review, coding qualitative interview data, GIS site analysis, artifact classification, and report writing — all areas where AI tools are already materially useful, and remote-sensing plus machine vision are accelerating site detection and artifact typology. However, the core remains fieldwork: excavation, on-site survey, ethnographic observation and interviewing, and physical handling of artifacts in unpredictable outdoor settings that AI cannot substitute for. Demand is largely driven by fixed regulatory triggers (Section 106 compliance tied to construction volume) and grant/federal budget allocations rather than price, so cheaper analysis unlocks only modest additional work, though faster compliance review could slightly expand throughput. Because disruption stays at or below 6 with the physical and regulatory core intact, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with AI reshaping the desk-work portion of the job rather than the profession itself.

title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
rationale: Much of the preparatory and documentary side of this work — reviewing claim files, records, and precedents, drafting settlement agreements, scheduling, and summarizing positions — is language-based and squarely in AI's path, and AI-assisted 'e-mediation' triage tools already exist for high-volume, low-value disputes. However, the core of the job is live, emotionally charged, in-person facilitation where perceived neutrality, credibility, and legally recognized authority (binding arbitral awards, court-certified mediators) rest on a human third party that disputants consent to, which caps disruption in the moderate range. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster ADR would unlock substantial latent demand from small claims, consumer, workplace, and family disputes that currently go unresolved, but growth is constrained by public-sector budgets, certification rules, and the fact that parties must voluntarily agree to the process. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in resilient — AI reshapes the paperwork and analytical periphery while the human-presence core, and a small 9,100-person workforce with steady projected growth, remains intact.

title: Architects
rationale: Architecture is predominantly digital knowledge work — conceptual design, CADD/BIM modeling, code and zoning research, specification writing, renderings, cost estimating, and contract documentation are all directly in AI's path, and generative design plus AI-assisted BIM tools are already reshaping early-stage design and documentation workflows. However, meaningful portions of the job resist automation: licensure liability and stamping, client relationship management, site visits, construction administration, and negotiating among stakeholders. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design could unlock more custom design for small commercial and residential projects that currently use stock plans or skip architects entirely, but total demand is anchored to construction volume, which is capped by capital costs, permitting, land, and labor availability rather than design fees. So the profession persists with fewer hours spent on drafting and documentation and more on project orchestration, regulatory navigation, and client-facing judgment — a skill-set shift rather than wholesale replacement or explosive growth.

title: Architectural and engineering managers
rationale: Much of this role is knowledge work — planning, budgeting, scheduling, technical review, documentation — where AI tools already help materially, and AI-assisted design/simulation will reshape how their teams work. But the core of the job is accountability, leadership, hiring, negotiation, stakeholder coordination, and technical judgment on physical projects (plants, infrastructure, buildings), which resists automation and often requires on-site presence. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper engineering capacity means more projects (infrastructure, grid, renewables) get designed and built, but management headcount scales with number of teams and projects, not with output volume alone, and each manager can plausibly oversee larger AI-augmented teams. Net effect is resilient because disruption stays at or below the threshold — AI restructures the workflows of the engineers they supervise more than the manager's own core responsibilities.

title: Archivists, curators, and museum workers
rationale: Cataloging, metadata creation, transcription, digitization triage, and research/writing for exhibit labels are language-and-data tasks squarely in AI's path, and archivists in particular already use automated description and OCR/handwriting recognition tools — pushing disruption toward the high end. But a large share of the work is irreducibly physical and judgment-laden: handling fragile objects, conservation treatment, exhibit fabrication and installation, provenance authentication of unique items, public tours, donor and loan negotiation, and institutional administration. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper description could unlock large hidden backlogs of undescribed archival material and expand digital access, but headcount is capped by fixed institutional budgets, grant funding, and public/government appropriations rather than by service demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6 with the physical and stewardship core intact, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with AI reshaping the metadata and research workflow rather than the job itself.

title: Art directors
rationale: Art direction is almost entirely visual-digital knowledge work — concepting, mood boards, layout, image selection, and reviewing designs — and generative image/video tools already transform how visual concepts are produced and iterated, so disruption is very high. However, the role's core value is taste, judgment, client persuasion, and directing teams, which shifts rather than eliminates the job; the biggest displacement risk lands on the production designers beneath them. Elasticity is high because visual content demand is heavily cost-suppressed: cheaper production means far more campaigns, variants, personalized creative, and video/web assets per client, and small businesses that never had an art director can now afford directed creative. That combination — very high disruption absorbed by expanding output per director — fits augment, though junior pipeline entry may narrow.

title: Assemblers and fabricators
rationale: The core work is manual, dexterity-intensive assembly with hand tools in physical plants — language and digital AI barely touches it, though AI-driven vision inspection and collaborative robotics do affect quality-control and some repetitive tasks. The disruption that does occur comes from robotics/automation rather than from AI per se, and delicate small-batch and aerospace assembly remains stubbornly manual. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: manufacturing output is bounded by capital investment, supply chains, and consumer goods demand rather than by assembly labor cost, so productivity gains flow to fewer workers (as BLS's -1% projection reflects). Because AI-specific disruption to the core hands-on tasks stays low, this is 'resilient' in the AI sense even though headcount is flat-to-declining for automation and offshoring reasons.

title: Athletes and sports competitors
rationale: The core work — physically competing in officiated athletic events — is inherently embodied and cannot be performed by AI; the value proposition is human bodies competing for spectator entertainment. AI touches only peripheral elements like performance analytics, opponent scouting video review, injury-prevention modeling, and training optimization, which coaches and analysts largely handle. Elasticity is low because roster spots are fixed by league structures and expansion is rare and capital-intensive, so cheaper analytics cannot multiply the number of professional athletes. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Athletic trainers
rationale: Athletic training is overwhelmingly hands-on: taping, bracing, on-field emergency response, palpation-based injury evaluation, and manually guided rehabilitation require physical presence at practices and games. AI can help with documentation, injury-risk analytics from wearable data, rehab program design, and concussion protocol compliance, but these are peripheral to the core physical work. Elasticity is high because athletic trainer coverage is currently rationed by cost — most youth and high school programs lack coverage — so cheaper support tools could expand access, but that expansion requires more human bodies on sidelines, not fewer. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient and BLS's projected 11% growth remains plausible.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: The core work — running numerical models, analyzing large observational datasets, writing code, generating graphics and forecast narratives — is almost entirely digital and already being transformed by AI weather models (GraphCast/GenCast/Aurora-class systems) that match or beat traditional NWP at a fraction of the compute cost, plus LLM-generated forecast discussions and broadcast graphics. Physical elements (field campaigns, on-air presence, court testimony) are peripheral and don't shield the analytic core. Elasticity is moderate: cheap, hyper-local, probabilistic forecasting genuinely unlocks latent demand from energy traders, insurers, agriculture, logistics and event planners, but the largest employer segment is federal/publicly funded and budget-capped, and consumers don't need 10x more forecasts — the value accrues largely to platforms rather than to headcount. Hence restructure: the occupation persists but shifts toward ML model development, verification, decision-support communication and domain-specific consulting, with routine shift-based forecasting and generic broadcast roles thinning out.

title: Audiologists
rationale: Core audiology work is hands-on and in-person: otoscopic examination, cerumen removal, physically administering audiometric and vestibular testing, fitting and adjusting hearing aids and cochlear implant mappings, and counseling patients who often have communication difficulties. AI and automated/self-administered audiometry, algorithmic hearing-aid fitting, and OTC self-fitting devices do encroach on the routine testing and programming layer, and AI will assist with interpretation and documentation — but diagnosis of complex pathology, pediatric and balance work, and the empathetic counseling role require human presence and licensure. Elasticity is high because untreated hearing loss is massively under-served (only a minority of candidates ever get hearing aids), so cheaper, faster screening and fitting would pull far more patients into care, reinforced by an aging population. With disruption at 4, the occupation remains resilient: AI reshapes the periphery and some device-fitting revenue, but does not displace the clinical core, and demand tailwinds support headcount growth.

title: Automotive body and glass repairers
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on — hammering dents, welding panels, aligning frames, cutting out and sealing windshields in awkward positions and at customer locations — none of which AI can perform without hardware that does not exist at commercial scale. AI touches only peripheral tasks: photo-based damage assessment, cost estimating, insurance claim processing, and ADAS calibration guidance, which may shift some estimating work away from repairers but not the core repair. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because demand is driven by accident frequency and insurance economics, not by the cost or speed of repair; cheaper estimating does not create more collisions, and ADAS adoption may actually reduce crash volume. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient, though technicians must keep retraining on sensors, cameras, and new materials.

title: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling components, lifting tires, working in cramped positions — which AI cannot perform without embodied robotics that remains far from shop-floor deployment. AI does meaningfully improve the diagnostic portion of the job (interpreting fault codes, guided troubleshooting, service documentation retrieval) and customer-facing estimates and paperwork, so peripheral disruption is real but limited to a modest fraction of daily tasks. Elasticity is moderate: vehicle repair demand is tied to the physical fleet and driven by miles driven and vehicle age rather than by service cost, though faster diagnosis could capture some deferred maintenance work. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient — AI becomes a better diagnostic tool in the technician's hands rather than a substitute for the technician.

title: Bakers
rationale: Baking is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: measuring, kneading, shaping, monitoring ovens, decorating, and cleaning equipment. AI touches only peripheral functions like inventory forecasting, recipe scaling, ordering, and demand prediction for shop owners; automation in commercial baking is driven by mechanical equipment rather than AI, and that trend long predates current AI tools. Demand for baked goods is moderately expandable with lower cost, but it is fundamentally capped by food consumption and requires physical production capacity. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — BLS projects 6% growth and the core craft remains human.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
rationale: The core work is entirely manual, tactile, and interpersonal — cutting, coloring, and styling hair on a live client in an unpredictable physical setting that robotics is nowhere near replicating. AI touches only peripheral tasks: booking and scheduling apps, marketing, inventory, client records, and virtual style previews/consultation tools. Demand is bounded by hair growth rates and personal grooming budgets, so cheaper back-office automation would not multiply appointments, though slight expansion is possible via better marketing and add-on services. Very low disruption places this firmly in the resilient category regardless of elasticity.

title: Bartenders
rationale: Bartending is almost entirely physical and interpersonal: mixing and pouring drinks, checking IDs, judging intoxication, conversing with patrons, and hauling kegs. AI touches only peripheral elements like POS systems, inventory forecasting, and scheduling; automated drink dispensers are robotics rather than AI and remain niche in a business where hospitality and social atmosphere are the product. Demand for bars and restaurants could expand moderately with income growth and lower operating costs, but people don't consume unlimited drinks and the experience itself is the constraint. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: The work is almost entirely phone- and screen-based: skip tracing via databases, scripted disclosures, negotiation of standardized payment plans, and record-keeping — all directly in the path of AI voice agents, automated dialers, and LLM-driven negotiation and compliance workflows. Debt collection volume is bounded by the amount of delinquent debt outstanding, not by the cost of collection, so cheaper collection does not create meaningfully more debt to collect; regulatory constraints (FDCPA, state rules, contact frequency caps) further limit expansion. Productivity gains therefore flow to headcount reduction, consistent with BLS's projected -10% decline. High disruption plus inelastic demand places this squarely in the replace category.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
rationale: Roughly half of the work is wet-lab and instrument-based, but the intellectual core — literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, protein structure and function prediction, omics data analysis, molecular design, grant and paper writing — is squarely in AI's path, and tools like AlphaFold, generative protein design, and LLM-based literature mining are already reshaping daily practice, justifying a high-but-not-maximal disruption score. Demand elasticity is high because the space of unexplored targets, diseases, enzymes, crops, and biomaterials is effectively unbounded and currently rate-limited by the cost and slowness of experimentation; cheaper, faster discovery cycles pull forward far more programs rather than simply reducing scientist headcount, though grant funding caps and lab capital costs keep it below the top tier. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 7, the occupation lands in augment: each scientist orchestrates far more computational and automated experimentation, with skill demands shifting toward computational and AI-fluent experimental design rather than headcount contraction.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
rationale: Much of the work — simulation, statistical modeling, software for instruments, design iteration, regulatory documentation, technical reports, and literature synthesis — is digital and squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven protein/molecule design and generative CAD already materially change R&D workflows; however, a substantial share involves physical prototyping, lab experimentation, clinical validation in hospitals, and hands-on device support, capping disruption at the lower end of 'high'. Demand elasticity is high because biomedical innovation is strongly cost- and cycle-time-constrained: cheaper, faster design and testing unlocks more device programs, more personalized implants, more drug-delivery and diagnostic products, and broader access in underserved markets, so productivity gains largely convert into more projects rather than fewer engineers. Regulatory approval timelines (FDA) and clinical trial requirements do throttle expansion somewhat, keeping elasticity from reaching 9-10. Net effect is augment: each engineer will supervise AI-driven design and simulation pipelines while total demand for biomedical devices and therapies expands enough to sustain or grow headcount.

title: Biological technicians
rationale: Core work is substantially physical and hands-on — pipetting, culturing, staining, maintaining instruments, collecting field samples — which AI alone cannot perform; disruption comes from the knowledge-work slice (data analysis, modeling, report writing, protocol documentation) plus growing AI-driven lab automation platforms that could compress routine bench tasks over the decade. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper and faster experimentation genuinely unlocks more biotech, synthetic biology, and screening work, but research volume is gated by grant funding, capital equipment, regulatory validation, and physical lab capacity rather than purely by labor cost. With disruption at 5, the occupation lands in the resilient band — AI reshapes the analytical and documentation periphery and raises expectations for computational literacy, but the wet-lab core remains human. Technicians who add data/automation skills will be advantaged, yet aggregate headcount should hold roughly stable.

title: Boilermakers
rationale: Boilermaking is overwhelmingly physical: welding, rigging, cutting, and crawling into confined vessels at height in unpredictable field conditions. AI touches only peripheral elements such as blueprint interpretation, inspection analytics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and drone/robotic inspection assistance, none of which displace the hands-on assembly and repair core. Demand is driven by the installed base of boilers and pressure vessels and the energy transition away from coal, not by the cost of cognitive labor, so productivity gains from AI would not unlock much new demand. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient; its projected decline stems from energy-sector shifts rather than AI.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — transaction entry, coding, reconciliation, report generation, error checking — are routine digital data processing already heavily automated by bank feeds, OCR receipt capture, and rules-based ledger software, with LLMs extending automation to exception handling and client communication. Demand is structurally inelastic: a business has a fixed number of transactions to record, and cheaper bookkeeping does not generate more transactions; the only expansion is marginal (very small firms and gig workers getting real books instead of shoeboxes). BLS already projects a 6% decline attributed to automation, and generative AI likely accelerates that. High disruption plus low elasticity means productivity gains convert to fewer headcount, with surviving roles shifting toward advisory work that increasingly resembles the accountant occupation.

title: Broadcast, sound, and video technicians
rationale: A large share of this work is physical and on-site: rigging cables, hauling and mounting speakers, lights, and cameras, focusing fixtures, climbing towers, and troubleshooting hardware in real time at live events. AI meaningfully touches the software-side portions — automated audio mixing, camera switching, noise reduction, auto-tracking cameras, lighting presets, and remote/centralized broadcast operations — which is why BLS explicitly cites AI as reducing crew sizes in broadcast, lighting, and sound roles. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper AV production expands corporate video, streaming, houses of worship, and digital signage installations, but live events, venues, and productions are physically capped in number. Because the core hands-on setup, maintenance, and on-location presence remains human, disruption stays at or below the moderate range, making this occupation resilient with slow headcount growth rather than restructured or replaced.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Budget analysis is almost entirely digital knowledge work: consolidating spreadsheets, variance analysis, forecasting, cost-benefit modeling, and writing explanatory reports — all tasks squarely in the path of current AI and modern FP&A automation tools. Demand is highly inelastic because the number of budgets is fixed by the number of organizations, agencies, and fiscal cycles; nobody produces 10x more budgets because analysis got cheaper, and government headcount is tied to appropriations rather than analytic throughput. The residual human value lies in defending recommendations to legislators and executives and navigating political tradeoffs, which will keep a leaner core of senior analysts but shrink the preparatory and reconciliation workload that occupies most junior roles. High disruption plus structurally capped demand yields net headcount contraction.

title: Bus drivers
rationale: Core work is physical driving plus in-person passenger management — supervising children, assisting riders with disabilities, handling unruly passengers, and safety judgment — none of which language-model AI touches. Autonomous vehicle technology is the real threat, but full self-driving buses carrying schoolchildren face steep regulatory, liability, union, and public-trust barriers that make meaningful displacement within 10 years unlikely; AI's near-term impact is on routing, scheduling, dispatch, and driver-monitoring systems that assist rather than replace. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper transit operation could expand service frequency and rural/paratransit coverage where demand is currently cost-suppressed, but ridership is structurally bounded by school enrollment and municipal budgets. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient over the next decade, with the caveat that autonomy could shift the picture sharply in the following decade.

title: Butchers
rationale: Butchering is almost entirely manual, dexterity-intensive physical work performed in cold, wet environments on variable animal carcasses — a task that resists both AI and robotics for the foreseeable term. AI touches only peripheral functions like inventory forecasting, ordering, and demand planning, which are a small fraction of daily tasks. Demand for retail meat cutting is driven by food consumption and the structural shift toward pre-packaged cuts, not by the cost or speed of cognitive work, so productivity gains from AI wouldn't unlock much latent demand. With disruption far below the threshold, the occupation is resilient to AI even though its overall employment growth is slow for unrelated reasons (centralized pre-packaging and automation in processing plants).

title: Calibration technologists and technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on: physically inspecting, adjusting, and testing instruments on shop floors and in labs, requiring dexterity, presence, and sometimes lifting heavy equipment. AI and self-calibrating instrumentation will absorb the documentation, scheduling, drift-prediction, and report-writing portions, and may reduce routine verification passes, but the physical adjustment and traceability-to-standard work remains human. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper calibration could expand coverage as instrumented equipment and sensors proliferate across manufacturing and healthcare, but calibration volume is largely tied to installed device counts and regulatory intervals rather than latent unmet demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the paperwork and diagnostics around the job without displacing its hands-on core.

title: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on and patient-facing: positioning patients, prepping catheterization sites, attaching electrodes, monitoring vitals during invasive procedures, and standing/lifting in procedure rooms — none of which AI can perform. AI does touch the interpretive layer (automated EKG interpretation is already standard, and AI arrhythmia/waveform analysis is advancing fast), which could compress the 'analyze results and summarize findings' portion of the job, but physicians retain final read responsibility anyway. Elasticity is moderate: aging demographics and cheaper screening could expand cardiac testing volumes somewhat, but procedures are capped by physician availability, capital equipment, reimbursement rules, and clinical indication rather than by analysis cost. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the reporting and quality-check periphery while the physical, procedural core remains human.

title: Career and technical education teachers
rationale: CTE teaching is anchored in hands-on, supervised skill demonstration in workshops and labs — welding, auto repair, cosmetology, culinary — which requires physical presence, safety oversight, and tactile feedback that AI cannot replicate. AI meaningfully helps with the knowledge-work periphery: lesson planning, curriculum updates, assessment, grading, and personalized theory instruction, but the core instructional activity remains embodied. Elasticity is moderate: reskilling demand could rise as AI displaces workers into trades, and cheaper curriculum development lowers program costs, but school budgets, facility capacity, credentialing requirements, and declining student populations cap expansion. Because disruption stays well below the 7 threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes prep and admin work while classroom and lab instruction persist largely unchanged.

title: Carpenters
rationale: Carpentry is overwhelmingly physical, dexterity-intensive work in unpredictable, unstructured jobsite environments — measuring, cutting, framing, and installing materials that AI cannot perform without robotics that remain far from cost-competitive. AI touches only peripheral tasks: bidding, estimating, material takeoffs, scheduling, and blueprint interpretation, which matter mainly for the 27% who are self-employed. Elasticity is high because housing and renovation demand is genuinely suppressed by cost and labor scarcity, so cheaper construction would unlock substantial latent building. But since core disruption is minimal, the occupation is resilient; the larger structural threat is prefabrication and modular construction, not AI itself.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: The core work — extracting features from satellite/aerial imagery and LiDAR, georeferencing, digitizing, data QC, and map production — is almost entirely digital and sits squarely in the path of computer vision and automated feature-extraction models that already outperform manual digitizing; the residual human work is fieldwork validation, judgment about accuracy/relevance, licensure-backed certification, and stakeholder communication, keeping it below a 9. Demand has real latent expansion: cheaper mapping enables far more frequent basemap refresh, digital twins, autonomous-vehicle and precision-agriculture layers, and disaster response mapping in jurisdictions that currently cannot afford it. But 45%+ of employment is in local/state/federal government with fixed appropriations and procurement cycles, which caps how fast productivity gains convert into new headcount, so elasticity is moderate rather than high. With very high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation persists but shifts toward geospatial data science, model supervision, accuracy auditing, and licensed sign-off — classic restructuring rather than wholesale replacement or growth.

title: Cashiers
rationale: Core cashier tasks — scanning, tallying, processing payments, and answering routine policy questions — are highly routine transaction processing that self-checkout, mobile payment, computer-vision 'just walk out' systems, and AI-driven kiosks already substitute for at scale; the physical elements (bagging, light stocking, ID checks) provide only partial insulation, so disruption is high though not maximal. Demand elasticity is very low: the number of retail transactions needing supervision is set by shopping volume, not by the cost of checkout labor, and cheaper checkout does not induce people to buy dramatically more trips or items — productivity gains convert almost directly into fewer staffed lanes. Combined with continuing migration of sales to e-commerce, the result is headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS -10% projection. Surviving roles will consolidate into fewer 'checkout attendants' overseeing banks of automated stations.

title: Chefs and head cooks
rationale: The core work — cooking, tasting, plating, supervising a hot fast-paced kitchen, and hands-on quality inspection — is physical, sensory, and requires real-time presence that AI cannot replicate. AI meaningfully touches only peripheral tasks: menu ideation, recipe development, inventory and purchasing forecasting, scheduling, cost/margin analysis, and social media marketing, which may modestly reduce administrative burden. Demand elasticity is moderate: dining out is somewhat cost-sensitive and cheaper back-office operations could support more restaurant openings, but a chef can only oversee one kitchen and meal consumption is physically bounded. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI becomes a back-office assistant rather than a substitute for culinary craft and kitchen leadership.

title: Chemical engineers
rationale: Much of chemical engineering is computational and analytical — process simulation, modeling, cost estimation, regulatory documentation, and materials research — all areas where AI and ML-driven design tools (e.g., molecular/process optimization) are already materially useful, pushing disruption toward high. However, a substantial share of the role involves plant walkdowns, physical experimentation, pilot-scale validation, safety oversight of hazardous processes, and PE-stamped accountability that cannot be delegated to software, capping disruption at 6. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper simulation and faster materials discovery could unlock more R&D projects and process optimization, but demand is ultimately tied to capital-intensive physical plant construction and domestic manufacturing volumes, which are constrained by capital costs and offshoring. Because core work still requires human presence, physical judgment, and legal sign-off, the occupation is best classified as resilient with AI reshaping the analytical periphery and accelerating design cycles.

title: Chemical technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on wet-lab and plant-floor activity: preparing solutions, setting up and maintaining precision instruments, sampling, and troubleshooting equipment — tasks that require physical presence and dexterity. AI (and lab automation more broadly) does meaningfully reshape the data-analysis, reporting, QC-documentation, and experiment-design portions of the job, so disruption is moderate rather than low, and increasing lab robotics could compress routine sample throughput. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster analytical testing would expand demand in environmental monitoring, materials discovery, and pharma R&D screening, but much testing volume is set by regulatory requirements and production schedules rather than price. Because the physical laboratory core is not displaced by language/cognitive AI within a decade, the occupation lands in the resilient band, with the skill mix tilting toward automation-instrument operation and data interpretation.

title: Chemists and materials scientists
rationale: A large share of chemists' and materials scientists' work is already computational and language-based — literature review, hypothesis generation, molecular modeling, spectral and analytical data interpretation, statistical analysis, and technical report writing — and AI systems (generative molecular design, ML interatomic potentials, structure prediction, autonomous experiment planning) are already reshaping these steps, pushing disruption to the high end; the counterweight is the irreducible physical wet-lab component of synthesis, sample handling, instrument operation, and QC testing that keeps it from scoring 8-9. Elasticity is moderate: latent demand for new materials, batteries, semiconductors, and drug candidates is genuinely large and cost-suppressed, so cheaper discovery cycles will expand screening and R&D volume, but throughput is capped by capital-intensive lab infrastructure, regulatory validation timelines, and the fact that routine compliance/testing-lab work (a big employment segment) has essentially fixed volume. That combination — core cognitive tasks absorbed by AI, with real but bounded demand expansion — fits restructure: headcount likely holds roughly flat while the job shifts toward computational fluency, AI-assisted experimental design, and orchestrating automated labs, with routine bench analysts most at risk and hybrid computational-experimental scientists gaining.

title: Childcare workers
rationale: Childcare is almost entirely physical, hands-on, and supervisory work — feeding, diapering, safety monitoring, emotional care, and play — with staff-to-child ratios legally mandated and parents demanding human presence. AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, progress record-keeping, parent communication apps, and activity/curriculum ideas, leaving the core work untouched. Elasticity is high in principle because childcare demand is heavily suppressed by cost, but AI cannot lower the dominant labor cost, so this latent demand stays locked. With disruption at the bottom of the scale, the occupation is resilient; its projected decline stems from falling birth rates and affordability, not automation.

title: Chiropractors
rationale: Chiropractic work is fundamentally hands-on: manual spinal adjustment, physical examination, palpation, and in-person patient contact cannot be performed by AI. Disruption is limited to peripheral functions — intake, documentation, imaging interpretation support, practice marketing, scheduling, and patient education materials — which may free up modest amounts of clinician time. Elasticity is moderate because demand for drug-free pain treatment is genuinely price- and access-sensitive and could expand with cheaper administration and better referral integration, but the binding constraint is licensed practitioner hours and insurance coverage, not information processing. With disruption well below the threshold, this is a resilient occupation where AI touches back-office and diagnostic support rather than the core therapeutic act.

title: Civil engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Roughly half the work — CAD drafting, cost estimating, specification writing, data analysis, and report preparation — is squarely in AI's path, and generative design plus automated documentation tools are already compressing drafting hours. But the other half requires physical presence: field surveys, soil and materials testing, jobsite inspection for code conformance, and coordination with construction crews under real-world, weather-dependent conditions that AI cannot substitute for. Elasticity is low because infrastructure volume is governed by public capital budgets, permitting, and licensed-engineer sign-off rather than by the cost of technician labor, so cheaper drafting mostly means fewer technician hours per project rather than many more projects. With disruption capped at 6 by the irreducible fieldwork component, the occupation lands in resilient — headcount likely flat, with the office/drafting share of the role shrinking and the inspection/field-data share growing.

title: Civil engineers
rationale: A substantial portion of civil engineering work is digital and analytical — CAD drafting, structural and hydraulic calculations, cost estimating, code and permit research, report writing — all areas where AI tools are already materially useful and generative design is advancing fast. However, the core of the job also involves site presence, construction oversight, soil and materials testing interpretation, stakeholder negotiation, and PE-stamped legal accountability for public safety, which anchors judgment with a licensed human and limits full automation. Elasticity is moderate at best: infrastructure volume is set by federal, state, and local capital budgets and permitting timelines rather than by engineering design cost, which is a small share of total project cost, so cheaper design unlocks only modest extra project throughput and some latent small-municipality work. With disruption at 6 and demand structurally capped, the occupation lands in resilient — AI reshapes the drafting and analysis periphery and raises per-engineer output, but the licensed, field-facing, accountability-bearing core remains, and headcount should continue its slow growth.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: Core work is document review, policy interpretation, damage estimation from photos, and rule-based payment authorization — almost all digital, language- and data-driven tasks squarely in AI's path; photo-based estimating and automated straight-through claims processing are already deployed at scale, though a minority of field inspection, negotiation, and surveillance work still requires human presence. Demand is structurally fixed: the number of claims is driven by accidents, illness, and disasters, not by the cost or speed of adjudicating them, so faster and cheaper processing yields fewer adjusters rather than more claims. Only marginal expansion is plausible (more thorough fraud detection, more subrogation recovery, disaster-driven surges). High disruption paired with near-inelastic demand points to replace, consistent with BLS's own projected -5% decline attributed explicitly to AI and automated photo estimation.

title: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians
rationale: Much of the work is hands-on specimen handling, instrument calibration, quality control, and physical presence in a regulated lab, which limits AI's reach; however, image-based tasks (cytology, hematology slide review, microbiology plate reading) and result flagging are directly in AI's path, and automation plus AI-assisted digital pathology is already reshaping high-volume workflows, so disruption is at the upper end of moderate. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: test volumes are driven by physician orders, reimbursement, and clinical necessity rather than lab cost, so cheaper analysis mainly consolidates workload rather than multiplying it, though genetic and screening testing offers some genuine latent expansion. Because the core of the job remains physical, regulated, and CLIA-supervised work that AI touches at the analytic periphery, the occupation scores as resilient, consistent with BLS's slow-but-positive growth projection with automation dampening demand.

title: Coaches and scouts
rationale: Coaching is fundamentally an in-person, physical, motivational and relational job: running practices, correcting technique, managing team dynamics, and making live in-game decisions cannot be delegated to AI. However, meaningful portions of the work are analytic and increasingly AI-assisted — video breakdown, opponent tendency analysis, conditioning program design, and especially scouting, where AI-driven player evaluation and data models already displace some traditional scouting legwork. Elasticity is high because personalized athletic instruction is currently rationed by cost and coach availability, so cheaper analysis and planning tools would let each coach serve more athletes and expand youth/recreational instruction. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate range — AI touches the analytical periphery while the coaching core remains embodied human work — the occupation is resilient, though scouting subroles will see real restructuring.

title: Community health workers
rationale: Core work is field-based: home visits, in-person outreach, trust-building with specific cultural communities, basic screenings, and physical presence at community events — AI can assist with recordkeeping, referral lookup, translation, report writing, and grant proposals, but these are peripheral to the relational core. Demand elasticity is high because community health outreach is heavily suppressed by funding and staffing constraints, with vast unmet need in underserved populations, so cheaper administrative overhead would let programs reach more people. Since disruption is low, the occupation is resilient: AI tools make these workers modestly more efficient without reshaping what they do, and projected growth continues to be driven by chronic disease burden and public health funding rather than technology.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: The core work — analyzing wage and benefits data, benchmarking against market surveys, modeling plan costs, monitoring regulatory compliance, and preparing presentations and recommendations — is almost entirely digital, analytical, and language-based, and AI plus HRIS/benefits platforms already automate much of it. Residual human elements (vendor negotiation, executive persuasion, supervising staff, accountability for pay decisions) keep it below the very-high tier. Demand is highly inelastic: an organization needs one pay structure and one benefits program regardless of how cheap the analysis becomes, and the trend toward outsourcing to consulting firms and automated vendors further concentrates the function. With high task disruption and structurally capped demand, productivity gains flow into fewer positions per organization rather than expanded output, so modest headcount contraction (against an already flat 0% BLS projection) is the likely outcome.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language/data-based: writing and classifying job descriptions, benchmarking survey data, running cost analyses, monitoring regulatory changes, and producing reports — all tasks where current AI already performs well and HRIS/compensation platforms are rapidly embedding automated benchmarking and job-architecture generation. Elasticity is low because demand is bounded by the number of organizations and positions that need pay structures; a company does not need 10x more compensation plans or job classifications just because analysis becomes cheap, though slightly more small and mid-sized employers may gain access to formal comp/benefits design and regulatory complexity (pay transparency, healthcare cost pressure) sustains some need for human judgment and negotiation with brokers. High disruption combined with structurally capped demand points to fewer specialists per organization, with surviving roles concentrated in strategy, vendor negotiation, and compliance sign-off rather than analysis production.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Compliance work is overwhelmingly document- and language-based: tracking changing regulations, mapping rules to policies, reviewing transactions and records, drafting reports and training materials, and flagging potential violations. LLMs and regtech tools already do regulatory horizon-scanning, policy drafting, and automated monitoring/screening well, putting a large share of daily tasks in AI's direct path, though accountability, judgment calls, investigations, and onsite inspections still require humans. Elasticity is moderate: regulatory volume keeps expanding and cheaper compliance means smaller firms and more business lines get monitored continuously rather than sampled, but demand is ultimately capped by the regulatory regime, and much of the field is government employment with fixed budgets and mandated headcounts. High disruption with moderate demand expansion means the occupation persists but shifts toward AI oversight, model validation, exception handling, and accountable sign-off, displacing those doing routine review.

title: Computer and information research scientists
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — algorithm design, coding experiments, literature synthesis, data analysis, paper writing — are digital and directly in AI's path, and AI research assistants already materially accelerate experiment pipelines and code generation, so disruption is very high. However, demand for computing research is heavily supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained: AI itself is the frontier research field, and cheaper/faster experimentation unlocks vastly more research directions in AI safety, robotics, cybersecurity, quantum, and domain-specific science. These scientists are also the primary designers and stewards of the AI systems doing the automating, giving them a complementary rather than substitutive relationship. High disruption plus high latent demand means each researcher becomes dramatically more productive while headcount continues to grow, fitting the augment category.

title: Computer and information systems managers
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — planning IT architecture, evaluating vendors, budgeting, security policy, and reporting to executives — and AI already assists heavily with analysis, documentation, project tracking, and technical evaluation; however, a large share of the role is accountability, negotiation, stakeholder persuasion, and people management that AI cannot own, which keeps disruption at the low end of 'high.' Elasticity is high because AI itself dramatically expands the surface area of technology that organizations must adopt, integrate, secure, and govern — more systems, more data, more AI deployments all require human oversight and decision authority. As AI makes IT teams more productive, organizations tend to build and run more technology rather than shrink IT leadership, and someone must be accountable for AI-driven systems and their risks. Thus headcount should hold or grow even as the skill mix shifts toward AI governance, vendor/model management, and orchestrating smaller, higher-leverage technical teams.

title: Computer hardware engineers
rationale: Core hardware engineering work is overwhelmingly digital: RTL/HDL coding, schematic capture, simulation, verification, timing analysis, place-and-route, and documentation — all areas where AI-assisted EDA tools (reinforcement-learning floorplanning, AI verification/coverage closure, LLM-generated RTL and testbenches) are already materially productive, though physical bring-up, lab debug, and manufacturing oversight keep it short of maximum. Demand elasticity is high because custom silicon and embedded design is currently gated by enormous NRE cost and multi-year design cycles: if design effort drops 10x, far more domain-specific accelerators, ASICs, and connected devices become economically viable, and the AI infrastructure buildout is itself pulling hardware demand upward. Combined with a small, credentialed workforce (77k) and severe talent scarcity in semiconductors, productivity gains are far more likely to be absorbed by more chips and more design starts than by headcount cuts. Hence augment: each engineer covers more of the stack, with role emphasis shifting toward architecture, specification, and validating AI-generated designs.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: The work is predominantly knowledge work — designing topologies, writing configurations, capacity modeling, documentation, and troubleshooting logs — all of which AI coding/config assistants and AIOps tools already meaningfully accelerate; only occasional server-room hardware work and high-stakes cross-team negotiation resist automation, holding disruption just below the very-high tier. Demand is elastic because network infrastructure is itself the substrate for the AI and cloud buildout: cheaper, faster design means more organizations (including smaller ones previously priced out of proper architecture) get modernized, segmented, zero-trust networks, and every AI workload expansion creates new bandwidth and interconnect design work. Productivity gains are therefore likely to be absorbed by a larger volume of network projects rather than by headcount cuts, consistent with BLS's 12% growth projection. The role restructures toward automation-driven, code-defined networking skills, but total employment should hold or grow — an augment outcome.

title: Computer programmers
rationale: Computer programmers do almost entirely digital work — translating specifications into code, testing, and debugging — which is precisely the task class where LLM code generation is already strongest, so disruption is at the top of the scale. Unlike software developers, this occupation is defined by the implementation step rather than architecture, requirements gathering, or stakeholder judgment, so there is less residual human-only work to migrate into. Elasticity is only low-to-moderate: cheaper code does expand total software output, but that latent demand accrues mainly to developers, architects, and product owners who define what to build, while the pure code-translation role gets absorbed rather than multiplied. BLS already projects a 6% decline, and AI acceleration points to steeper contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: Help-desk and user support work is overwhelmingly language-based troubleshooting — reading ticket descriptions, diagnosing from symptoms, walking users through steps, documenting resolutions — which is squarely in the path of current LLM chatbots and agentic IT automation; self-healing endpoint tools and AI knowledge bases already resolve a large share of tier-1 tickets. Some hands-on hardware setup, physical repair, and onsite network maintenance keeps disruption below the maximum. Elasticity is low: support demand is derived from an installed base of users and devices, and organizations treat IT support as a cost center to minimize rather than a service to consume more of — cheaper support does not make firms want 10x more tickets. High disruption plus inelastic, cost-center demand yields headcount contraction, consistent with BLS's projected decline, though the residual complex-escalation and onsite tier-2/3 roles will remain and command higher skill.

title: Computer systems analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language-based: requirements gathering, data modeling, cost-benefit analysis, system configuration, testing, documentation, and some programming — all directly in AI's path, and AI tools already draft specs, diagrams, test plans, and integration code. Elasticity is high because organizational demand for system modernization, integration, and AI-enabled workflow redesign is currently gated by scarce analyst capacity and project cost; cheaper analysis means far more systems get evaluated, upgraded, and customized, including at smaller firms previously priced out. The stakeholder-liaison and domain-knowledge component also resists full automation, keeping humans central while their throughput multiplies. Hence augment: substantial task transformation with demand expansion absorbing the productivity gains, though the mix shifts toward business judgment and AI orchestration over hands-on documentation and coding.

title: Concierges
rationale: Much of a concierge's informational work — recommendations, reservations, travel arrangements, message-taking — is language-based and already being absorbed by apps and AI assistants, which BLS explicitly cites as reducing hotel concierge roles. However, the core value proposition is in-person hospitality: greeting people, physical package handling, running errands, responding to resident needs, and creating a human welcome that is itself the product being sold, so disruption stays moderate. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper concierge-style service does expand into residential and senior-living settings where amenity competition drives demand, but the physical staffing at a desk is roughly fixed per building rather than scaling with output. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI hollows out the information-lookup periphery while the in-person presence remains the job.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
rationale: A meaningful share of the work is analytical and digital — GIS mapping, remote sensing, drone and satellite imagery analysis, growth modeling, plan writing, and regulatory compliance documentation — all of which AI can substantially accelerate. But the core of the job remains field-based: site inspection, controlled burns, fire suppression, physical timber measurement, supervising crews, and negotiating with landowners in person, which caps disruption at moderate. Demand is largely set by government budgets, public land acreage, and regulatory mandates rather than by the cost of analysis, so cheaper monitoring expands coverage somewhat (more parcels assessed, more private landowners advised) but does not multiply headcount. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the mapping and reporting periphery while the field-management core, and the wildfire-driven demand growth BLS projects, remain intact.

title: Construction and building inspectors
rationale: Core work requires physical site presence — climbing ladders, crawling in attics, using moisture meters and electrical testers — which AI cannot replace, though plans examination, code lookup, report writing, and photo/video-based remote inspection are genuinely in AI's path and already reducing site visits (BLS explicitly cites remote inspection as a headcount drag). That puts disruption in the moderate band: a meaningful slice of the job (plan review, documentation, code interpretation) is digitizable while the field verification remains hands-on. Elasticity is low because inspection volume is set by construction activity and mandated code checkpoints, not by inspection cost — nobody orders extra inspections because they got cheaper, and regulatory frameworks fix the number of required checks. Since disruption is at 5, the occupation lands in 'resilient': AI reshapes the paperwork and enables some remote consolidation, causing slow erosion rather than a structural transformation of the core role.

title: Construction equipment operators
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical and site-based: maneuvering heavy machinery in unpredictable outdoor terrain, coordinating with crews via hand signals, and performing hands-on maintenance. GPS/machine-control and semi-autonomous grading systems are real and growing, and mining sites already run autonomous haulage, but general construction sites are too variable, cluttered, and liability-sensitive for broad autonomy within a decade, so AI mainly assists with grade guidance, telematics, and maintenance prediction. Demand is moderately elastic — cheaper earthmoving would unlock some deferred infrastructure and site work — but is capped by permitting, funding cycles, and land availability rather than operator cost. With disruption well under the threshold, the occupation is resilient; the main change is operators supervising increasingly automated machines rather than being replaced by them.

title: Construction laborers and helpers
rationale: The work is almost entirely physical: hauling materials, digging, cleaning sites, erecting scaffolding, and operating handheld power tools in unpredictable outdoor environments. AI has essentially no path to these tasks in the next decade; robotics remains far from cost-effective for varied, unstructured jobsite labor, and the only AI touchpoints are peripheral (scheduling, safety monitoring, dispatch). Demand is fairly elastic in the sense that cheaper construction would unlock substantial latent building and infrastructure demand, but that expansion would come from AI-driven efficiencies elsewhere (design, permitting, project management) rather than automating laborers themselves. With disruption at the floor, the occupation is resilient — headcount is driven by construction volume and demographics, not AI.

title: Construction managers
rationale: A meaningful slice of the job — cost estimating, scheduling, bid analysis, contract and code interpretation, progress reporting — is digital knowledge work that AI tools (and increasingly integrated project-management platforms) already accelerate. But the core of the role is onsite presence: physically inspecting work, negotiating with subcontractors, resolving unpredictable field emergencies, and holding legal/licensed accountability for safety and compliance, none of which AI can assume. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper project management could unlock more small-scale renovation, retrofit, and infrastructure work, but construction volume is ultimately capped by capital, labor availability, permitting, and land rather than by management cost. Since disruption stays at or below 6 — AI reshapes the paperwork and estimating periphery while the supervisory core remains human — the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 9 percent growth.

title: Cooks
rationale: Cooking is overwhelmingly physical and sensory — knife work, heat management, plating, taste and smell — performed in crowded, fast-paced kitchens that resist automation; AI touches only peripheral functions like menu planning, inventory forecasting, and order routing. Robotic fry stations and automated assembly do threaten the fast food and short order segments (BLS already projects -13% and -6%), but these are robotics rather than AI cognition, and the larger restaurant cook category is projected to grow 15%. Demand for prepared food expands with income and convenience, so cheaper kitchen operations plausibly mean more outlets and more meals served rather than fewer cooks overall. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the back-office and some highly standardized stations but not the core craft.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
rationale: Core work is physical presence, supervision, restraint, and de-escalation inside secure facilities — tasks AI cannot perform. AI touches only the periphery: surveillance analytics, contraband detection, automated headcounts, and report/log generation, which may modestly reduce paperwork and per-officer staffing ratios but not replace the post. Elasticity is very low because demand is set by incarceration policy and court schedules, not by the cost of guarding; cheaper monitoring does not create more prisoners.
