Projected decline stems from sentencing reform and budgets rather than AI, so the occupation is resilient to AI disruption even as headcount shrinks for unrelated reasons.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Cost estimating is almost entirely digital analytical work: reading blueprints and specs, quantity takeoffs, database lookups of material and labor costs, calculation, and report writing — all directly in the path of AI plus BIM/estimating software automation, with multimodal models increasingly able to parse drawings and generate itemized estimates. Demand is largely derived from the volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which is capped by capital, permitting, and physical building capacity rather than by the cost of producing estimates; cheaper estimating might unlock somewhat more bid coverage and more frequent re-estimation on smaller jobs, but not proportionally more work. Site visits, client negotiation, and accountability for costly errors preserve some human role, but they are a minority of the task mix. High disruption combined with low elasticity implies headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS -4% projection, so 'replace' fits.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
rationale: The core task — converting spoken language into accurate verbatim text in real time — is precisely what modern automatic speech recognition and diarization systems now do at near-human accuracy and a tiny fraction of the cost; the remaining human work (speaker identification, certification, editing, exhibit handling) is peripheral to the transcription itself, so disruption is very high even though courtroom presence and state certification rules slow adoption. Demand is highly inelastic: the number of depositions, hearings, and broadcast hours is set by litigation volume and captioning mandates, not by transcription price, so cheaper transcription does not generate proportionally more proceedings. Some latent demand exists for captioning more meetings, classes, and live events, but that expansion is being served almost entirely by automated captioning rather than by hiring more human captioners. High disruption plus inelastic demand points to headcount contraction, with surviving roles shifting toward reviewing and certifying machine-generated records.

title: Craft and fine artists
rationale: The occupation is sharply bifurcated: digital and commercial subsegments (illustrators, cartoonists, concept and digital artists, some medical/scientific illustration) are squarely in the path of generative image models and are already seeing commissioned work absorbed, while the majority of the field — ceramics, glass, fiber, furniture, jewelry, sculpture, tattooing, public installations — is hands-on material work where AI at most assists with ideation, marketing, and online sales. That mix places overall disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than the high band. Elasticity is low because the value of fine and craft art rests on scarcity, provenance, and human authorship rather than on production cost; making images 10x cheaper does not make collectors buy 10x more paintings, and cheap machine-made lookalikes historically suppress rather than expand demand for handmade goods. Net effect is resilient overall (core physical and reputational work persists, BLS projects flat employment), though the commercial illustration niche within it faces genuine replacement pressure and those workers will need to shift toward physical media, direct-to-audience brands, or AI-augmented art direction.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: Core tasks — gathering financial information, assessing income/debt/expenses, calculating repayment capacity, generating debt management plans, and drafting client documents — are cognitive, numeric, and language-based, and current AI tools plus automation software already handle much of the analysis and document generation; the BLS itself notes automation may temper growth. Disruption is capped below 8 because trust-building, emotional counseling for distressed borrowers, live negotiation with creditors, and referral to community resources still favor a human intermediary. Elasticity is moderate: there is large latent demand for personal financial guidance that cost has suppressed, but most jobs sit in institutionally budgeted settings (colleges, hospitals, nonprofit agencies) whose headcount is funded by fixed budgets and enrollment rather than client willingness to pay, and much unlocked demand will be met by self-serve AI tools rather than more counselors. That combination — high task exposure with only partial demand absorption — fits restructure: the role shifts toward high-touch case management, complex negotiation, and oversight of AI-generated plans, with fewer routine-intake positions.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: Core tasks — listening to inquiries, retrieving account information, explaining products, processing orders and returns, and logging interactions — are almost entirely language-based and conducted through phone, chat, and email channels that LLM agents already handle at scale today. Voice AI and chatbots are being deployed aggressively because labor is the dominant cost of contact centers, and only a minority of work (in-person retail assistance, escalated or regulated inquiries) requires human presence. Demand is inelastic: customers do not want more service interactions, they want fewer and shorter ones, so cheaper support resolves the same fixed volume of contacts with less human labor rather than expanding volume. High disruption plus low elasticity, reinforced by BLS's own -5% projection, points squarely to headcount contraction.

title: Dancers and choreographers
rationale: Dance is an inherently embodied, physical craft: auditioning, rehearsing for hours, and performing live before audiences cannot be delegated to AI. Choreographers may use AI for idea generation, motion-capture visualization, music selection, or admin/marketing tasks, and AI-generated video may compete at the margins for some commercial/background dance content, but the core work remains human presence and athleticism. Elasticity is moderate — cheaper production tools and social media distribution can expand the market for dance content and instruction, though live performance demand is capped by venue funding and audience attention. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient; AI touches peripheral creative and promotional tasks only.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Nearly every core task — data cleaning, coding, model building, statistical analysis, visualization, and even written interpretation of results — is fully digital and squarely in the direct path of current LLMs and AutoML tooling; AI agents already handle substantial portions of exploratory analysis and pipeline code, so disruption is very high. Elasticity is also high because the vast majority of organizational data is never analyzed at all: cost and scarce talent currently suppress demand, and cheaper analysis means far more questions get asked, more models get built and monitored, and smaller firms and departments gain access to analytics they previously could not afford. Data scientists also sit on the supply side of AI adoption, building and validating the very systems that expand, meaning their work shifts toward problem framing, data governance, evaluation, and stakeholder translation rather than disappearing. Headcount should grow even as the day-to-day skill mix changes sharply, fitting 'augment,' though workers who remain purely script-writing analysts will be squeezed.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital — SQL, schema design, query tuning, scripting, monitoring, documentation — all directly in AI's path, and cloud automation plus AI copilots already handle much of the routine maintenance, backup, and optimization work. Elasticity is moderate: the AI data boom itself increases demand for well-governed data infrastructure, pipelines, and security, and cheaper database work means more organizations get proper architecture, but the number of enterprise data estates that need designing is structurally bounded and cloud consolidation lets fewer people serve more clients. This splits the occupation: pure administration/maintenance roles contract (BLS already projects -1%) while architecture, governance, and AI-data-readiness roles grow, meaning the skill set shifts substantially rather than the occupation disappearing. Hence restructure.

title: Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers
rationale: Core work is physical and unpredictable: driving congested urban streets, lifting and carrying packages, navigating buildings, and handling last-mile customer interaction. AI already touches the periphery through route optimization, dispatch, and delivery scheduling, and autonomous vehicles plus sidewalk robots pose a long-run threat, but within 10 years the last-100-feet handoff in messy real-world environments keeps human drivers essential. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster delivery reliably unlocks more e-commerce and on-demand ordering volume, as the BLS 8% growth projection reflects. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the routing and logistics layer around the driver rather than the driver's core tasks.

title: Dental and ophthalmic laboratory technicians and medical appliance technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on fabrication, shaping, polishing, and fitting of physical devices, which AI itself cannot perform; however, the design phase is increasingly digital (CAD/CAM, intraoral scans, 3D printing), so AI-assisted design and automated milling/printing meaningfully change part of the workflow — hence a moderate disruption score. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand is driven by demographics (aging, diabetes, vision correction) and clinical need rather than price, so cheaper crowns or lenses do not lead people to buy many more of them, though some latent demand exists for higher-quality or more accessible prosthetics and orthoses. Because disruption stays at or below 6 — the physical fabrication and fitting core remains human — the occupation is classified resilient, even though automation (as BLS notes) will slowly erode dental lab technician headcount and shift skills toward digital design and machine operation.

title: Dental assistants
rationale: Core work is hands-on chairside assistance: sterilizing instruments, passing tools, suctioning, taking impressions and intraoral x-rays, and calming anxious patients — all physical tasks requiring presence and dexterity that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral duties like scheduling, billing, charting/documentation, and x-ray image quality checks, which may modestly reduce administrative time per assistant but not core headcount. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper administrative overhead and aging-population demand support practice growth, and assistants could take on expanded clinical duties, though dental visits are constrained by dentist capacity and insurance. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the front office, not the operatory.

title: Dental hygienists
rationale: Core work is hands-on manual care inside a patient's mouth requiring fine motor skill, physical presence, and licensure — AI cannot perform scaling, polishing, sealant application, or x-ray positioning. AI touches only peripheral elements: charting/documentation automation, radiograph caries and bone-loss detection (already FDA-cleared and in use), scheduling, and patient education materials. Demand is moderately elastic — an aging population retaining more teeth, expanded scope-of-practice laws, and unmet preventive care needs mean more hygiene services could be consumed, but chair time and licensing constraints cap expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, this is a resilient occupation where AI augments diagnosis support and paperwork rather than reshaping the core clinical task.

title: Dentists
rationale: Dentistry is overwhelmingly a manual, in-mouth procedural craft requiring fine dexterity, physical presence, and licensure; AI touches mainly the periphery — radiograph and intraoral scan interpretation, caries/perio detection, treatment planning, CAD/CAM appliance design, charting, and practice administration. These are real and already-deployed tools, which lifts the score above minimal, but they do not displace drilling, extracting, anesthetizing, or restoring teeth. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper diagnostics and faster digital workflows plus cosmetic dentistry could unlock some latent underserved demand, though patient chair time and access remain the binding constraint. Because disruption to core tasks stays low, the occupation is resilient with AI mostly boosting throughput per dentist and shifting some tasks to hygienists and technicians.

title: Desktop publishers
rationale: Desktop publishing is almost entirely digital: importing text and images, adjusting typography, formatting layouts, and exporting print/web files. Generative AI and template-driven tools (Canva, Adobe's AI layout features, automated typesetting) already perform much of this work, and the residual judgment is largely absorbed by graphic designers and editors using those tools themselves. Demand elasticity is low because layout is a derivative, fixed-volume input to a publication pipeline — cheaper layout does not cause organizations to produce vastly more brochures or pages, and much output is shifting to templated electronic formats. High disruption plus inelastic demand, consistent with the BLS -12% projection, points squarely to replacement.

title: Diagnostic medical sonographers
rationale: Core work is hands-on: positioning patients, manipulating a transducer with real-time hand-eye coordination, and interacting with anxious or immobile patients — tasks AI cannot perform without robotics that remain immature. AI does meaningfully assist the image-quality, measurement, and preliminary abnormality-flagging portions (AI-guided acquisition tools already help novices capture standard views), plus documentation, so disruption is moderate rather than low. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, AI-guided point-of-care ultrasound could expand imaging into primary care, rural clinics, and screening settings, but exam volume is ultimately gated by clinical indications, reimbursement, and scanner/room time. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the interpretive periphery and may even broaden ultrasound's use, while the scanning job itself remains human.

title: Diesel service technicians and mechanics
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling engines, lifting heavy components, working in awkward positions on trucks and roadside — which AI cannot perform without mature robotics that don't exist for this variable environment. AI does touch the diagnostic layer: computerized fault-code interpretation, predictive maintenance telematics, and AI-assisted access to service manuals will speed troubleshooting and shift some diagnostic skill from the technician to software. Elasticity is moderate: fleets have a fixed number of vehicles requiring maintenance, so cheaper diagnostics don't multiply repair volume, though predictive maintenance could shift work toward more frequent preventive service. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the diagnostic periphery while the wrench-turning core remains human.

title: Dietitians and nutritionists
rationale: A large share of dietitians' work is language- and analysis-based — assessing intake, translating research, building meal plans, writing educational materials, documenting progress — and consumer AI nutrition tools already generate credible personalized plans, so disruption is meaningful. But the core value sits in licensed clinical judgment integrated with lab data and care teams, empathetic behavior-change counseling, and hands-on food service management in hospitals, schools, and long-term care, which AI does not replace; that caps disruption at moderate. Elasticity is high because nutrition counseling is heavily suppressed by cost and access, and cheaper screening/plan generation plus growing preventive-care and aging-population demand would expand rather than shrink the total volume of nutrition services. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in 'resilient': AI reshapes documentation, plan drafting, and patient education workflows at the periphery while the counseling and clinical core, and its licensure moat, persist.

title: Drafters
rationale: Drafting is almost entirely digital work — translating engineer/architect specifications into CAD/BIM models — which is squarely in the path of generative design, parametric automation, and AI text/sketch-to-model tools; CAD/BIM already absorbed much of the routine work and AI accelerates that trend, letting engineers and architects produce their own documentation directly. Demand is inelastic because drawing volume is derived from the number of buildings, machines, and circuit boards actually being designed and built, which is capped by capital budgets, permitting, and construction capacity rather than by drafting cost; cheaper drafting does not induce many more projects. With very high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains flow to fewer drafter headcount, consistent with BLS projections of flat-to-declining employment concentrated in mechanical and electrical specialties. Some architectural/civil drafters with BIM coordination and site-collaboration duties will persist, but the occupation overall contracts.

title: Drywall installers, ceiling tile installers, and tapers
rationale: The work is almost entirely physical: lifting and hanging heavy panels, working on stilts and scaffolds, cutting, taping, and sanding in variable, unfinished job-site conditions. AI has essentially no path to these core tasks in the next decade; at most it touches peripheral functions like takeoff/material estimating, bidding, and scheduling, which are often handled by supervisors or estimators anyway. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper construction and remodeling would unlock more projects, but that expansion depends on overall construction costs, not on AI-driven productivity in this trade. With disruption at the very low end, the occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Economists
rationale: Economists' work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — data collection, statistical modeling, forecasting, literature review, report writing and visualization — all directly in AI's path, and current LLM/code-agent tools already handle much of the econometric coding and drafting. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis lets more firms, agencies, and smaller organizations commission economic modeling and expands data-driven pricing and policy evaluation, but the field is small, credential-gated, and heavily dependent on fixed government budgets and institutional demand rather than price-sensitive consumption. The result is substantial skill-set change — value shifts toward framing causal questions, judgment, credibility, and communicating with policymakers rather than executing analysis — with roughly flat headcount, matching BLS's 1 percent projection. That combination of very high disruption and moderate demand expansion fits restructure.

title: Editors
rationale: Editing is almost entirely text-based cognitive work — copyediting, grammar and style correction, fact-checking, rewriting for clarity, headline generation — and current LLMs already perform these tasks at or near professional quality, making disruption very high. The copy-editing tier in particular is directly substitutable, while editorial judgment, sourcing ethics, writer management, and brand voice stewardship remain human-anchored but employ far fewer people. Elasticity is limited: while AI floods the world with more content needing review, the willingness to pay for human editorial oversight is capped by shrinking media budgets and the fact that AI can also do the review layer itself; audience attention and publication slots are structurally finite. Net effect is replacement — productivity gains accrue to fewer, more senior editors overseeing AI-assisted pipelines rather than to expanded headcount, consistent with already-flat BLS projections.

title: Electrical and electronic engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Roughly half the work is hands-on: assembling prototypes, soldering, calibrating instruments, bench machining, and physically troubleshooting hardware in labs and factories — tasks AI cannot perform without robotics that remains costly and slow to deploy. AI does materially affect the documentation, diagram drafting, test-data analysis, and report-writing portions, and automated test systems continue to absorb routine measurement work, which justifies a moderate disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper electronics design and validation would expand hardware prototyping and instrumentation work somewhat (semiconductors, utilities, defense), but demand is capped by capital costs, fab capacity, and physical production cycles rather than technician labor cost. Because disruption stays at or below 6 given the irreducible physical core, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with skill shifts toward automated test and software-defined instrumentation.

title: Electrical and electronics engineers
rationale: Most of the work — circuit and system design in CAD/EDA tools, simulation, requirements documentation, firmware and control code, test analysis — is digital and squarely in AI's path, with AI-assisted EDA, layout optimization, and code generation already materially useful; but physical prototyping, lab testing, site visits, and supervision of manufacturing keep a meaningful human core, capping disruption at the low end of 'high.' Elasticity is high because demand for electrical engineering is currently supply- and cost-constrained: grid modernization, electrification, data center power, semiconductors, and defense electronics all have large backlogs that cheaper, faster design capacity would unlock rather than eliminate. Combined with PE licensure and liability requirements that keep accountable humans in the loop, productivity gains should translate into more projects completed per engineer rather than fewer engineers, fitting 'augment.'

title: Electrical and electronics installers and repairers
rationale: Core work is hands-on: physically inspecting, disassembling, replacing, and testing electrical and electronic equipment in factories, substations, and vehicles, often lifting 50+ pound components in awkward positions. AI can assist with diagnostics, predictive maintenance alerts, manual lookup, and documentation, which shifts troubleshooting somewhat but doesn't remove the need for a technician on site with tools. Elasticity is moderate: grid strain and electrification expand maintenance demand, but the volume of equipment needing repair is set by installed physical infrastructure, not by the cost of diagnosis. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient — AI becomes another diagnostic tool alongside multimeters and oscilloscopes.

title: Electrical power-line installers and repairers
rationale: The core work is almost entirely physical and hazardous: climbing poles and towers, stringing high-voltage cable, operating bucket trucks and augers in all weather conditions. AI can improve peripheral functions like predictive maintenance analytics, drone/aerial inspection triage, outage prediction, and crew dispatch optimization, but it cannot perform the field repair itself, so disruption is low. Demand elasticity is high because grid buildout for electrification, data centers, EVs, and renewables is constrained by workforce capacity, not by lack of need — any productivity gain gets absorbed by more grid work. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient and BLS-projected growth is likely to hold or exceed expectations.

title: Electricians
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical installation, troubleshooting, and repair in varied, unpredictable built environments — pulling wire, bending conduit, working in cramped spaces and at heights — which AI cannot perform without robotics that remain far from deployment. AI touches only peripheral elements: code lookup, diagnostic assistance, estimating, scheduling, and design support, plus AI-enabled test instruments. Demand elasticity is high in principle because electrification, data centers, EV charging, and renewables create large latent demand currently constrained by labor supply, but that demand expansion is limited by human throughput rather than AI. With disruption well below the threshold and strong projected growth, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on: soldering, calibrating hydraulic and pneumatic assemblies, machining housings, physically installing and repairing automated machinery on factory floors. AI meaningfully helps with the knowledge portions — interpreting schematics, diagnostic troubleshooting, predictive maintenance analytics, test documentation and report writing — which raises disruption above the purely manual trades, but the dexterity and on-site presence requirements are not automatable in a 10-year window. Elasticity is moderate: broader deployment of robotics and automated lines expands the installed base needing technicians, and cheaper automation deployment could unlock demand among smaller manufacturers, though total demand is bounded by industrial capital spending. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes diagnostics and paperwork at the periphery while the physical maintenance core endures.

title: Elementary, middle, and high school principals
rationale: Much of a principal's day is in-person leadership: student discipline, teacher observation and coaching, parent and community relations, crisis and safety management — work requiring physical presence, authority, and accountability that AI cannot assume. AI will meaningfully compress the administrative layer (scheduling, budget tracking, compliance reporting, test-score analysis, drafting communications), which is real but peripheral to the core role. Elasticity is low because principal headcount is structurally tied to the number of school buildings, enrollment, and public budgets, not to productivity — one school gets one principal regardless of how efficient the job becomes. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the paperwork burden but not the fundamental leadership function, and BLS-projected decline stems from demographics rather than automation.

title: Elevator and escalator installers and repairers
rationale: Core work is intensely physical and site-specific: lifting 200-pound components, working in shafts and crawl spaces, wiring control panels, and hands-on troubleshooting of hydraulics and brakes. AI's contribution is peripheral — predictive maintenance analytics from IoT sensors, diagnostic assistance on computerized controllers, and digital service records — which may shift some work from reactive to scheduled repair but does not remove the need for a licensed mechanic on site. Demand is structurally capped by the installed base of equipment and new building construction, plus regulatory inspection requirements, so cheaper diagnostics wouldn't multiply the number of elevators needing service. Low disruption places this squarely in the resilient category, consistent with BLS's above-average growth projection.

title: Emergency management directors
rationale: A large share of the job is document- and analysis-heavy — drafting emergency operations plans, hazard and risk modeling, grant applications and reporting, damage assessments, public messaging — all of which AI can substantially accelerate. But the core of the role is human leadership under crisis conditions: on-scene command, live interagency coordination, politically accountable decisions like ordering evacuations, and in-person training and community outreach that AI cannot assume. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper planning capacity could let smaller jurisdictions and more private organizations get real continuity programs, but positions are capped by public budgets, statutory structures, and the fixed number of jurisdictions and facilities needing a director. Because disruption is confined to the paperwork and analytic periphery while the authoritative human command role remains, the occupation is resilient with each director simply covering more planning ground.

title: EMTs and paramedics
rationale: Core work is intensely physical and situational: lifting patients, hands-on airway management, IV placement, driving ambulances, and improvising in chaotic uncontrolled environments — none of which AI can perform. AI touches the periphery through dispatch optimization, decision-support protocols, EKG interpretation aids, automated documentation, and remote physician telemedicine consults, which may modestly shift paramedic judgment tasks but not replace them. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because 911 call volume is driven by demographics and acute events, not by cost or speed of service, though cheaper documentation could expand community paramedicine and interfacility transport roles. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — demand is fundamentally tied to human physical presence at emergencies.

title: Entertainment and recreation managers
rationale: Core work is on-site, interpersonal, and physical: leading activities, inspecting equipment, staffing programs, handling customers in real time, and responding to emergencies. AI meaningfully helps with the administrative layer — scheduling, budgeting, marketing copy, feedback analysis, program design ideas — but cannot substitute for presence, leadership, and live experience delivery, so disruption is moderate. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper program administration could let more community centers, clubs, and small venues run more offerings, but headcount is ultimately tied to facilities and participants, not to output speed. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient; AI trims paperwork while leisure demand and in-person supervision keep employment growing.

title: Environmental engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: A substantial share of the work is hands-on field and lab activity — collecting air, soil, and water samples, operating pumps and monitoring instruments, handling hazardous materials, and inspecting facilities — which AI cannot perform. AI (plus sensor automation and remote telemetry) does meaningfully affect the documentation, recordkeeping, regulatory-compliance review, and data-analysis portions of the job, and automated testing is already cited by BLS as a productivity constraint on employment growth, putting disruption in the moderate range. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster monitoring could expand the number of sites and parameters continuously tracked, but demand is largely driven by regulatory mandates and project budgets rather than latent consumer appetite. Because the core work remains physically situated and only the reporting/analysis layer is automated, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with flat headcount and a modest shift toward instrumentation and data-oversight skills.

title: Environmental engineers
rationale: A large share of environmental engineering work is document- and analysis-heavy — permit applications, compliance reports, environmental impact statements, modeling of air/water dispersion, and data QC — all directly in AI's path, so disruption is substantial. However, core value also comes from site inspections, fieldwork, stamped PE design sign-off, regulatory negotiation, and legal/expert testimony that require licensed human accountability and physical presence, capping disruption at moderate-high. Demand is partly latent (many small facilities and municipalities underinvest in remediation and compliance because it is costly), but growth is ultimately gated by regulation, public budgets, and capital project pipelines rather than analysis cost, giving moderate elasticity. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in resilient: AI reshapes the reporting and modeling workflow and boosts per-engineer throughput, but the licensed, field-based, regulatory core of the job persists.

title: Environmental science and protection technicians
rationale: Core work centers on physical field activity — inspecting sites, setting up monitoring equipment, collecting air, soil, and water samples, and handling hazardous materials — which AI cannot perform, though sensors and automated monitoring may reduce some manual sampling. AI does meaningfully assist the knowledge-work portion: data analysis, regulatory compliance checking, and report writing, which is a substantial minority of the job. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper monitoring could expand environmental testing coverage of contaminated sites and small facilities, but demand is largely set by regulatory mandates and government budgets rather than price. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes reporting and analysis workflows at the periphery while field inspection and sampling remain human-performed.

title: Environmental scientists and specialists
rationale: A large share of the work — data analysis, modeling, regulatory compliance review, permit and impact-statement writing, literature synthesis — is digital and language-based, and AI already accelerates NEPA documentation, remote sensing interpretation, and report drafting. However, the occupation retains substantial non-automatable components: field sampling and site inspection, lab work, professional sign-off and legal accountability under environmental statutes, stakeholder negotiation, and expert testimony, which holds disruption just below the high band. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper assessments could expand monitoring coverage and let smaller municipalities and firms afford environmental review, but total demand is largely set by regulatory mandates and construction/permitting volume rather than by price. Given disruption at 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes the reporting and analysis workflow but not the regulated, field- and accountability-anchored core.

title: Epidemiologists
rationale: Core epidemiological work — statistical modeling, large-database analysis, literature synthesis, report and grant writing, surveillance dashboards — is precisely the kind of quantitative/language work AI already accelerates substantially, pushing disruption high; only the fieldwork, interviewing, sample collection, community outreach and inter-agency leadership components resist automation. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analytics would let more hospitals, local health departments, and low-resource jurisdictions run real surveillance and outbreak investigation programs that are currently cost-suppressed, but the bulk of employment sits in state/local government and academia where headcount is capped by appropriations and grant funding rather than by latent demand. That combination means the occupation persists and may still grow modestly, but the job shifts from hands-on data wrangling and manual analysis toward study design, AI-output validation, interpretation, and policy communication. Hence restructure rather than replace or augment.

title: Exercise physiologists
rationale: Program design, data analysis of stress-test results, and health education are genuinely AI-assistable, and consumer apps/wearables already generate personalized exercise plans — but the core work involves in-person testing with medical equipment, hands-on supervision of exercising patients with chronic conditions, motivation, and clinical judgment in a safety-critical setting. That keeps disruption moderate rather than high. Elasticity is high because preventive exercise medicine is heavily cost- and access-suppressed; cheaper personalized programming plus AI triage could expand referrals and the population served, and BLS already projects above-average growth. Since disruption sits at 5, the occupation is best classified as resilient: AI reshapes the plan-writing and data-crunching periphery while the human-facing clinical core endures.

title: Farmers, ranchers, and other agricultural managers
rationale: Core work is physical and place-based — planting, herding, equipment maintenance, animal husbandry, and supervising crews outdoors — which AI cannot perform, though precision-agriculture analytics, yield and weather forecasting, market/price optimization, and recordkeeping are genuinely improved by AI, placing this in the moderate band. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because agricultural demand is bounded by food consumption, land availability, and commodity markets; cheaper decision-making does not make people eat more, so productivity gains historically flow into farm consolidation and fewer operators rather than expanded headcount. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes the analytical and administrative periphery of farm management but leaves the hands-on, land-tied core intact. The BLS-projected slight decline stems from consolidation and mechanization trends that predate AI rather than from AI absorbing the core work.

title: Fashion designers
rationale: Core ideation and visualization work — trend research, sketching, colorways, print/pattern generation, CAD tech packs, virtual sampling on digital models — is squarely in generative AI's path, and tools like Midjourney, CLO3D and AI trend-forecasting platforms are already used in apparel design workflows. What resists automation is the tactile side: fabric sourcing, fit and drape on real bodies, sample review with factories, and the taste/brand authority that gives a collection commercial value. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design unlocks more SKUs, faster micro-seasons, personalization and more small DTC brands, but total apparel demand is capped by physical manufacturing, materials cost, and sustainability pushback, so output expansion won't scale one-to-one with design productivity. The result is restructuring — a small occupation where the job shifts toward AI-assisted curation, prompt/CAD fluency, materials expertise and brand direction rather than manual illustration, with adapters thriving and pure sketch-production roles shrinking.

title: Film and video editors and camera operators
rationale: Editing is almost entirely digital post-production work — cutting, color, sound sync, captions, rough assembly — and AI tools already automate scene detection, transcript-based editing, reframing, and even generative shot creation; camera operation remains physical and location-based, but robotic cameras and AI framing/tracking erode that too, so the blended occupation sits high on disruption. Demand elasticity is high because video content demand is far from saturated: lower production and post costs unlock vast latent volume from small businesses, creators, marketing, training, and localized/short-form variants, and the BLS itself cites growing content demand as the growth driver. The net effect is augment because output per editor rises sharply but total video produced expands even faster, though the mix shifts toward creative direction, supervision of AI pipelines, and high-end/live shooting while routine assembly and log-and-transfer assistant roles shrink.

title: Financial analysts
rationale: Financial analysis is almost entirely digital: building models, parsing filings and earnings transcripts, screening securities, and writing research reports — all squarely in the path of current LLM and analytics tooling, which already drafts memos, extracts data from documents, and automates spreadsheet work. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis means more assets, private companies, credit exposures, and mid-market deals get covered, and firms will expand risk and scenario analysis they previously couldn't afford, but AUM, deal flow, and the number of investable entities are structurally bounded and much investment demand is fixed rather than cost-suppressed. The net result is substantial restructuring rather than wholesale replacement — junior modeling and report-drafting roles shrink while the surviving work shifts toward judgment, client relationships, capital allocation decisions, and validating/overseeing AI-generated analysis. Regulatory accountability and the need for a named human to own investment recommendations further preserve headcount at the senior level while compressing the entry-level pipeline.

title: Financial clerks
rationale: Financial clerk work is almost entirely digital document processing: generating bills, verifying data, processing claims and applications, reconciling records, and answering routine account questions. These are exactly the rule-based, language-and-numbers tasks that current AI plus RPA already automate, and BLS already projects decline before accounting for generative AI. Demand is highly inelastic: the number of invoices, payrolls, claims, and loan files is determined by underlying business activity, not by the cost of clerical processing, so cheaper processing yields fewer clerks rather than more transactions. High disruption with near-fixed demand points squarely to headcount contraction, with the residual work concentrated in exception handling and customer-facing judgment.

title: Financial examiners
rationale: Core tasks — reviewing balance sheets and loan documentation, testing regulatory compliance, flagging risky assets, and drafting safety-and-soundness reports — are almost entirely document- and data-based, exactly where LLMs and analytics tooling are already deployed in RegTech and bank internal audit; only the onsite inspection, management interviews, and judgment/accountability portions resist automation. Demand is anchored by statutory examination mandates and agency budgets rather than by price, so cheaper analysis does not proportionally multiply the number of exams, but there is real latent expansion: continuous rather than periodic monitoring, deeper transaction-level coverage, fair-lending testing on full populations instead of samples, and smaller institutions gaining affordable compliance support. That places elasticity in the moderate band, not high. High disruption plus moderate elasticity means the occupation persists and may still grow modestly, but the skill mix shifts from manual sampling and report drafting toward model oversight, exception adjudication, and defending AI-generated findings to regulators — hence restructure.

title: Financial managers
rationale: Core outputs — financial statements, forecasts, variance analysis, budgeting, risk and cash modeling, regulatory reporting — are almost entirely digital, structured, and language/numeric based, which puts a large share of the analytical workload directly in AI's path; the residual human core is judgment, accountability, negotiation with executives, and supervising staff, which keeps this below the 8-9 range. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper analysis means smaller firms, divisions, and nonprofits get real-time treasury, risk, and scenario management they previously couldn't afford, and risk/compliance scope keeps expanding, but each organization only needs so many financial decision-makers and headcount scales with entity count rather than analytic throughput. The likely outcome is a shift in the role toward oversight of AI-generated analysis, data governance, capital strategy, and signing-off responsibility, with fewer subordinate analyst-heavy layers beneath the manager. That combination of high task disruption with mid-range elasticity fits restructure rather than outright replacement.

title: Fire inspectors
rationale: Core work is onsite physical inspection, evidence collection at fire scenes, testimony, and interviewing — tasks requiring human presence, legal authority, and sometimes police powers. AI meaningfully assists the knowledge-work periphery: code compliance checking against blueprints, report writing, documentation, fire-cause pattern analysis, and drone/sensor-based wildfire risk monitoring, which could raise throughput per inspector. Elasticity is moderate because inspection demand is set by building stock, statutory schedules, and municipal budgets rather than price, though cheaper inspection could allow more frequent code enforcement and expanded wildfire risk assessment. Since disruption stays well below 7 given the irreducibly physical and legally authorized nature of the work, this occupation is resilient.

title: Firefighters
rationale: Firefighting is overwhelmingly physical and situational: entering burning structures, hauling hoses, ladder work, extrication, patient care, and driving apparatus cannot be delegated to AI in this decade. AI touches only peripheral elements — dispatch triage and call routing, incident reporting, predictive wildfire spread modeling, drone/thermal reconnaissance, and training simulation — which may modestly change situational awareness but not the core job. Demand is inelastic and budget-driven: staffing is set by municipal budgets, union agreements, and NFPA minimum-crew standards rather than by cost per incident, so productivity tools do not unlock new consumption. With very low disruption, the occupation is clearly resilient; headcount tracks population and call volume, and BLS projects steady modest growth.

title: Fishing and hunting workers
rationale: The work is almost entirely physical and outdoors — hauling nets, setting traps, operating vessels in unpredictable sea and weather conditions — with only marginal AI relevance through better fish-finding sonar, navigation, and weather/stock prediction tools. Demand is hard-capped by biological fish stocks and regulatory quotas and catch shares, so even dramatic productivity gains cannot expand output; any efficiency gain simply fills quotas faster with fewer workers. Because disruption is minimal, the occupation is classified as resilient to AI, though its projected 5 percent decline stems from resource and regulatory constraints rather than automation.

title: Fitness trainers and instructors
rationale: Core work is in-person physical demonstration, motivation, form correction, and safety supervision — AI can generate workout plans and nutrition guidance (the knowledge-work slice) but cannot replace embodied coaching, accountability, or the social dynamic of a group class. AI apps may siphon off the lowest-touch program-design tasks and some at-home users, yet they also broaden fitness engagement and funnel clients toward human coaching. Elasticity is high because personalized fitness guidance is heavily cost-suppressed and latent demand for health coaching is large, so cheaper AI-assisted programming likely expands rather than shrinks the human coaching market. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes peripheral planning and marketing tasks while the human-presence core remains intact and growing.

title: Flight attendants
rationale: Flight attendant work is almost entirely physical and interpersonal — safety demonstrations, emergency response, evacuation, first aid, serving passengers, and managing unruly behavior in a confined cabin — none of which AI can perform. Federal regulations mandate a minimum number of attendants per aircraft, effectively locking headcount to flight volume rather than to productivity. Elasticity is moderate only in the sense that air travel demand grows with cheaper flights, but AI does not lower the marginal cost of cabin crew, so staffing scales strictly with seats flown. With disruption at the very low end, the occupation is clearly resilient; AI may touch only peripheral tasks like scheduling, incident report drafting, and training simulations.

title: Flooring installers and tile and stone setters
rationale: This is near-entirely physical, hands-on work performed on-site in unpredictable, varied environments — kneeling, cutting, spreading mortar, matching patterns by eye — none of which AI can perform. AI's only touchpoints are peripheral: design visualization, material estimation, quoting, and scheduling for the 26% who are self-employed. Demand is driven by construction and renovation cycles and homeowner budgets rather than the cost of cognitive labor, so productivity gains from AI tools would barely shift total volume. With disruption at the very low end, the occupation is clearly resilient; BLS-projected 6% growth reflects housing and remodeling demand, not AI effects.

title: Floral designers
rationale: Floral design is overwhelmingly physical and tactile — cutting, wiring, conditioning, and assembling perishable flowers, plus in-person customer interaction and on-site event setup — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks: design inspiration imagery, order intake, inventory forecasting, marketing copy, and e-commerce visualization. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate: flower purchases are tied to fixed occasions (weddings, funerals, holidays) and gift budgets, so cheaper design labor would not dramatically expand consumption. The projected decline stems from retail consolidation and online order aggregation rather than AI, so the occupation is best classified as resilient with low disruption.

title: Food and beverage serving and related workers
rationale: Core work is physical and in-person: carrying trays, clearing tables, heating food, stocking stations, and face-to-face customer interaction. AI touches only the order-taking and payment layer — kiosks, app ordering, and voice AI at drive-thrus do shift some tasks (notably hosts/hostesses and order-taking portions of fast food work), but these are automation/interface changes rather than AI reshaping the underlying job, and the manual food handling and cleaning remain. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster service supports more dining occasions and delivery/takeout volume, though appetite for meals is ultimately bounded by population and stomachs. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient, with modest erosion concentrated in pure order-intake roles.

title: Food preparation workers
rationale: The core work is almost entirely physical and hands-on — chopping, slicing, cleaning, lifting, stocking — performed in cluttered, variable kitchen environments that remain difficult for robotics and irrelevant to language-model AI. AI touches only peripheral elements like inventory forecasting, scheduling, and prep-list generation, so disruption is low. Demand elasticity is modest: food consumption is bounded by appetite and dining occasions, and the observed decline stems from supply-chain substitution (precut, prewashed ingredients) and role consolidation rather than AI. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, even though BLS projects a mild secular decline for non-AI reasons.

title: Food processing equipment workers
rationale: The core work is physical and plant-floor based: loading equipment, lifting 50-pound ingredient boxes, monitoring temperatures and consistency, cleaning machinery, and visually/sensorially checking product quality. AI touches only peripheral elements such as batch data recording, process optimization, and vision-based quality inspection; the bigger threat is conventional automation (auto-weighing/mixing lines), which is capital-intensive and rolls out slowly. Elasticity is low because food consumption is bounded by population and appetite, so cheaper processing does not meaningfully expand total volume. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient, though incremental automation will keep headcount growth modest rather than robust.

title: Food service managers
rationale: Core work is on-premise, physical and interpersonal — supervising kitchen and dining staff, inspecting equipment, handling customer complaints, expediting service during rushes, and even serving or cleaning tables. AI meaningfully helps with the back-office slice: scheduling, inventory ordering and forecasting, payroll, food-cost analytics, and compliance recordkeeping, which is a real but minority share of daily tasks. Elasticity is moderate: restaurant demand is tied to physical locations and consumer dining spend, so cheaper administration doesn't multiply the number of establishments much, though better tools could let more small/independent operators run professionally and could enable managers to oversee more units (which cuts the other way). With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the paperwork periphery while the floor-level leadership core remains human.

title: Forensic science technicians
rationale: Roughly half the work — evidence collection at scenes, chain-of-custody handling, physical lab bench procedures, and court testimony — requires hands-on human presence and legally accountable human judgment, while the analytic portions (fingerprint and ballistics matching, DNA interpretation, statistical reports) are already being enhanced by AI pattern-recognition and automation, keeping disruption in the moderate range. Elasticity is high because forensic throughput is severely constrained by cost and backlogs (untested rape kits, unprocessed DNA and digital evidence), so cheaper, faster analysis would unlock large latent demand from law enforcement and courts rather than reducing needed staff. Legal admissibility standards and accreditation requirements also mean a credentialed human must verify and testify to results, anchoring headcount. Because core tasks are only partially in AI's path, the occupation is resilient — technicians will use AI as a triage and matching tool while BLS-projected growth from caseloads continues.

title: Forest and conservation workers
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical and outdoors — planting seedlings, clearing brush, operating saws, spraying vegetation, fire suppression — none of which AI can perform directly. AI-adjacent technologies (remote sensing, drone surveying, automated inventory) do erode the measurement/monitoring portion of the job and BLS explicitly cites automation as a driver of the projected 5% decline, but that affects a minority of tasks. Elasticity is moderate: forest health, fuel reduction, and wildfire mitigation represent genuine latent need, yet demand is gated by public agency budgets and appropriations rather than by cost of analysis. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient in character even though headcount is projected to slip slightly for reasons of mechanization rather than AI.

title: Fundraisers
rationale: Much of fundraising work is digital and language-based: donor prospect research, segmentation and wealth screening, drafting appeals and grant copy, personalizing outreach at scale, social media campaigns, and performance analytics — all areas where AI tools are already materially reshaping workflows. However, the highest-value portion (major gifts, planned giving, board and donor relationship cultivation, in-person events) depends on trust and human presence, which caps disruption below the very-high range. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper personalization lets smaller nonprofits run sophisticated campaigns and expands mid-level donor cultivation, but total charitable giving is roughly capped by donor capacity (~2% of GDP), so productivity gains do not proportionally multiply demand. The result is restructuring — headcount stays roughly flat while the skill mix shifts from writing, list management, and administrative execution toward relationship management, strategy, and AI-assisted campaign orchestration.

title: Funeral service workers
rationale: Core work is physical and deeply interpersonal: body removal and preparation, embalming, staging services, transporting remains, and in-person grief counseling with families in a compressed 24-72 hour window. AI can meaningfully help with the administrative periphery — death certificate filings, insurance and VA/SSA paperwork, obituary drafting, scheduling, prearrangement sales and funeral home marketing — but that is a minority of the job and does not displace the licensed, present human. Elasticity is very low because demand is set by the death rate, not by price or speed; cheaper administration will not produce more funerals, and the industry's cost trend (cremation) is already shrinking service intensity. With low disruption and inelastic demand, headcount tracks demographics rather than AI, making this occupation resilient.

title: Gambling services workers
rationale: Core work is physically and socially embodied: dealing cards, managing dice and chips, monitoring players in person, and providing the entertainment experience customers pay for. AI touches only the periphery — surveillance analytics, player-tracking, scheduling, and automated sports-book wagering (which mainly pressures the small writers/runners category). Elasticity is low-to-moderate because gambling demand is capped by regulation, licensing, and the fixed number of physical venues, and the shift to online betting substitutes automated platforms rather than expanding in-person dealer headcount. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient in structure, though flat overall employment reflects channel shift rather than AI displacement.

title: General maintenance and repair workers
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair across varied, unpredictable environments — plumbing, electrical, painting, machinery — requiring dexterity, ladders, cramped spaces, and on-site presence that AI and robotics cannot replicate in the next decade. AI touches only peripheral aspects: diagnostic assistance, predictive maintenance scheduling from sensor data, parts ordering, work-order documentation, and AR-guided troubleshooting that may modestly broaden what a generalist can handle. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper diagnosis could shift some work from licensed specialists to generalists and enable more preventive maintenance, but building stock and equipment volume ultimately cap demand. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is clearly resilient — headcount is driven by physical building and equipment needs, not by information-processing productivity.

title: General office clerks
rationale: Core tasks — typing and formatting documents, data entry, filing, routing calls and mail, processing bills, answering routine questions — are almost entirely digital, routine, and language-based, placing them directly in AI's path; automated phone systems, electronic records, and document generation tools already erode this work today. The residual physical elements (moving paper, greeting visitors, operating copiers) are minor and increasingly obsolete. Demand is highly inelastic: organizations do not want more memos filed or more calls transferred as clerical throughput gets cheaper, and the work is a fixed overhead cost absorbed by other staff via self-service software. High disruption plus near-zero latent demand expansion means productivity gains flow straight to headcount reduction, consistent with BLS's projected -7% decline.

title: Genetic counselors
rationale: Much of the work is information-intensive cognitive labor — collecting pedigrees, interpreting variant data against literature, calculating risk, drafting documentation and letters to referring physicians — all directly in AI's path, and clinical decision-support tools already automate variant curation and risk modeling. The counter-weight is the irreducible human element: delivering emotionally charged results, psychosocial support, and shared decision-making with distressed families, plus state licensure gatekeeping, which keeps disruption at high-but-not-extreme. Elasticity is high because with only ~4,000 counselors nationally, genetic counseling is severely supply-constrained while genomic and pharmacogenomic testing volume is exploding; population screening, oncology, and prenatal care all have large latent unmet demand that cheaper, faster counseling would unlock. Since disruption is high and demand expansion should more than absorb productivity gains, the occupation is augmented — each counselor supervises AI-generated interpretations and handles far more cases, with headcount stable or growing.

title: Geographers
rationale: Geographers' core work — GIS analysis, remote sensing interpretation, spatial statistics, map production, and report writing — is almost entirely digital and squarely in AI's path; foundation models for satellite imagery segmentation, automated geospatial pipelines, and LLM-assisted report generation already displace substantial portions of routine analysis and cartographic production. Some fieldwork and stakeholder-facing advisory work resists automation, but it is a minority of tasks. Elasticity is low because 68% of employment is federal government positions whose headcount is set by appropriations rather than by demand for spatial analysis; cheaper geospatial insight tends to be absorbed by existing staff and by GIS-enabled workers in other occupations (planners, geoscientists, analysts) rather than by hiring more geographers. With very high task exposure, a tiny 1,500-person budget-constrained occupation, and an already-declining BLS projection, contraction is the likely outcome.

title: Geological and hydrologic technicians
rationale: Roughly half of this work is physical and site-based — installing and maintaining field instruments, collecting mud/water samples in remote locations, lab sample prep — which AI cannot perform, though drones and automated sensors substitute for some manual data collection. The data-analysis, mapping, and report-writing half is squarely in AI's path, so the office-based portion of the role will be substantially automated or accelerated. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper monitoring could expand water-quality and mineral exploration coverage (more sensors, more sites analyzed), but demand is anchored to commodity cycles and federal budgets, which cap growth. Because the core hands-on field and lab component remains human-dependent, disruption stays at or below 6 and the occupation is best classified as resilient, with a gradual shift toward sensor/drone operation and data interpretation skills.

title: Geoscientists
rationale: A substantial share of geoscientists' work is data-heavy and digital — seismic interpretation, remote sensing analysis, GIS modeling, report writing — all areas where AI already materially accelerates output, pushing disruption toward the high end. But the occupation retains an irreducible physical core: field surveys in remote locations, sample collection, laboratory testing, and licensed professional judgment on regulatory and engineering projects, which caps disruption at moderate-high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper subsurface analysis could unlock more exploration, hazard mapping, and environmental assessment work (especially for critical minerals and geothermal), but demand is ultimately tethered to capital-intensive drilling, mining, and construction projects and to government budgets rather than to analysis cost. With disruption at 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes the interpretation and reporting workflow but does not displace the fieldwork, licensure, and stakeholder-facing core.

title: Glaziers
rationale: Glazing is almost entirely physical: measuring, cutting, lifting, and securing heavy glass at heights in variable jobsite conditions, none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like estimating, blueprint interpretation, and scheduling, leaving the core work unchanged. Demand is tied to construction cycles and building stock rather than the cost of cognitive labor, so productivity gains from AI would barely shift total volume. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Graphic designers
rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital creative production — layouts, logos, illustration, photo editing, iteration on client feedback — and generative image and layout tools already produce usable output for much of the commodity end of this market. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper visuals do expand total demand (every small business, social channel, and product variant can now be designed, and volume of visual content is exploding), but much of that expanded demand is absorbed by non-designers using AI tools directly rather than by hiring designers, and brand-level work is capped by budgets and the number of clients. The net result is a substantial skill shift — toward art direction, brand strategy, prompt/AI-pipeline curation, and client-facing judgment — with the routine production tier, especially freelance commodity work, contracting. BLS's own 2 percent projection with an explicit AI caveat is consistent with restructuring rather than outright collapse or growth.

title: Grounds maintenance workers
rationale: Core work is almost entirely physical outdoor labor in unstructured environments — mowing, pruning, planting, climbing trees, applying chemicals — with essentially no digital or language-based task content for AI to absorb. Robotic mowers and autonomous equipment represent a mechanization trend rather than an AI one, and they address only a slice of duties on the most uniform terrain; scheduling, routing, and estimating are peripheral admin tasks. Demand for lawn and landscape services is moderately price-sensitive (households substitute their own labor when costs rise), so cheaper service could expand the market somewhat, but the total addressable amount of grounds needing upkeep is physically bounded. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Hand laborers and material movers
rationale: Core tasks are almost entirely physical: lifting, carrying, packing, bagging, cleaning, and collecting refuse in unstructured environments. AI's language and cognitive capabilities touch only the peripheral record-keeping and scanning elements; the real threat is warehouse robotics and mechanization, which is capital-intensive, incremental, and largely separate from the current AI wave — dexterous picking in cluttered settings remains unsolved at scale. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper logistics does expand e-commerce volume and order-filling demand (as BLS projects for stockers), but total goods movement is bounded by physical consumption. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient over the next decade, though pockets like machine feeders and hand packagers will continue to erode from automation rather than AI.

title: Hazardous materials removal workers
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: scraping asbestos, operating sandblasters, wearing protective suits in confined spaces, and responding to spills in unpredictable field conditions. AI touches only peripheral tasks such as compliance recordkeeping, hazard identification support, monitoring/sensor analytics, and job planning, and robotics for remediation remains niche and expensive over a 10-year horizon. Demand is driven by regulation, remediation funding cycles, building renovation, and nuclear decommissioning schedules rather than by labor cost, so cheaper knowledge work would unlock only modest additional cleanup activity. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient, though supervisory and documentation roles will use AI tools.

title: Health and safety engineers
rationale: Much of the work is document- and analysis-heavy — interpreting regulations, drafting safety programs, reviewing designs, writing incident reports — all directly in AI's path, and AI plus sensor/computer-vision monitoring can accelerate hazard identification. But the core still requires on-site inspection, interviewing workers after accidents, building rapport, directing physical installation of safety devices, and bearing professional/legal accountability for compliance sign-off, which caps disruption around 6. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper safety engineering would let smaller firms and more facilities get proper safety review, and regulation keeps a floor under demand, but total demand is largely tied to regulatory requirements and the number of worksites rather than price. With disruption at 6 the occupation lands in the resilient band — AI reshapes the paperwork and analytics periphery while the inspection, investigation, and accountability core remains human.

title: Health education specialists
rationale: A substantial share of the work — drafting educational materials and campaigns, designing and analyzing needs-assessment surveys, writing grant proposals, evaluating program effectiveness — is language- and data-based and is already meaningfully accelerated by current AI tools, pushing disruption to the high end of moderate. However, the core value proposition rests on in-person program delivery, one-on-one patient teaching, community trust-building, coalition work, and policy advocacy, which resist automation and keep disruption at 6 rather than 7+. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, more tailored health content could unlock real latent demand for personalized prevention and outreach, but headcount is largely determined by government, hospital, and grant budgets rather than by market price, capping expansion. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the content-production and analytics periphery while the relational and community-facing core endures, though workers will be expected to produce far more materials and evaluation output per person.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital: abstracting clinical records, assigning classification codes, validating data integrity, and generating reports are precisely the document-extraction and structured-data tasks that LLMs and NLP-based abstraction tools already perform in pilot deployments at cancer registries and health systems. Registry abstraction volume is largely fixed by patient case counts, so cheaper abstraction does not create 10x more cases; however, healthcare organizations have deep latent demand for analytics, quality measurement, interoperability projects, and system implementation support that is currently rationed by cost and staffing, which supports moderate elasticity. The net result is that pure abstraction/coding roles contract while the occupation shifts toward data governance, AI output validation, informatics implementation, and analytics interpretation. That skill-set migration with roughly stable-to-modest headcount is the definition of restructure rather than outright replacement.

title: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical labor in unpredictable, cramped, varied real-world environments — installing, soldering, wiring, lifting, and diagnosing equipment on-site — which AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral functions: remote diagnostics and IoT sensor data, scheduling and dispatch optimization, parts lookup, quoting, and recordkeeping, plus AI-assisted training and troubleshooting guidance that may raise junior technician productivity. Demand is moderately elastic (cheaper diagnostics and predictive maintenance could expand service contracts and retrofit work), but it is fundamentally capped by the physical building stock and technician time per call. With disruption at 2, the occupation is clearly resilient; BLS projects above-average growth driven by construction and energy-efficiency retrofits.

title: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
rationale: Core work is physical driving, cargo securement, inspections, and navigating unpredictable real-world conditions — largely outside the reach of language-model AI, though autonomous driving is a genuine embodied-AI threat on long-haul highway segments and is already in limited commercial deployment in the Sunbelt. Over a 10-year horizon, disruption is moderate rather than high: regulatory approval, insurance, weather/urban edge cases, and the persistence of first/last-mile, drayage, and specialized loads mean most of the 2.2 million jobs remain human-operated, with AI more likely to reshape routing, dispatch, compliance logging, and safety monitoring than to replace the driver. Elasticity is moderate — cheaper freight would modestly increase ton-miles shipped, but demand for goods movement is tied to physical consumption rather than suppressed by trucking cost, so productivity gains largely substitute for labor in the segments where automation succeeds. Because disruption over the decade stays at or below 6, the occupation lands in 'resilient,' albeit with the highest embodied-AI tail risk of any large occupation and likely erosion concentrated in the highway line-haul niche.

title: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling engines, replacing hydraulic pumps, lifting heavy parts, working in awkward positions and at remote worksites — none of which AI can perform. AI's contribution is confined to the diagnostic and documentation periphery: smarter fault-code interpretation, predictive maintenance telemetry, AI-assisted access to manuals and repair procedures, which may modestly shift time from troubleshooting to wrench time. Elasticity is moderate: equipment fleets grow with construction and agriculture and predictive maintenance could increase scheduled service events, but total demand is capped by the physical stock of machines, and better diagnostics could equally reduce some repair volume. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient — AI becomes another tool in the technician's kit rather than a replacement for the labor itself.

title: High school teachers
rationale: Lesson planning, grading, assessment design, and parent communication are language-based tasks squarely in AI's path, and teachers are already using AI tools for these — a meaningful share of the workday. But the core of the job is in-person classroom management, motivating and supervising adolescents, and custodial/social functions that AI cannot perform, and public school staffing is bound by credentialing rules, union contracts, and class-size norms. Demand is structurally capped by student enrollment (projected to decline) rather than by cost or speed, so productivity gains show up as less teacher overtime rather than more teaching or fewer teachers. With disruption at 6 and demand fixed by demographics and regulation, the occupation is best classified as resilient — restructured workflows, roughly stable headcount.

title: Historians
rationale: Historians' core work — searching archives, reading and translating primary sources, synthesizing evidence, and writing reports, articles, and exhibit text — is almost entirely text and document based, precisely where LLMs and digitized-archive search tools already provide material leverage; only artifact handling, site visits, and public programming require physical presence. Demand is highly inelastic because employment is dominated by government agencies, museums, and nonprofits whose budgets come from fixed appropriations and donations rather than from market demand for historical output; cheaper history production does not generate new funded positions. With disruption around 8 and elasticity around 3, the occupation falls in the replace band, though the very small base (3,400 jobs) and the credentialing/institutional inertia mean absolute losses will be modest and slow, with surviving roles skewing toward public engagement, curation, and provenance verification.

title: Home health and personal care aides
rationale: Core work is intensely physical and interpersonal — bathing, dressing, lifting, transferring, housekeeping, cooking, driving, and emotional companionship in unpredictable home environments — none of which AI can perform without robotics that remain far from deployment. AI touches only peripheral functions: scheduling, care documentation, remote monitoring alerts, and translation, which may modestly reduce paperwork burden. Elasticity is very high because unpaid family caregiving and unmet need are enormous; cheaper care would unlock massive latent demand, and demographic aging guarantees growth regardless. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the administrative periphery while the hands-on core, and headcount, continue to expand rapidly.

title: Human resources managers
rationale: HR management is predominantly knowledge and language work — policy drafting, recruiting workflows, benefits administration, compliance documentation, payroll oversight, and reporting — much of which AI already automates or accelerates, though the interpersonal core (mediation, discipline, negotiation, executive counsel, and accountability for legally sensitive decisions) still requires a human. Demand is largely a function of headcount and regulatory complexity in the organizations served, not of the cost of HR services, so cheaper HR administration mostly shrinks the ratio of HR staff to employees rather than expanding the total volume of HR work; outsourcing to AI-enabled service providers reinforces this. Some latent demand exists (small firms gaining real HR capability, richer workforce analytics), which lifts elasticity modestly above lawyer-like levels but not into expansion territory. High disruption combined with structurally capped demand implies flatter or contracting headcount per organization, with surviving roles concentrated in strategic and relationship-heavy work — placing this at the replace/restructure boundary and closer to replace.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: HR specialist work is overwhelmingly digital and language-based: resume screening, sourcing, scheduling, policy Q&A, records processing, onboarding paperwork, and compliance checks are all directly in AI's path, and applicant-tracking and AI screening tools already reshape recruiting workflows today. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate: hiring volume is driven by business headcount needs and economic conditions, not by the cost of HR processing, and employee-relations and compliance work scales with workforce size rather than expanding when it gets cheaper — though cheaper HR services could let smaller firms access more professional HR support. Because the transactional bulk of the role can be automated while total demand is structurally capped, headcount pressure is likely, with surviving roles concentrating in strategic advising, negotiation, and sensitive human judgment (investigations, disputes, culture). That combination of very high disruption and constrained demand expansion places it in the replace category, even though a meaningful strategic-advisor core remains.

title: Hydrologists
