rationale: A large share of hydrologists' work is data analysis, modeling, forecasting, and report writing — all squarely in AI's path, and ML-based hydrologic forecasting already outperforms some traditional models. However, the occupation retains substantial field components (streamflow measurement, sampling, sensor deployment, site assessment) plus regulatory, permitting, and expert-testimony roles that require credentialed human judgment and accountability, holding disruption to moderate. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper modeling could expand watershed-scale analysis, flood risk mapping, and monitoring of smaller aquifers, but roughly two-thirds of employment is government-funded and capped by public budgets rather than by cost of analysis. With disruption at 6, AI reshapes the toolkit and shifts hydrologists toward interpreting AI-generated models rather than eliminating the core role, making 'resilient' the fitting category.

title: Industrial designers
rationale: Core tasks — ideation, sketching, rendering, 2D/3D CAD modeling, user research synthesis, and client presentations — are overwhelmingly digital and squarely in the path of generative image models, text-to-3D tools, and AI-assisted CAD/generative design, which already materially accelerate concept exploration and visualization. Physical prototyping, materials evaluation, factory visits, and stakeholder negotiation remain human-anchored, keeping disruption below the maximum. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design unlocks more concept variants, faster iteration, and design attention for products and smaller manufacturers previously priced out, but total demand is ultimately gated by tooling costs, manufacturing capacity, and product launch cycles rather than design cost, and BLS already flags manufacturing decline as a drag. Thus the occupation persists but shifts toward AI-directed curation, engineering integration, user insight, and taste-making rather than manual rendering and modeling — a restructure.

title: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: A substantial portion of this work is data analysis, statistical production studies, charting workflows, and CAD/layout documentation — all directly in AI's path, and sensors plus analytics software already automate much of the data collection and time-and-motion measurement. However, the role is anchored to the physical plant floor: observing actual operations, assessing prototypes, verifying machinery performance, and conferring in person with production staff and engineers, which keeps disruption at the upper edge of moderate rather than high. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper process-improvement analysis would let more mid-size manufacturers and service operations pursue continuous improvement, but demand is ultimately tied to the number of physical facilities and capital projects, which does not scale rapidly. Net effect is resilient: AI reshapes the analytical toolkit and likely suppresses growth in pure data-gathering tasks, but the on-site, judgment-and-verification core of the job remains human.

title: Industrial engineers
rationale: Much of industrial engineering is analytical and digital — data collection, statistical analysis, simulation modeling, layout optimization, CAD work — all directly in AI's path, and AI-driven process mining and optimization tools already reshape parts of the job. However, a substantial share of the work requires physical presence on factory floors, in hospitals, and railyards: observing workers, time studies, validating equipment, and negotiating implementation with cross-functional stakeholders, which caps disruption around 6. Elasticity is high because optimization is chronically under-applied — most small and mid-sized manufacturers, hospitals, and service operations never get an industrial engineer's attention due to cost, so cheaper analysis would unlock large latent demand, and AI/automation deployment itself creates work for these engineers. Because core disruption stays at or below 6 with the human-in-the-plant element intact and demand tailwinds strong, the occupation is resilient, with tooling shifting rather than eliminating the role.

title: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, disassembly, welding, rigging, and reassembly of heavy industrial machinery in unpredictable plant environments — tasks far outside AI's reach. AI touches the periphery meaningfully via predictive maintenance analytics, sensor-based diagnostics, and AR/LLM-assisted access to technical manuals, which can shift some troubleshooting effort and reduce routine lubrication/inspection rounds (hence the projected decline for machinery maintenance workers), but it does not replace the wrench turn. Elasticity is high because AI-driven automation of factories increases the installed base of machinery requiring skilled upkeep, and downtime costs make more frequent, condition-based servicing economically attractive. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes diagnostics and scheduling while headcount continues to grow.

title: Industrial production managers
rationale: Roughly half the job is analytical/digital — production scheduling, data analysis, reports, quality-defect root-cause work — all areas where AI and predictive analytics already provide material help. But the core of the role is physical plant presence, on-call emergency response, walking the floor, supervising and motivating unionized workers, and negotiating across departments and suppliers, which AI cannot absorb. Elasticity is low-moderate: plant management headcount is tied to the number of physical facilities and shifts, not to how fast analysis can be produced, so productivity gains don't spawn more plants. With disruption at 5, AI reshapes the analytical toolkit these managers use rather than the core accountability of running a plant, making the occupation resilient.

title: Information clerks
rationale: Core tasks — answering routine inquiries, entering and retrieving records, filling out forms, processing orders and applications, drafting standard correspondence — are almost entirely language-based digital work squarely in AI's path, and self-service portals plus conversational agents already substitute for much of it. Some segments (hotel front desk, ticket agents handling bags, in-person eligibility interviews) retain a physical or trust-based human component, which tempers the score slightly below maximum. Demand is inelastic: the underlying volume of orders, filings, permits, and guest check-ins is set by external activity levels, not by the cost of clerical processing, so cheaper processing means fewer clerks rather than more transactions. High disruption with low elasticity yields replacement, consistent with BLS's projected decline and the steep drops in file clerks, order clerks, and interviewers.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital — log monitoring, alert triage, vulnerability scanning, threat research, report writing, policy drafting — and AI/ML-driven SOC tooling and LLM copilots already automate large portions of tier-1 detection and documentation, so disruption is very high. However, demand is strongly elastic: attack surfaces are expanding, adversaries are themselves using AI to scale offense, and vast numbers of small and mid-sized organizations currently go under-secured because expert coverage is unaffordable, so cheaper security capacity unlocks large latent demand rather than just cutting headcount. Security is also an adversarial arms race with no fixed ceiling on output, plus accountability, regulatory, and incident-response duties that keep humans in the loop. The role restructures toward AI oversight, threat hunting, and architecture, but headcount should keep growing — hence augment.

title: Instructional coordinators
rationale: Core tasks — developing curriculum materials, analyzing student test data, reviewing textbooks, designing training modules, and writing implementation procedures — are predominantly document-based cognitive work directly in AI's path; generative AI already produces lesson plans, standards-aligned units, and assessment analytics quickly. The in-person components (classroom observation, teacher coaching, relationship-building with principals) preserve a meaningful human core, capping disruption around 7. Elasticity is low because demand is set by school district budgets, enrollment, and state accountability mandates rather than by the cost of curriculum production; cheaper curriculum development does not cause districts to hire more coordinators, and centrally produced or vendor AI curricula could serve many districts at once. High disruption with budget-constrained, structurally fixed demand points to modest headcount contraction, consistent with the already-flat BLS projection.

title: Insulation workers
rationale: Insulation work is almost entirely physical: measuring, cutting, stapling, spraying foam, crawling through attics and confined spaces, and working at heights in unpredictable jobsite conditions. AI touches only peripheral tasks like takeoff estimating from blueprints, energy modeling, and scheduling, none of which change the hands-on core. Demand is moderately elastic in principle, since energy-efficiency retrofits are a large latent market gated by cost, but labor productivity is set by physical installation speed rather than by cognition, so AI cannot unlock much of it. With disruption at the very low end, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Insurance sales agents
rationale: Core tasks — prospecting, needs analysis, comparing policy features, quoting, explaining coverage, processing renewals, and maintaining client records — are overwhelmingly digital, language-based, and rules-driven, which is squarely in AI's path; direct-to-consumer online quoting and AI-assisted comparison tools already substitute for much of the agent's informational role, and generative AI can handle personalized explanation and cross-sell recommendations at scale. Demand is structurally inelastic: households and businesses buy a roughly fixed number of policies dictated by assets, regulation, and lender requirements, so cheaper, faster sales support does not multiply premiums — it mainly unlocks modest gains from better-matched coverage among the underinsured and small commercial segment. Because high disruption meets low elasticity, productivity gains flow into fewer agents per book of business, with survivors concentrated in complex commercial lines, high-net-worth life/annuity advising, and claims advocacy where trust and negotiation still require a human. Hence 'replace,' though contraction will be gradual given licensing requirements and entrenched agency distribution.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Underwriting is almost entirely digital, rule-based risk assessment: reading applications, pulling structured and unstructured data, applying actuarial criteria, and outputting a price decision — precisely what predictive models and LLMs handle well, and automated underwriting engines already dominate personal lines. Demand is inelastic because the number of insurance applications is bounded by the number of people and businesses buying policies, not by underwriting cost or speed; cheaper underwriting expands the market only marginally (some thinner-margin niches, micro-policies, or previously uninsurable specialty risks). With very high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains flow to headcount reduction, consistent with BLS's projected decline. Residual demand concentrates in complex commercial, specialty, and workers' compensation lines requiring judgment, relationship management, and on-site property assessment.

title: Interior designers
rationale: Core creative-visual work — concept generation, mood boards, renderings, space planning, material specification, and CAD/BIM drafting — is highly digital and already being transformed by generative image and design tools, so disruption is high; however, site measurement, client relationship management, contractor coordination, installation oversight, and code compliance still require physical presence and judgment, capping it below 8. Demand elasticity is high because design services are currently priced out of reach for most homeowners and small businesses: cheap instant visualization and iteration unlocks a large latent market for renovation, staging, and small commercial projects, and clients typically want more options and iterations than budgets allow. The main risk is commoditization of pure rendering/decor advice, but the professional role shifts toward curation, procurement, and project execution while total volume of designed spaces expands. That combination — high disruption with substantial latent demand — fits augment, with individual designers handling far more projects each.

title: Interpreters and translators
rationale: Translation is the canonical language-to-language task that modern LLMs and neural MT already perform at near-human quality for most language pairs and domains, and even simultaneous interpreting is being addressed by real-time speech translation on phones and conferencing platforms; the vast majority of core tasks are linguistic and digital, so disruption is very high. Some latent demand does exist — far more content, meetings, and documents will get translated when the cost approaches zero — but that expansion is captured almost entirely by the machines rather than by human headcount, and the segments that will keep humans (court certification, ASL in-person settings, high-stakes medical, literary and legal liability, sworn/certified translations) are capped by regulation, budget, and fixed population need rather than price. Human roles shift toward post-editing and quality assurance, which requires far fewer workers per unit of output. Net effect is replacement pressure: high disruption with only modest, regulation-bounded demand expansion, so headcount in the general translation market contracts while a smaller certified/in-person niche persists.

title: Ironworkers
rationale: Ironworking is almost entirely physical: rigging, welding, bolting, tying rebar, and walking narrow beams at height in unpredictable outdoor conditions. AI touches only peripheral elements like digital blueprints/BIM models, layout planning, and safety monitoring, and robotic rebar-tying or steel erection remains niche and slow to scale over a 10-year horizon. Demand is moderately elastic in that cheaper construction could unlock more building, but it is gated by capital, permitting, and land rather than by ironworker productivity. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity; employment tracks construction cycles and infrastructure spending, not AI.

title: Janitors and building cleaners
rationale: The work is almost entirely physical and hands-on — mopping, trash removal, restroom sanitation, minor repairs — performed in cluttered, variable environments that remain hard for robotics and irrelevant to language-model AI. Autonomous floor scrubbers already exist but handle only large open floors, leaving the bulk of tasks untouched over a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: cleaning demand is tied to fixed square footage and occupancy rather than price, though marginally cheaper cleaning could raise frequency in some facilities. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is resilient, and headcount will be driven by building stock and labor supply rather than AI.

title: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers
rationale: Core work is highly manual and dexterity-intensive: soldering, stone setting, polishing, and repair at a bench cannot be done by AI, though design (CAD), gem grading/certification, appraisal research, and cost estimation are digital tasks AI can meaningfully assist or automate, pushing disruption to the moderate range. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate: jewelry consumption is driven by discretionary luxury spending, occasions, and material costs rather than by design or labor cost, so cheaper design does not multiply demand much, and imports plus 3D printing/robotic polishing already convert productivity gains into fewer domestic workers. The occupation is projected to decline for reasons largely independent of generative AI — automation of physical processes and offshoring. Because disruption to the core hands-on craft stays at or below 6, the correct category is resilient even though headcount is slowly shrinking.

title: Judges and hearing officers
rationale: The work is heavily language- and analysis-based — reading briefs, researching law, drafting opinions — all squarely in AI's path, and judges already benefit from AI-assisted research, transcript summarization, and drafting support. But the core of the role is constitutionally and statutorily vested authority: presiding in a courtroom, judging credibility of live witnesses, exercising discretion, and bearing accountability for decisions that must be made by a human officeholder, which caps disruption in the moderate range. Elasticity is low because judicial headcount is set by legislative authorization and budget appropriations, not by demand for adjudication; faster decisions would reduce backlogs rather than create more judgeships. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes chambers workflow and may shrink clerk and staff support more than the judges themselves.

title: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers
rationale: Core work is in-person care, supervision, behavior management, and socialization of young children — physically embodied, custodial, and relational tasks that AI cannot assume, especially at K-5 ages where adult presence is legally and developmentally required. AI does meaningfully change the peripheral knowledge work: lesson planning, differentiation, worksheet and assessment generation, progress reporting, and parent communication, which is why disruption sits at moderate rather than low. Elasticity is low because headcount is driven by student enrollment (projected to decline), state class-size rules, and school budgets rather than by the cost or speed of producing instruction; cheaper lesson prep does not create more children to teach. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — the job survives largely intact, with AI absorbing administrative burden rather than displacing the teacher.

title: Labor relations specialists
rationale: A substantial share of the work is document-heavy and language-based — drafting handbooks and collective bargaining language, researching labor law and precedent, summarizing grievance files, preparing training materials — and AI already meaningfully accelerates those pieces. But the defining core of the job is adversarial, high-stakes human negotiation, credibility-building with union and management representatives, and misconduct investigations requiring in-person interviews and judgment, none of which delegate well to AI or to a party that lacks standing at the table. Elasticity is low because demand is structurally tied to union density, statutory bargaining requirements, and the number of grievances filed rather than to the cost of producing labor relations advice; cheaper drafting does not generate more contracts or disputes. With disruption at 6 and demand essentially fixed, the occupation fits resilient — AI reshapes the paperwork periphery while headcount stays roughly flat, consistent with the BLS 0% projection.

title: Landscape architects
rationale: Most of the daily work — site plans, CADD drafting, renderings, cost estimates, GIS/drainage analysis, specification writing, and client presentations — is digital and directly in AI's path, with generative design and image tools already producing concept visualizations and automating drafting; site inspections and stakeholder negotiation remain human, capping disruption at the low end of 'high'. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper design could unlock more small residential, municipal green-infrastructure, and stormwater/restoration projects that are currently priced out, but total volume is ultimately gated by construction budgets, land availability, permitting, and state licensure requirements rather than design cost. So productivity gains will partly expand the market and partly compress the drafting/rendering labor that junior staff perform. The occupation persists but shifts toward ecological judgment, regulatory navigation, client relationships, and construction oversight, with less time spent producing drawings — a restructuring rather than wholesale replacement or headcount boom.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Lawyering is overwhelmingly language- and document-based work — research, drafting, contract review, discovery, memo writing, and advisory analysis — all squarely in the path of current LLM capability, and AI legal research/drafting tools are already materially changing firm workflows. Elasticity is limited: there is real latent demand (unmet needs among individuals and small businesses, more contracts reviewed, more compliance work), but unauthorized-practice rules, bar licensure, court capacity, and the fact that much high-value legal work is adversarial and zero-sum cap how much volume can expand. Billable-hour economics also mean efficiency gains tend to compress revenue rather than multiply matters. High disruption with only low-to-moderate demand expansion points to contraction concentrated in associate-level research and document work, with human judgment, advocacy, negotiation, and client relationships retaining value at the top.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: The information-retrieval core of librarianship — reference queries, literature searches, cataloging/metadata, collection research, and readers' advisory — sits squarely in AI's path, and special/corporate/law/medical librarians who mainly do research on demand are highly exposed. But the majority of the occupation (63% in public libraries and K-12 schools) spends its day on in-person patron service, children's and community programming, information-literacy instruction, budgets, contract negotiation, staff supervision, and physical collection management, which AI touches only peripherally. Elasticity is low because library headcount is set by municipal and school district budgets and physical facility staffing needs, not by the price of an information search; cheaper research does not cause taxpayers to fund more librarian positions. With disruption at 6 and inelastic public funding, the occupation is best classed resilient — slow, flat growth with skill shifts toward programming, digital literacy teaching, and AI-tool instruction rather than sharp contraction, though specialized corporate research roles will thin.

title: Library technicians and assistants
rationale: A majority of daily tasks — cataloguing, maintaining bibliographic databases, handling interlibrary loan records, answering routine reference and research questions, and general clerical work — are information-handling tasks squarely in AI's path, and automated cataloguing, self-checkout, and conversational search already absorb much of it; only shelving, desk coverage, and in-person programming resist. Demand is highly inelastic: library staffing is set by fixed public and institutional budgets and by open hours rather than by output volume, and overall library patronage is already declining as patrons substitute digital search and e-resources, so productivity gains do not unlock new consumption. With high task exposure and essentially no demand expansion, gains convert directly into fewer positions, consistent with the BLS -7 percent projection. The residual physical and interpersonal duties will keep some headcount, but the trajectory is contraction rather than restructuring into a larger role.

title: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses
rationale: LPN/LVN work is overwhelmingly hands-on physical care: vital signs, bathing, dressing changes, feeding, wound care, and bedside interaction with patients who cannot be served remotely. AI touches mainly the documentation and charting periphery — ambient scribing and automated record-keeping could reduce paperwork burden and free time for direct care — plus decision-support prompts for monitoring, but none of that displaces the core caregiving. Demand elasticity is high because an aging population and chronic disease burden create enormous unmet need for basic nursing care, and cost is currently the binding constraint on how much care patients in nursing homes and home health receive. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes admin overhead rather than the job itself, and headcount continues to grow with demographics.

title: Loan officers
rationale: The core work — collecting and verifying financial documents, analyzing credit and income data, checking regulatory compliance, and producing an underwriting recommendation — is already largely automated by rules-based software and is squarely in the path of document-processing and reasoning AI; the remaining human parts are sales, relationship-building, and exception handling, which keeps this from a 9-10. Demand elasticity is low because loan volume is driven by macroeconomic credit appetite, interest rates, home purchases, and business investment cycles, not by the cost of processing an application; a 10x cheaper underwriting process does not make people buy 10x more houses or cars, though it modestly expands credit access for thin-file borrowers and small businesses. Combined with the ongoing decline of bank branches and the shift of origination to digital platforms, productivity gains flow to headcount reduction rather than output expansion. High disruption plus inelastic demand places this firmly in the replace category, with survivors concentrated in complex commercial lending and commission-driven mortgage origination where relationships still matter.

title: Lodging managers
rationale: Lodging management blends on-site physical presence — inspecting rooms, greeting guests, supervising housekeeping and front-desk staff, resolving in-person complaints — with genuinely AI-exposed knowledge tasks like revenue management, dynamic pricing, occupancy forecasting, scheduling, budgeting, and guest communications. Revenue managers and front-desk managers face the highest exposure (algorithmic pricing and chatbots already handle much of this), but general managers' core work of leading people and handling unpredictable real-world service failures resists automation, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is middling: room inventory is physically capped and travel demand is driven by macro factors, not management efficiency, though cheaper professional-grade management could extend to small independents, B&Bs, and short-term rental portfolios that previously couldn't afford it. Because disruption sits at 5 with the core supervisory and hospitality role intact, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the analytical periphery and may consolidate revenue-management roles rather than eliminating the function.

title: Logging workers
rationale: Logging is overwhelmingly physical work performed outdoors on rough, unpredictable terrain — felling trees, operating skidders and harvesters, rigging cable systems — none of which AI addresses directly in the near term. The main AI-adjacent slice is log grading/scaling and harvest planning, where machine vision and sensor-equipped harvester heads can automate measurement and optimize bucking, but that is a small share of headcount and continues a decades-long mechanization trend rather than a new AI shock. Demand elasticity is low because timber consumption is driven by construction, paper, and pulp markets plus land access and environmental regulation, not by the cost of logging labor; cheaper harvesting would not meaningfully expand how much wood society consumes. With disruption well under 6, the occupation is resilient — headcount continues its slow mechanization-driven drift downward for reasons largely unrelated to AI.

title: Logisticians
rationale: Logisticians' core work — demand forecasting, route and inventory optimization, cost analysis, exception handling, and reporting inside ERP/TMS/WMS systems — is largely digital and already the focus of AI-driven supply chain planning tools, giving a high disruption score; the residual human element is supplier/customer relationship management, cross-functional negotiation, and on-the-ground troubleshooting at plants and distribution centers. Elasticity is moderate: e-commerce complexity, nearshoring, and tariff volatility keep expanding the number of supply chains needing management, and cheaper optimization lets smaller firms and more product lines get professional logistics attention, but each physical supply chain has a finite planning need, so demand cannot expand proportionally to a 10x productivity gain. The result is restructuring rather than replacement — headcount likely still grows modestly (BLS projects 17%), but the job shifts from spreadsheet analysis and manual coordination toward supervising AI planning systems, scenario judgment, and vendor/stakeholder management. Workers who remain primarily data-wranglers and report-builders will be displaced by those who can interpret and override algorithmic recommendations.

title: Machinists and tool and die makers
rationale: Core work is hands-on: setting up machines, fixturing, aligning cutting tools, deburring, polishing, and measuring parts to ten-thousandths of an inch on the shop floor. AI meaningfully touches the digital slice — CAD interpretation, CAM/CNC program generation, toolpath optimization, and in-process quality inspection — which is why tool and die makers (more programming-heavy) are projected to decline faster than machinists, but physical setup and skilled judgment remain human. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster precision machining could unlock more custom low-volume and prototype work and reshoring, though capital equipment, materials, and lead-time constraints cap expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the programming and inspection periphery while the machinist's core role shifts toward supervising more automated cells.

title: Management analysts
rationale: Core management analyst work — gathering and organizing information, analyzing financial and operational data, building models, drafting recommendations, and producing slide decks and written reports — is almost entirely digital, language- and analysis-based, and already substantially assisted by current LLM and analytics tools. Client relationships, onsite observation, interviewing personnel, trust-building, and accountability for recommendations remain human-anchored, which caps disruption below the very top. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis lets many mid-market and smaller organizations afford advisory work they previously skipped, and internal teams can run more improvement projects, but consulting spend is gated by client budgets, executive attention, and the relational/credibility nature of the sale rather than purely by production cost. The result is restructuring — leverage models shift as junior research and deck-production roles compress, while workers who combine domain judgment, client trust, and AI-augmented analysis capture the value.

title: Manicurists and pedicurists
rationale: The core work is entirely manual, tactile, and delivered in physical proximity to a client's hands and feet — nail shaping, callus removal, massage, and intricate hand-painted design require fine dexterity and human presence that AI cannot substitute for. AI touches only peripheral elements: appointment booking, inventory and accounting for salon owners, and design inspiration or AR previews of nail art. Demand is moderately elastic in principle (a low-cost luxury service that grows with disposable income), but productivity per technician is capped by the physical time a service takes, so no AI-driven cost collapse is available to unlock latent demand. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient; BLS-projected 7 percent growth reflects demographic and lifestyle trends rather than technology.

title: Marine engineers and naval architects
rationale: A substantial share of the work is digital — CAD modeling, hydrodynamic and structural simulation, cost estimating, specification writing, and technical reporting — all areas where AI-assisted design optimization and generative simulation tools are already materially useful, pushing disruption toward the high end. However, the core role remains anchored in physical validation: shipyard oversight, prototype testing, sea trials, offshore rig and port site work, and regulatory/classification-society coordination that requires accountable licensed human judgment on safety-critical structures. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design could unlock more custom vessel and offshore wind platform engineering, but demand is fundamentally capped by shipbuilding capacity, capital costs, and defense procurement cycles rather than engineering hours. With disruption at 6, AI reshapes the toolset without absorbing the core accountability and field presence, so the occupation is resilient with continued modest growth.

title: Market research analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language/data based: gathering competitor and consumer information, running statistical analyses, building charts, and writing up reports and presentations. All of these are squarely in the path of current LLM and AI analytics tools, which can already draft survey instruments, code and interpret analyses, synthesize open-ended responses and social listening data, and generate polished decks. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper research means many small and mid-sized firms that never bought market research will start consuming it continuously rather than episodically, and analysis can be run on far more segments and geographies — but a large share of the demand is tied to fixed corporate marketing budgets and to the value of the human relationship in interpreting and defending findings to executives. Net effect is restructure: headcount likely holds roughly flat while the job shifts from data collection and report production toward framing questions, validating AI output, and translating insight into business strategy.

title: Marriage and family therapists
rationale: The core work is language-based conversation, which superficially sits in AI's path, but the therapeutic value derives from human empathy, trust, licensure, and real-time relational dynamics among multiple family members — things AI chatbots supplement rather than substitute. AI will materially affect the periphery: documentation, notes, treatment-plan drafting, insurance billing, client intake/triage, and between-session support tools, plus AI companions may absorb some low-acuity demand. Elasticity is high because mental health care is heavily cost- and access-constrained, with large unmet demand; cheaper administrative overhead lets therapists see more clients and expand reach. Because disruption stays at or below 6 — the relational core is not reshaped — this occupation is resilient, with BLS projecting strong growth.

title: Masonry workers
rationale: Masonry is almost entirely physical craft work performed in variable outdoor jobsite conditions, requiring dexterity, strength, and hand-eye coordination that AI cannot replicate; only peripheral tasks like blueprint reading, material estimating, and bidding are touched by AI tools. Bricklaying robots exist but remain niche, slow, and limited to simple straight walls, so the trajectory over 10 years is incremental at best. Demand is tied to construction cycles, building codes, and material cost trends (prefabricated panels and polished concrete are already substituting), so productivity gains would not unleash large latent demand. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI affects planning and estimating around the edges while the core trowel work stays human.

title: Massage therapists
rationale: Massage therapy is almost entirely physical, hands-on work requiring human touch, dexterity, and in-person presence; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, marketing, client notes, and billing for the 42% who are self-employed. Demand is genuinely elastic — massage is a discretionary wellness service currently suppressed by cost and time, and cheaper access would expand consumption — but AI cannot reduce the cost of the core service since labor time is the product. With disruption at the floor, the occupation is clearly resilient; BLS projects 15% growth driven by demographics and wellness trends independent of AI.

title: Material moving machine operators
rationale: The core work is physical machine operation in semi-structured environments, so language-model AI is largely irrelevant; however, robotics and warehouse automation (autonomous forklifts, AMRs, automated conveyor and container-crane systems) are a real and advancing threat in the most structured settings like warehousing and ports, which pushes disruption to moderate rather than low. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: material movement demand is derived from physical goods volume and e-commerce growth, so cheaper handling doesn't dramatically expand the tonnage that needs moving, though slightly lower logistics costs do support some throughput growth. Because the disruption vector is robotics rather than AI cognition, and unstructured sites (construction, mixed-SKU yards, dredging, crane rigging) still require human judgment and presence, the occupation is best classified as resilient with slow headcount growth. Warehouse forklift roles are the most exposed subsegment and may see gradual erosion even as crane and construction roles hold.

title: Material recording clerks
rationale: The core work — recording shipments, reconciling inventory data, compiling production reports, scheduling, computing freight costs — is routine data handling that AI combined with RFID/barcode automation, warehouse management systems, and computer vision can absorb almost entirely; only a modest physical component (moving packages, hands-on defect inspection) resists, holding disruption just at the high threshold. Demand is highly inelastic: businesses need each shipment recorded exactly once, and cheaper recordkeeping does not create more goods to track, so productivity gains flow straight to reduced headcount. BLS already projects -6% employment on the strength of automated storage and retrieval and RFID adoption, a trend AI accelerates. High disruption plus near-fixed demand puts this squarely in the replace category, though the physical warehouse tasks mean contraction is gradual rather than abrupt.

title: Materials engineers
rationale: Materials engineering is heavily computational — simulation, property prediction, literature synthesis, failure analysis, and report writing are all directly in AI's path, and ML-driven materials discovery (e.g., GNoME-style property prediction, generative candidate screening) is already reshaping the discovery pipeline. However, a substantial portion of the work remains physical: lab synthesis, characterization, processing trials, factory-floor troubleshooting, and supervising technicians, which caps disruption around 7. Elasticity is high because materials discovery and qualification are currently severely rate-limited by cost and time — decades-long development cycles mean vast latent demand across batteries, semiconductors, aerospace alloys, and sustainable materials that becomes economically viable when screening is cheap. Cheaper computational discovery actually increases the need for humans to validate, synthesize, and qualify the exploding number of candidate materials, so headcount should hold or grow while the skill mix shifts toward ML-augmented workflows.

title: Mathematicians and statisticians
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — coding, modeling, statistical analysis, data interpretation, and report writing — all directly in the path of current AI capabilities, and AI coding/analysis assistants already materially change how these tasks are done. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis means more organizations, smaller studies, and more datasets get rigorous statistical treatment, and biostatistics/regulated clinical work has genuine expansion room, but much of the demand is anchored to a fixed number of trials, surveys, and government programs, with federal funding a hard cap for mathematicians. Net effect is restructure: headcount likely holds roughly steady while the role shifts toward problem formulation, causal reasoning, study design, validation of AI-generated analyses, and stakeholder communication rather than hands-on computation. Practitioners who remain manual analysts will be displaced; those who orchestrate and audit AI-driven pipelines will gain leverage.

title: Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: Roughly half the work is digital and cognitive — CAD layouts, drawings, calculations, data recording and analysis, test reporting — all squarely in AI's path, and generative design tools already automate much routine drafting and analysis. But the other half is hands-on: setting up instrumentation, assembling and machining parts, installing and troubleshooting equipment on factory floors, and physically running tests, which AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design iteration and testing support could expand prototyping and product development somewhat, but demand is anchored to physical manufacturing capital investment rather than knowledge-work volume. Because disruption stays at or below 6 given the substantial irreducible physical component, the occupation is resilient, though the digital drafting/analysis portion of the role will visibly shift toward AI-assisted workflows.

title: Mechanical engineers
rationale: Mechanical engineering is largely office-based knowledge work — CAD modeling, FEA/CFD simulation, tolerance and thermal analysis, spec generation, documentation — all of which AI-assisted generative design and simulation surrogates already accelerate materially; this pushes disruption to 7, though physical prototyping, lab testing, failure investigation on site, and manufacturing floor oversight keep it from being higher. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper and faster design iteration does unlock more product variants, more optimization, and more small-firm access to real engineering analysis, but total demand is anchored by capital costs of tooling, materials, factories, and regulatory qualification that AI does not cheapen, so latent demand is real but capped. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation persists and even grows modestly, but the skill mix shifts sharply toward simulation orchestration, AI-tool validation, systems integration, and physical verification rather than manual drafting and routine calculation. Engineers who become adept at directing and auditing AI design pipelines will absorb the productivity gains; those whose value was routine CAD/analysis throughput are most exposed.

title: Medical and health services managers
rationale: Much of the work is knowledge-based — budgeting, scheduling, compliance reporting, records oversight, and metrics analysis — all areas where AI already offers material productivity gains, so disruption is at the upper end of moderate. But the core of the job is on-site human leadership: hiring, motivating and supervising clinical staff, negotiating with physicians and payers, handling emergencies, and bearing regulatory and licensure accountability, which AI cannot assume. Elasticity is moderate: healthcare delivery is expanding with an aging population and growing regulatory complexity, so administrative capacity freed by AI tends to be reabsorbed into more oversight of more facilities rather than eliminated, though headcount is ultimately tied to facility and department counts rather than to price of administration. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in the resilient band — AI reshapes the reporting and analytics periphery while the accountable-leadership core persists, and BLS-projected growth is likely to hold even if per-manager administrative staff shrinks.

title: Medical assistants
rationale: Roughly half of the job is hands-on clinical work — taking vital signs, drawing blood, giving injections, prepping specimens, assisting exams — which requires physical presence and patient interaction that AI cannot replicate. The administrative half (scheduling, insurance forms, coding, charting, phone triage) is genuinely in AI's path and ambient documentation/scheduling tools are already reducing that workload, but it is the peripheral rather than defining portion of the role. Demand elasticity is high because healthcare access is cost- and capacity-constrained, and an aging population plus AI-driven administrative relief lets practices see more patients, which increases need for hands-on support staff. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the clerical tasks and may shift the job mix further toward clinical duties, but headcount should keep growing.

title: Medical dosimetrists
rationale: Core work is computer-based: reviewing CT/MRI images, contouring, and optimizing radiation dose distributions in treatment planning software — exactly the domain where AI auto-segmentation and knowledge-based/automated planning tools are already commercially deployed and validated, often producing plans in minutes that took hours. Only a small share of the job (immobilization devices, occasional patient positioning, QA on physical equipment) requires hands-on presence, so disruption is very high. Demand is driven by cancer incidence and physician-prescribed treatment courses, not by planning cost or speed; patients will not receive 10x more radiotherapy because plans are cheaper, so elasticity is low with only modest expansion from aging demographics and better access in underserved clinics. High disruption plus inelastic demand in a small (4,800-person) occupation means productivity gains concentrate into fewer dosimetrists per center, shifting the surviving role toward plan review, QA, and physicist-adjacent oversight.

title: Medical equipment repairers
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical repair, calibration, and installation of equipment in clinical settings — requiring dexterity, physical strength, and on-site presence that AI cannot substitute. AI does touch peripheral and diagnostic layers: predictive maintenance analytics, AI-assisted troubleshooting from manuals and error logs, and documentation could make each technician more efficient, and the growing software/cybersecurity component of connected devices shifts skills somewhat. Demand is moderately elastic — aging equipment fleets, expanding imaging and monitoring installations, and more IoT-connected devices mean more maintenance work, though hospital budgets and equipment counts cap growth. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient; BLS already projects 13% growth.

title: Medical records specialists
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital text processing: reading clinical documentation and assigning standardized codes, entering and retrieving data in EHR systems. Computer-assisted coding and NLP already automate much of this, and LLMs are rapidly closing the gap on the ambiguous cases that previously required human coders. Demand is structurally fixed — coding volume tracks the number of patient encounters and claims, not the cost of coding, so 10x cheaper coding produces no more encounters and only modest new demand for auditing, denial management, and compliance review. High disruption paired with inelastic demand means productivity gains convert to headcount reduction, with surviving roles concentrated in exception handling and AI output validation.

title: Medical scientists
rationale: Medical research is heavily knowledge- and data-intensive: literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, study design, statistical analysis, grant writing, and manuscript preparation are all directly in AI's path, and AI-driven protein structure prediction, target identification, and trial-data analysis are already reshaping workflows. Wet-lab experimentation, clinical trial oversight, and biosafety work still require human presence, which keeps disruption below maximum. Elasticity is high because the space of unanswered biomedical questions is effectively unbounded and currently rationed by cost, time, and funding — cheaper discovery expands the number of targets pursued, diseases studied, and trials run, and existing job growth projections already reflect strong latent demand. Because productivity gains are likely absorbed by more research output rather than fewer researchers, with the human role shifting toward directing AI-assisted programs and validating results in the lab, this is augmentation rather than replacement.

title: Medical transcriptionists
rationale: The work is entirely digital audio-to-text conversion and editing — precisely what modern ASR and LLM-based ambient documentation tools already perform at or above human accuracy, and AI scribes are being adopted rapidly across physician offices and hospitals. Demand is strictly bounded by the number of patient encounters; cheaper documentation does not create more clinical notes, so productivity gains flow directly into fewer workers. With maximal disruption and near-zero elasticity, headcount contraction is the only outcome, consistent with the BLS decline projection, which likely understates the pace.

title: Meeting, convention, and event planners
rationale: A substantial slice of the job — vendor research, RFPs, budget spreadsheets, contract drafting, registration systems, attendee communications, post-event surveys and reporting — is digital and already being compressed by AI and event-tech platforms, which will meaningfully change how planners spend their days. But the core of the occupation remains in-person and relational: site inspections, live negotiation with venues and caterers, on-site crisis management, reading a client's or attendee's mood, and physically running the event, none of which AI performs. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper planning labor lets more mid-size organizations and individuals afford professional coordination, yet total event volume is capped by the hard costs of venues, food, travel, and calendar time, so the planner fee is not the binding constraint on demand. With disruption at 5, this fits 'resilient' — AI reshapes the back-office workflow and raises the number of events one planner can juggle, but the human, on-the-ground core keeps headcount roughly on its modest growth path.

title: Metal and plastic machine workers
rationale: Core work is physical machine setup, loading, tool changing, and inspection on the shop floor — AI language/vision models touch only the programming (CAM/CNC), quality-inspection, and process-optimization slices, and the CNC programmer subgroup is the one segment squarely in AI's path. The bigger threat here is conventional automation and robotics rather than AI per se, which is why BLS already projects a 7 percent decline driven by CNC adoption and offshoring, not by generative AI. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand for machined parts is derived from manufacturing output and constrained by global competition and capital investment, so cheaper programming does not multiply part volumes proportionally, though some reshoring and cheaper short-run/custom fabrication could unlock modest new demand. Net effect is 'resilient' in the classification sense — AI reshapes the periphery (programming, inspection, predictive maintenance) rather than the hands-on core — even though total headcount continues to erode from automation trends predating AI.

title: Microbiologists
rationale: Microbiology blends substantial wet-lab bench work — culturing organisms, handling specimens, operating microscopes and incubators, field sampling — with knowledge work like experimental design, genomic/sequence analysis, literature review, grant writing, and reporting, where AI is already materially useful. The physical, hands-on, and biosafety-constrained portion of the job caps disruption at moderate-to-high rather than very high, though lab automation plus AI-driven analysis will reshape workflow significantly. Elasticity is high: drug discovery, antimicrobial resistance surveillance, environmental and food-safety testing, and biomanufacturing all have large latent demand currently gated by research cost and cycle time, so cheaper/faster analysis tends to expand the number of experiments and programs rather than shrink staff. Because core disruption stays at 6 given the irreducible bench and field component, the occupation lands in the resilient category, with AI acting as a productivity multiplier on the analytical side.

title: Middle school teachers
rationale: Lesson planning, grading, assessment design, and parent communication are language-based tasks where AI tools are already materially useful, so the knowledge-work portion of the job is genuinely disrupted. But the core of middle school teaching is in-person supervision, behavior management, motivation, and social-emotional development of adolescents — custodial and relational work that requires physical presence and cannot be automated, which caps disruption at the upper edge of moderate. Elasticity is moderate at best: student enrollment is demographically fixed and publicly funded, so cheaper instruction does not produce more students, though it could deepen individualized support and tutoring within existing staffing. Because disruption stays at 6 and the core classroom role remains intact, the occupation is resilient — teachers' workflows shift toward AI-assisted planning and grading rather than the job disappearing.

title: Military careers
rationale: Military careers span a vast range of specialties, but the bulk of personnel (combat arms, transportation, maintenance, logistics, protective service) perform physically embodied, presence-dependent work in unpredictable environments; AI will heavily reshape intelligence analysis, cyber, targeting, ISR processing, and administrative/logistics planning, and autonomous systems will change some crew and pilot roles, giving a moderate overall disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because force size is set by congressional appropriations, geopolitical threat assessment, and recruiting pools rather than by the cost or speed of producing military output — cheaper analysis does not cause the nation to buy 10x more soldiers. Headcount is politically determined and has been roughly stable for decades, so productivity gains show up as capability shifts and reallocation across specialties rather than large contraction or expansion. Because disruption remains at or below the moderate range for the aggregate occupation, the resilient category fits, though specific specialties (intelligence analyst, admin, imagery interpretation) will be restructured internally.

title: Mining and geological engineers
rationale: A substantial part of the job — geological modeling, ore-body estimation, mine planning optimization, environmental/reclamation analysis, and technical report writing — is digital and squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven exploration analytics and autonomous mining systems are already reshaping these workflows. But the core role remains anchored in site-specific physical reality: supervising shaft and tunnel construction, inspecting walls and roofs, monitoring air quality, verifying equipment hazards, and signing off as a licensed PE in remote field conditions. Demand is inelastic because mine development is gated by commodity prices, capital intensity, permitting, and land access rather than by engineering cost or speed — cheaper analysis does not create more ore bodies or approved mines. With disruption at 6 and elasticity at 4, the occupation lands in resilient: AI reshapes the analytical toolkit of a small, licensure-protected workforce without displacing the field-based, accountability-bearing core.

title: Models
rationale: Although modeling is a physically embodied job, its economic output is an image or video — precisely what generative AI now produces synthetically, and brands are already substituting AI-generated or AI-reused model imagery for paid shoots (BLS explicitly flags this). Segments that require literal physical presence (runway, fit modeling, trade shows, art-class and clinical/standardized-patient posing) are insulated, which caps disruption below the very-high range, but the large commercial print/e-commerce/catalog segment is squarely in AI's path. Elasticity is very low: cheaper imagery expands the volume of advertising content, yet that extra volume is fulfilled by synthetic models rather than more human bookings, so productivity gains accrue to brands and AI tools, not to model headcount. High disruption plus demand that does not flow back to human workers yields replacement, consistent with the already-projected employment decline.

title: Music directors and composers
rationale: The occupation is bifurcated: composers do largely digital, creative knowledge work that generative music models already touch directly (jingles, stock/production music, arranging, mockups, scoring drafts), while music directors — the majority of employment, concentrated in churches, schools, and performing arts companies — spend their days rehearsing, auditioning, conducting live ensembles, and building relationships with musicians and donors, tasks that require embodied presence and real-time human judgment. Blending the two yields moderate disruption: AI reshapes the composer workflow and erodes the low-end commercial music market, but leaves live direction essentially intact. Elasticity is moderate — cheap music unlocks far more scored content for video, games, and advertising, yet the concert/church/school ensembles that employ most of these workers are funding-constrained and their headcount is fixed by the number of ensembles, not by production cost. Because over half of the workforce sits in roles whose core work AI cannot perform, the occupation scores at the resilient boundary, though individual commercial composers will face genuine restructuring pressure.

title: Musicians and singers
rationale: The core of this occupation — live performance in concert halls, clubs, and houses of worship (nearly half self-employed, 35% in religious/civic organizations) — depends on embodied human presence, physical technique, and audience connection that generative AI cannot substitute for. AI does materially threaten specific adjacent segments: session work, background vocals, jingles, library/stock music, and demo recording, where synthetic audio is already commercially usable, and it changes promotion and production workflows, which lifts disruption to the middle of the range. Elasticity is low because live-music demand is capped by venue capacity, ticket spending, leisure time, and declining classical and church attendance; cheaper music production does not create more paid performance slots, and it may actually flood the recorded market and depress rates. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation lands in the resilient category — AI reshapes the recording-adjacent periphery and income mix, but not the live performance core.

title: Natural sciences managers
rationale: Much of the role's paperwork — drafting operational reports, reviewing research, writing proposals, budgeting, literature synthesis, and status communication — is language- and analysis-heavy and already materially aided by AI, and the scientific work being supervised is itself being reshaped by AI-driven discovery tools. However, the core of the job is accountable human leadership: hiring, evaluating, and motivating scientists, negotiating resources across units, ensuring lab safety and supply, and bearing responsibility for regulatory and scientific judgment — activities that require presence, authority, and trust rather than text generation. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster R&D should expand the volume of research projects and product development that organizations undertake, but management headcount is capped by span-of-control flexibility and by budget-constrained funders like the federal government and grant agencies. With disruption at 6, the periphery of the job changes considerably while the supervisory core persists, placing this occupation in the resilient category with a gradual skill shift toward AI-literate research portfolio management.

title: Network and computer systems administrators
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital — configuration, monitoring, scripting, patching, log analysis, ticket triage, user provisioning — all directly in the path of AI agents, infrastructure-as-code, and AIOps tooling, though a residual hands-on component remains for physical hardware, cabling, and on-site incident response. Demand elasticity is low: organizations need a roughly fixed amount of network and server uptime, and cheaper administration does not lead firms to consume dramatically more 'administered infrastructure'; the same forces (cloud, Networks-as-a-Service, DevOps consolidation) actually pull the function out of the occupation entirely. BLS already projects a 4 percent decline before accounting for accelerating automation. High disruption combined with inelastic, structurally shrinking demand puts this squarely in the replace category, with surviving roles skewing toward senior automation/cloud engineering.

title: News analysts, reporters, and journalists
rationale: Journalism is predominantly language-based knowledge work — researching, drafting, editing, summarizing, and repurposing content across platforms — all directly in AI's path; automated wire copy, earnings and sports recaps, transcription, and multi-platform rewriting are already being generated by AI today. The residual human core (cultivating sources, on-scene reporting, on-air presence, investigative accountability work) keeps it from a 9-10. Elasticity is low: total news consumption is bounded by audience attention and, critically, by advertising and subscription revenue that does not grow when production gets cheaper — cheaper content production floods an already saturated market and further erodes the ad revenue base rather than expanding paid employment. With high task disruption, a structurally declining revenue model, and BLS already projecting -4%, productivity gains accrue as smaller newsrooms rather than more journalists, fitting 'replace,' though a premium tier of brand-name investigative and on-air talent will persist.

title: Nuclear engineers
rationale: A large share of nuclear engineering is computational — neutronics and thermal-hydraulic simulation, shielding and dose calculations, safety-case analysis, and voluminous regulatory documentation — all of which AI can meaningfully accelerate, so disruption is real and already visible in design and licensing workflows. However, the core work is anchored in physical plant oversight, onsite construction and maintenance monitoring, NRC-licensed accountability, and safety-critical judgment that must be signed by a credentialed human, capping disruption at the upper-moderate range. Elasticity is moderate: there is genuine latent demand from SMRs and data-center power needs, but the binding constraints are capital, siting, supply chains, and regulatory throughput rather than engineering labor cost, so cheaper analysis unlocks only some additional projects. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the safety/regulatory core resists automation, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with the skill mix shifting toward AI-assisted modeling and verification.

title: Nuclear medicine technologists
rationale: Core work is hands-on and physical: preparing and handling radiopharmaceuticals, positioning and reassuring patients, operating and maintaining imaging hardware, and following radiation safety protocols — none of which AI can perform without robotics. AI touches only peripheral portions such as image reconstruction/denoising, dose optimization, scheduling, and documentation, which may modestly speed workflow per scan. Demand is driven by clinical need, physician referrals, reimbursement, and radiopharmaceutical supply rather than technologist productivity, so cheaper scan processing unlocks only limited additional volume (some growth from expanding theranostics and cancer imaging). With low disruption to the physical core, the occupation is resilient; AI becomes a tool within an unchanged job.

title: Nuclear technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on and site-bound: calibrating and maintaining radiation detection instruments, collecting air/water/soil samples, donning protective gear, responding to contamination events, and training plant personnel in person. AI and automated sensor networks can enhance the data-analysis, monitoring, and reporting portions — and could modestly reduce staffing needs in control rooms — but NRC regulation, security clearance requirements, and physical inspection duties keep humans in the loop. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: the number of technicians is tied to the number of licensed reactors and regulatory staffing minimums rather than to the cost of the service, so cheaper analysis does not generate more demand (though a nuclear buildout for data-center power could offset the BLS-projected decline). With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI reshapes tools and reporting at the periphery, not the fundamental job.

title: Nurse anesthetists, nurse midwives, and nurse practitioners
rationale: Core APRN work requires hands-on physical presence — physical exams, administering anesthesia, delivering babies, procedures, and bedside monitoring — while AI meaningfully assists the cognitive layer (documentation, differential diagnosis, test interpretation, drug interaction checks, patient education), placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand elasticity is high: primary care access is severely supply-constrained, an aging population with chronic disease is expanding need, and expanding state practice authority plus AI decision support would let each APRN safely handle more panel volume, unlocking substantial latent care demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes documentation and diagnostic support around the edges but does not replace the licensed, physically present clinician. BLS's projected 35% growth reinforces that headcount will expand rather than contract.

title: Nursing assistants and orderlies
rationale: The core work — bathing, feeding, toileting, lifting, repositioning, and transporting patients — is intensely physical, hands-on, and requires human presence and compassion, none of which current or near-term AI addresses; only peripheral tasks like vital-sign logging, charting, and shift documentation are meaningfully touched by AI, which may free a small amount of time for direct care. Demand elasticity is high in principle because eldercare is heavily rationed by cost and labor scarcity, with enormous latent demand from an aging population, but this demand expansion is driven by demographics and reimbursement policy rather than AI productivity gains. Because disruption is very low, the occupation lands squarely in the resilient category regardless of elasticity. Headcount pressure comes from nursing-home financing, not automation.

title: Occupational health and safety specialists and technicians
rationale: A substantial share of the work — regulatory research, hazard analysis, incident reporting, training material development, and compliance documentation — is language- and data-driven and already benefits from AI assistance, plus sensors and computer vision can automate some monitoring. But the core of the job is on-site physical inspection, walking factories, tunnels, and construction sites, judging real-world conditions, and personally enforcing and coaching compliance, which AI cannot substitute for and which regulatory frameworks require a credentialed human to sign off on. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper safety analytics would extend proper safety programs to smaller employers and enable continuous rather than periodic monitoring, though total demand is anchored to headcount and regulatory cadence rather than price. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the reporting and analytic periphery while the inspection, training, and enforcement core remains human.

title: Occupational therapists
rationale: Occupational therapy is overwhelmingly hands-on: physically guiding clients through daily-living tasks, assessing homes and workspaces in person, fitting adaptive equipment, and building rapport with people who have disabilities or cognitive impairment. AI can meaningfully help with documentation, billing, progress tracking, treatment-plan drafting, and outcome analytics, but these are peripheral to the core in-person therapeutic work, and licensure plus the physical/relational nature of care keep the human in the loop. Elasticity is high because therapy access is genuinely suppressed by cost, therapist scarcity, and insurance limits, and an aging population plus growing pediatric developmental caseloads mean far more latent demand exists than is currently served. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI mainly reduces administrative burden and frees clinicians for more billable client contact.

title: Occupational therapy assistants and aides
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical therapy delivery — guiding exercises, transferring clients, demonstrating adaptive equipment use — all requiring in-person presence, physical strength, and human rapport with frustrated or disabled clients. AI touches only the periphery: documentation of client progress, scheduling, insurance paperwork, and possibly exercise-program suggestion tools, which could reduce administrative burden and free up more treatment time. Elasticity is high because occupational therapy demand is heavily suppressed by cost and reimbursement limits amid an aging population, so cheaper delivery would unlock substantial latent demand. Since disruption is low, the occupation is resilient; BLS-projected 18% growth reflects demographic drivers AI cannot offset.

title: Oil and gas workers
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical — assembling, moving, and repairing heavy drilling equipment outdoors, at heights, and in confined spaces — so AI itself touches little of the core task set. Automated drilling systems and remote monitoring (more robotics/mechanization than AI cognition) do modestly reduce crew sizes and shift some monitoring to control rooms, which justifies a low-but-nonzero disruption score. Elasticity is low because oil and gas output is governed by commodity prices, reserves, and energy policy rather than by labor cost or speed of rig crews; cheaper drilling yields more barrels per worker, not proportionally more crews. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient, though headcount growth stays flat as productivity gains absorb rising production.

title: Operations research analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — data collection, modeling, optimization, simulation, forecasting, and report writing — all directly in AI's path, and LLM-plus-solver tooling already automates much of the model formulation, coding, and documentation cycle. Elasticity is high because optimization analysis is currently rationed by cost and scarce quantitative talent: most mid-size firms never optimize their routing, pricing, scheduling, or inventory at all, and cheaper analysis would push these methods into far more processes and organizations. The bottleneck shifts from building models to framing problems, validating assumptions, and persuading decision makers, which remains human-mediated. High disruption plus substantial latent demand puts this in augment, though workers who can't move up the stack to problem framing and stakeholder work will be squeezed.

title: Opticians
rationale: Optician work is predominantly hands-on and in-person: measuring faces, fitting and adjusting frames, teaching contact lens insertion, and repairing eyewear. AI touches only peripheral elements — virtual try-on, frame recommendation, inventory, prescription record handling — and app-based measurement plus online eyewear retail is a real but modest channel-shift threat rather than task automation. Elasticity is low-moderate because eyewear demand is driven by prescriptions, aging demographics, and fashion cycles; cheaper fitting does not lead people to buy dramatically more pairs, though some latent demand for affordable eyewear exists. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient, with the main risk coming from e-commerce disintermediation rather than AI substituting for the core skill set.

title: Optometrists
rationale: AI is genuinely strong at the image-interpretation slice of optometry — automated retinal screening for diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and macular degeneration is already FDA-cleared, and autorefractors plus AI triage can pre-populate much of the diagnostic workup. But the core of the job remains a hands-on, in-person encounter: slit-lamp examination, refraction refinement with patient feedback, contact lens fitting, minor procedures, prescribing under state licensure, and counseling patients — none of which AI performs autonomously, and scope-of-practice regulation protects the role. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster screening could pull in currently under-served patients and raise exam frequency, but routine eye exams are habit- and insurance-bound rather than cost-suppressed, so expansion is real but bounded. With disruption at the middle of the range and the physical/regulated exam untouched, the occupation is resilient — AI compresses the interpretive workload and lets optometrists see more patients rather than displacing them.

title: Orthotists and prosthetists
rationale: Core work is hands-on: physically evaluating patients, taking molds and measurements, fitting, adjusting, and fabricating devices with tools, plus compassionate patient interaction. AI (with 3D scanning, generative design, and additive manufacturing) can accelerate design and documentation, but the clinical fitting and iterative adjustment require in-person dexterity, so disruption is low. Elasticity is high because O&P care is currently cost- and access-constrained — cheaper custom devices would unlock large latent demand among diabetic, aging, and underserved populations. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient; AI mostly boosts productivity in the lab portion while clinical headcount continues to grow.

title: Painters, construction and maintenance
rationale: Painting is almost entirely physical work: surface prep, ladder and scaffold work, brush/roller/sprayer application in highly variable, cluttered real-world environments that robotics has not solved outside limited industrial spray booths. AI touches only peripheral tasks like estimating, scheduling, color visualization, and customer lead generation, which matters mainly for the 34% who are self-employed. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper painting would prompt more frequent repainting and unlock DIY-substituted jobs, but the binding constraint is labor hours, not information cost. With disruption at the very low end, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Painting and coating workers
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical: surface prep, masking, spray gun handling, awkward-position touch-up, and lifting heavy parts. AI/software adds little beyond what industrial robotics already contributes in high-volume manufacturing lines, and the remaining jobs (auto body repair, custom and small-batch finishing, decorative work) resist automation because of part variability and human judgment on color matching and finish quality. Demand is tied to physical goods volumes and vehicle repair events, so cheaper finishing does not unlock much new consumption. Low disruption places this firmly in the resilient category, though continued robotic automation in factories caps growth.

title: Paralegals and legal assistants
rationale: Core paralegal work — legal research, document drafting, discovery review, summarizing transcripts, file organization — is almost entirely text-based cognitive work that current LLM and e-discovery tools already perform competently, making disruption very high. Some physical/logistical tasks (court filing, trial exhibit handling, client scheduling and relationship work) remain, but they are a minority of hours. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: cheaper legal support could unlock some latent demand for underserved individuals and small businesses, but legal volume is capped by court capacity, regulation on unauthorized practice of law, and the fact that lawyers (not paralegals) capture the billing — productivity gains are more likely absorbed by attorneys using AI directly than by hiring more paralegals. High disruption with constrained demand expansion points to headcount contraction, consistent with BLS's flat 0% projection which itself cites AI as a limiting factor.

title: Personal financial advisors
rationale: The analytical core of the job — portfolio construction, tax and estate scenario modeling, research, plan documentation, compliance notes, and client reporting — is almost entirely digital and squarely in AI's path, and robo-advisors plus AI copilots already reshape workflows; however, trust-building, sales, and emotional coaching in high-stakes life decisions keep a substantial human-presence component, holding disruption at 7 rather than higher. Elasticity is high because comprehensive financial advice is currently rationed by cost and minimum-asset thresholds: most middle-income households get no personalized planning at all, so a 10x drop in cost-to-serve unlocks a very large latent market, reinforced by demographic tailwinds from retiring baby boomers and the shift to self-directed retirement accounts. Fiduciary/licensing requirements and the need for a human accountable party also mean AI output still gets routed through a credentialed advisor rather than replacing one. Net effect is augment: each advisor serves far more clients with AI handling analysis and documentation, while total advised households expand, keeping headcount stable to growing even as the skill mix tilts toward relationship management and behavioral coaching.

title: Pest control workers
rationale: Core work is physical and site-specific: crawling through attics and crawl spaces, applying pesticides, sealing structures, setting traps.
