AI may help with pest identification from photos, route optimization, scheduling, estimating, and record-keeping/compliance, but these are peripheral to the hands-on treatment work that requires a licensed human on site. Demand is driven by infestations, invasive species, and regulation rather than cost of service, so productivity gains would mostly shave administrative overhead rather than unlock large latent demand. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient.

title: Petroleum engineers
rationale: Much of petroleum engineering is data-intensive modeling — reservoir simulation, production optimization, drilling program design — all squarely in AI's path, and ML-based subsurface interpretation and automated drilling optimization are already deployed in industry. However, a substantial share of the role involves on-site presence at rigs and well sites, equipment oversight, safety accountability, coordination with field crews, and PE-licensed sign-off, which caps disruption around moderate-high. Elasticity is low because oil and gas demand is set by commodity markets, capital budgets, reserve geology, and energy-transition policy rather than by engineering cost — cheaper analysis does not cause society to drill dramatically more wells, though some marginal recovery projects and adjacent carbon-storage/geothermal work could become viable. With disruption at 6, the occupation falls in the resilient band: AI reshapes the analytical toolkit while the core field-oriented, accountable engineering role persists at roughly flat headcount, consistent with BLS's 1% projection.

title: Pharmacists
rationale: A large share of pharmacist cognitive work — drug interaction and allergy checking, dosage verification, formulary and insurance adjudication, records management — is exactly the kind of rule-based, data-intensive task AI and automated dispensing systems already handle well, and retail volume is shifting to centralized mail-order fill operations. However, the core role remains anchored by legal sign-off requirements, state licensure, hands-on dispensing/compounding, immunizations, supervision of technicians, and face-to-face patient counseling, plus growing integration into clinical care teams for medication therapy management. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: total prescription volume is driven by physician prescribing, demographics, and insurance rather than by the cost or speed of pharmacy services, though cheaper clinical medication review could unlock some latent demand in ambulatory and long-term care settings. Because disruption stays at or below 6 given the regulatory and physical constraints, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with the mix shifting from retail dispensing toward clinical and consultative roles.

title: Pharmacy technicians
rationale: Core work is a mix of physical dispensing (counting, measuring, compounding, IV preparation, inventory handling, on-your-feet customer service) and digital tasks (data entry, insurance claim processing, prescription intake) that AI plus automated dispensing robotics can meaningfully absorb — hence moderate disruption, with automation pressure concentrated in high-volume mail-order and central-fill settings. Elasticity is moderate: prescription volume is driven by demographics, chronic disease prevalence, and prescriber behavior rather than by dispensing cost, so cheaper processing does not create many more prescriptions, though technicians are absorbing tasks delegated upward from pharmacists as pharmacists shift to clinical care. State regulation requiring pharmacist oversight and licensed technician involvement further stabilizes headcount. Because a substantial share of tasks require physical presence and hands-on patient-facing work, disruption stays at or below 6, making this occupation resilient with an internal skill shift toward oversight and clinical support rather than net contraction.

title: Phlebotomists
rationale: Phlebotomy is fundamentally a hands-on, physical task requiring fine dexterity, in-person patient interaction, and calming anxious patients — none of which AI touches directly. The only digital components are sample labeling, database entry, and scheduling, which are already largely automated by barcode/LIS systems; AI adds marginal help at the periphery. Demand for blood testing is moderately elastic (cheaper, more accessible draws and mobile/home collection could expand preventive and longitudinal testing), but expansion would be driven by robotics and decentralized testing rather than AI, and physical throughput per worker is the binding constraint. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient; the larger long-run risk is venipuncture robotics or micro-sampling devices, not language-model AI.

title: Photographers
rationale: Photography mixes physical presence (weddings, events, portraits, photojournalism) with heavily digital workflows — editing, retouching, culling, cataloging — that AI already automates well; more importantly, generative image models directly substitute for large segments of commercial, product, stock, and advertising photography, which is where much of the paid work sits. Event, portrait, and news photography still require a human on location with a camera and client rapport, capping disruption below the very-high tier. Demand elasticity is limited: people don't want 10x more wedding albums or headshots, and cheaper imagery is increasingly satisfied by synthetic generation or smartphones rather than by hiring more photographers. The combination of significant substitution in commercial/stock work with essentially fixed demand for ceremonial and portrait shoots points to headcount contraction, especially at the lower-paid commercial end.

title: Physical therapist assistants and aides
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical care: guiding exercises, manual therapy, gait training, moving patients, and setting up equipment — all requiring physical presence, dexterity, and human empathy that AI cannot substitute. AI touches only peripheral tasks like documentation, scheduling, insurance forms, and progress tracking, which may modestly reduce administrative burden (most relevant for aides' clerical duties). Demand elasticity is high because rehabilitation needs are large and currently rationed by cost and insurance reimbursement, and an aging population plus remote-monitoring tools could expand therapy volume. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes recordkeeping and possibly exercise adherence monitoring, not the treatment itself.

title: Physical therapists
rationale: Physical therapy is fundamentally hands-on: manual therapy, guided exercise, gait observation, and in-person motivation of patients in pain. AI can assist with documentation, referral review, exercise-program generation, motion-capture analytics, and remote adherence monitoring, but these are peripheral supports rather than replacements for the core physical encounter. Elasticity is high because demand for rehabilitation is currently suppressed by cost, visit caps, and access — an aging population and nonopioid pain management create large latent demand — but this expansion is realized through human clinicians plus PT assistants, not AI substitution. Because disruption stays well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient, with AI mainly reducing administrative burden and extending reach via hybrid telehealth models.

title: Physician assistants
rationale: PA work blends substantial cognitive/diagnostic tasks that AI can meaningfully support (history review, differential diagnosis, test interpretation, documentation, prescribing decision support) with hands-on physical care — physical exams, suturing, setting bones, injections, surgical assistance — plus licensure and supervision requirements that anchor the role to a human clinician. AI will reshape documentation burden and diagnostic workflow but cannot perform the physical or legally accountable core, keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is high: primary care access is severely supply-constrained, especially in rural and underserved areas, so any productivity gain gets absorbed by more patients seen rather than fewer PAs. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI acts as a throughput multiplier on top of already strong demographic-driven demand growth.

title: Physicians and surgeons
rationale: Physician work blends heavily cognitive components AI already touches — differential diagnosis, chart review, documentation, image and lab interpretation, patient messaging — with irreducible physical and interpersonal work: physical exams, procedures, surgery, emergency stabilization, and legally accountable judgment. Aggregate disruption lands at 6 because image-centric specialties (radiology, pathology, dermatology) face far more exposure than surgeons, anesthesiologists, and generalists whose value is hands-on presence; ambient documentation and decision support mostly remove drudgery rather than replacing the core role. Elasticity is high: access to physician care is severely cost- and supply-constrained (shortages, long waits, underserved rural and safety-net populations), so cheaper, faster care throughput would be absorbed by more patients seen and more preventive and chronic-disease management delivered. Because disruption stays at or below 6 — licensure, malpractice liability, and the need for a physical, accountable clinician anchor the job — the occupation is resilient, with AI reshaping workflow and documentation rather than headcount.

title: Physicists and astronomers
rationale: Core work — deriving and testing theory, writing simulation and analysis code, mining large observational datasets, drafting papers and grant proposals — is almost entirely cognitive and digital, and AI systems are already materially useful for literature synthesis, code generation, numerical modeling, and pattern-finding in telescope and accelerator data, so disruption is very high; the main non-digital residue is instrument design, lab work, and observatory operations. Elasticity is only moderate because headcount is set almost entirely by federal research budgets, fixed telescope/accelerator capacity, tenure lines, and grant cycles rather than by unit cost of analysis — cheaper science mostly means more papers per physicist, not proportionally more physicists — though applied segments (medical physics, quantum information, semiconductors, materials) do have genuine latent commercial demand that could absorb some gains. With disruption >= 7 and elasticity in the 5-6 band, the occupation persists but reshapes: value shifts toward posing good questions, designing experiments and instruments, and validating AI-generated results, while routine computation, coding, and manuscript production skills lose differentiation.

title: Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters
rationale: Core work is intensely physical and site-specific: crawling into tight spaces, soldering, cutting and fitting pipe, diagnosing leaks by feel and observation in unpredictable existing structures. AI touches only peripheral tasks — estimating and bidding, scheduling, dispatch, BIM-assisted layout, code lookup, and customer communication — which are a small share of the day for most workers. Demand is moderately elastic in that cheaper diagnostics and admin overhead could let small shops take more jobs and unlock some deferred maintenance, but the binding constraint is skilled labor hours and licensing, not information cost. With disruption well under 6, this is clearly resilient; AI is most likely a back-office productivity aid that slightly increases billable field time per plumber.

title: Podiatrists
rationale: Podiatry is heavily hands-on: physical exams of feet, surgery, wound debridement, orthotic fitting, and in-person patient care dominate daily work. AI can meaningfully assist with imaging interpretation (x-rays, diabetic foot ulcer risk screening), documentation, coding, and triage, which reduces administrative burden but leaves the core procedural and diagnostic touch work intact. Demand has moderate elasticity — aging populations, diabetes, and obesity create latent need, and cheaper AI screening could funnel more undiagnosed patients into treatment, but reimbursement limits and competition from other physicians cap expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the paperwork and screening periphery, not the clinical core.

title: Police and detectives
rationale: Core police work is physical, in-person, and unpredictable — patrol, traffic stops, arrests, crime scene response, and community interaction cannot be automated. AI meaningfully touches the paperwork and analytic periphery: report drafting from bodycam audio, evidence triage, license plate and facial recognition, predictive deployment, and digital forensics for detectives (the most exposed sub-group). Elasticity is moderate because public safety demand is real but headcount is capped by municipal budgets, civil-service structures, and political constraints rather than by cost of production, so productivity gains mostly free officers for more field time rather than expanding or shrinking rosters. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient: skill mix shifts toward tech-assisted investigation while headcount stays roughly flat.

title: Political scientists
rationale: Political scientists' core work — literature review, survey and voting data analysis, policy evaluation, forecasting, and report/article writing — is almost entirely digital, language- and analysis-based, placing it squarely in AI's path; LLMs already draft policy memos and code statistical analyses competently. Demand is highly inelastic because employment is dominated by federal government (67%) and grant/institution-funded roles where headcount is set by budget appropriations and organizational structure, not by the marginal cost of analysis; cheaper policy research does not create dramatically more funded positions, and BLS already projects decline. Some latent demand exists among smaller advocacy groups and firms wanting policy analysis they previously couldn't afford, but regulatory and budgetary caps limit it. High disruption plus low elasticity in a small, budget-constrained occupation points to headcount contraction rather than expansion.

title: Postal service workers
rationale: The bulk of this occupation (mail carriers, ~64%, plus handlers loading trucks) is physical last-mile delivery and parcel handling that AI software cannot perform; automation pressure here comes from mechanical sorting equipment and route consolidation rather than language-model AI, and that automation is already largely mature. Some disruption applies to sorters and clerks via OCR/automated sorting and self-service kiosks, but this is incremental rather than transformative. Demand elasticity is low: mail volume is structurally declining due to digital substitution and is not price- or speed-constrained, though parcel growth from e-commerce provides partial offset. Disruption is well below the threshold, so the occupation is classified resilient to AI specifically — even though headcount continues its slow secular decline for non-AI reasons.

title: Postsecondary education administrators
rationale: Much of this work is administrative knowledge work — reviewing applications, scheduling courses, maintaining records, producing enrollment data — which AI can substantially automate, and admissions/registrar functions are already being augmented by AI screening and scheduling tools. However, a large share of the role is interpersonal and institutional: advising students, managing staff, faculty tenure and budget decisions, campus events, governance, and accountability that institutions will not delegate to AI, which caps disruption at the upper edge of moderate. Elasticity is low because demand is tied to student enrollment and a fixed number of dean/provost slots — cheaper administration does not create more students or more institutions, so gains show up as leaner back offices rather than growth. Because the core relational and decision-authority work remains human while the routine processing thins out, the occupation is best classified as resilient with quiet contraction in the clerical-adjacent tiers.

title: Postsecondary teachers
rationale: Core tasks — lecturing, curriculum design, grading, advising, literature review, writing and publishing research — are overwhelmingly language- and cognition-based, and AI already materially changes syllabus creation, assessment design, feedback, and research workflows, while also forcing wholesale redesign of assignments because students use the same tools. Disruption is high but not maximal: live instruction, mentorship, lab supervision, accreditation requirements, and institutional credentialing keep humans central. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper instruction could expand access and lifelong/online learning, and health and nursing faculty face genuine unmet demand (a real bottleneck), but enrollment is demographically capped, degrees are the scarce good rather than teaching hours, and public funding plus tenure structures limit expansion. The result is restructuring — headcount roughly stable with continued adjunctification, while the skill mix shifts toward AI-resilient assessment, mentoring, and human-differentiated instruction.

title: Power plant operators, distributors, and dispatchers
rationale: Much of the work is instrument monitoring, data interpretation, and control-room decision-making, which is digital and squarely in the path of advanced automation, smart-grid analytics, and AI-assisted anomaly detection — so disruption is meaningful. However, the core role is legally and operationally anchored to licensed human presence (NRC licensing, NERC certification, physical rounds, hands-on switching orders, and emergency response accountability), which caps how far AI can absorb the job. Elasticity is very low: the number of generating units, substations, and control rooms is fixed by physical infrastructure, so efficiency gains convert directly into fewer operator seats rather than more output, consistent with the projected -10% decline. Net effect is 'resilient' because AI reshapes the tools and staffing ratios at the periphery while regulation and safety-critical human accountability preserve the core work, even though total headcount slowly shrinks from broader automation and plant retirements.

title: Preschool and childcare center directors
rationale: The role blends administrative work AI can help with (scheduling, budgets, compliance paperwork, parent communications, enrollment marketing, licensing documentation) with irreducibly in-person duties: supervising staff, being physically onsite while children are present, handling emergencies, facility oversight, and building trust with parents. Regulatory requirements mandate a licensed, credentialed human director onsite, which caps automation of the core function. Elasticity is moderate — childcare demand is suppressed by cost, so cheaper administration could marginally expand center capacity, but the binding constraints are teacher labor costs, physical space, ratio regulations, and declining birth rates, not administrative overhead. With disruption at 4, AI mainly relieves paperwork burden rather than reshaping the job, so the occupation is resilient even though BLS projects a slight decline for demographic rather than technological reasons.

title: Preschool teachers
rationale: Preschool teaching is overwhelmingly physical, custodial, and emotionally interpersonal work: supervising, feeding, comforting, and playing with children under five who cannot be left with software. AI may assist with lesson planning, developmental documentation, and parent communication, but these are peripheral to the core caregiving role, and child-to-staff ratios are fixed by licensing regulation. Demand elasticity is genuinely high — childcare is heavily cost-suppressed and many families would consume far more if it were cheaper — but AI cannot deliver those productivity gains because the binding constraint is physical supervision, not cognitive throughput. With disruption well under 6, this is clearly resilient.

title: Private detectives and investigators
rationale: A meaningful share of the work — public/court record searches, social media and OSINT research, skip tracing, and report writing — is digital and already being reshaped by AI-powered data aggregation and drafting tools, which pushes disruption toward the high end. However, the largest employer segment (retail loss prevention, 32%) plus field surveillance, in-person interviews, undercover work, and courtroom-defensible evidence collection require unpredictable physical presence and human judgment that AI cannot replace, capping disruption around 6. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster investigation could expand background screening, fraud detection, and due diligence volume, but privacy law, licensing, and the fixed nature of litigation and retail-shrink caseloads limit runaway growth. Because disruption stays at or below 6 with the physical core intact, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with AI absorbing the research-and-writing periphery while headcount continues modest growth.

title: Probation officers and correctional treatment specialists
rationale: A meaningful share of the job is documentation-heavy — case files, presentence investigations, progress reports, risk assessments — where AI drafting and predictive risk-scoring tools already reduce paperwork burden and are actively being piloted in corrections agencies. But the core work is in-person supervision: home and workplace visits, drug testing, building trust with hostile or vulnerable clients, court testimony, and legally accountable discretionary judgment that jurisdictions will not delegate to software. Elasticity is low-moderate because caseloads are determined by court sentencing volume and government corrections budgets, not by the cost of supervision; efficiency gains mostly raise caseload ratios rather than expand demand, though decarceration trends could shift more people into community supervision. With disruption at 5, AI reshapes the administrative periphery and may raise caseloads per officer, but does not reshape the core relational and field-based work, making the occupation resilient.

title: Producers and directors
rationale: Producing and directing blends on-set human leadership with heavy creative and logistical knowledge work — scripting decisions, storyboarding, budgeting, scheduling, casting review, editing supervision, and promotion — much of which generative AI already accelerates through previsualization, AI video generation, automated rough cuts, and budget/schedule optimization; this pushes disruption high even though live sets, talent management, and stage work still require human presence. Elasticity is high because content demand is structurally cost-suppressed: dramatically cheaper production unlocks far more video advertising, branded and short-form content, streaming series, and individual creator projects, and the 'producer/director' role scales down to small teams and solo creators who previously could not afford production. The result is more projects per dollar rather than fewer coordinators, since someone must still make creative and business judgment calls and be accountable for a final product. Hence augment: heavy task transformation, with expanding output absorbing productivity gains — though value shifts toward those fluent with AI toolchains and away from routine assistant-producer functions.

title: Project management specialists
rationale: A large share of the daily work — building schedules, tracking budgets and milestones, producing status reports, drafting project documents, synthesizing updates from teams — is digital, language- and data-based and already substantially assisted by AI-enabled project tools, pushing disruption high; however, the accountability, stakeholder negotiation, vendor selection, and human trust-building components resist automation, keeping it below the very-high band. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper coordination lets organizations run more, smaller projects with formal management and extends project discipline into work that previously went unmanaged, but PM headcount is fundamentally overhead tied to the number of projects and staff being coordinated, so productivity gains partly convert into leaner project offices rather than proportionally more coordinators. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 5, the occupation persists but the role shifts from administrative tracking and reporting toward exception handling, risk judgment, client relationship management, and orchestrating AI tooling — a restructuring in which workers who remain document-producers are displaced.

title: Property appraisers and assessors
rationale: The core work — pulling comparables, verifying public records, running valuation models, and writing standardized reports — is data analysis and document generation squarely in AI's path, and automated valuation models plus appraisal waivers have already displaced a meaningful share of residential work; only the physical site inspection and courtroom/hearing defense of assessments resist automation, and inspections are increasingly delegated to hybrid or third-party data collectors. Demand is highly inelastic: the number of appraisals is tied to real estate transaction volume, mortgage originations, and statutory tax assessment cycles, none of which expand because valuation gets cheaper or faster. Mass appraisal by government assessors is exactly the kind of batch task where one worker plus a model can cover an entire jurisdiction, so productivity gains flow to headcount reduction rather than more output. High disruption combined with structurally capped demand puts this in the replace category, with the surviving roles concentrated in complex commercial valuation and defending assessments in adversarial settings.

title: Property, real estate, and community association managers
rationale: A substantial share of the work is administrative and digital — rent collection, budgeting, financial reporting, lease documentation, listing vacancies, routing maintenance tickets — and AI plus property-management software already automates much of it. But the core of the job remains physically and socially anchored: inspecting grounds, showing units, supervising contractors, mediating disputes with residents and HOA boards, and responding to after-hours emergencies, which caps disruption at moderate. Elasticity is moderate: demand is driven by the fixed stock of managed properties and units, though cheaper management could push smaller landlords and single-family portfolios into professional management, expanding the addressable market somewhat. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI shrinks the paperwork burden and raises properties-per-manager, but the relationship and on-site functions preserve headcount.

title: Psychiatric technicians and aides
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical and interpersonal care: monitoring and de-escalating patients, assisting with bathing and eating, escorting, restraining violent individuals, and taking vital signs. AI touches only peripheral tasks like charting, documentation, shift handoff summaries, and possibly behavioral-monitoring sensors that flag risk, so disruption is low. Elasticity is high because mental health and substance use care is heavily supply- and cost-constrained with large unmet need, so any efficiency gains would be absorbed by serving more patients rather than cutting staff. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI may reduce paperwork burden but cannot substitute for physical presence, judgment, and compassion at the bedside.

title: Psychologists
rationale: Psychology is largely language-based cognitive work — interviewing, assessment, diagnosis, documentation, research writing — all areas where AI already assists meaningfully (note-taking, test scoring, report drafting, literature review, and increasingly AI chatbot-based therapeutic support). However, the therapeutic core depends on human rapport, trust, empathy, and legal/ethical accountability, and licensure plus liability structures strongly protect the role; school and forensic settings additionally require in-person observation and institutional participation. Elasticity is high because mental health care demand is enormously suppressed by cost, wait times, and clinician scarcity — cheaper support unlocks large latent demand, so productivity gains would be absorbed by more people served rather than fewer clinicians. Disruption sits at 6 because AI reshapes the administrative and low-acuity periphery and may siphon some self-help demand, but does not replace the core licensed clinical relationship, placing this in the resilient category with expanding, AI-augmented practice.

title: Public relations and fundraising managers
rationale: The work is predominantly language- and content-based — press releases, speeches, messaging strategy, media monitoring, donor research and segmentation, grant applications — all directly in AI's path, and AI tools already handle drafting, sentiment analysis, and donor prospecting well. However, a substantial share of the role is relationship-driven and judgment-heavy: face-to-face major-gift solicitation, crisis management with executives, spokesperson duties, and supervising staff, which caps disruption below the very-high tier. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper content and analytics let smaller organizations run sophisticated PR and fundraising programs and enable more personalized donor cultivation, but total demand is bounded by organizational budgets, donor pools, and the fixed number of institutions needing a communications leader. Net effect is restructure — the manager role persists but shifts toward orchestrating AI-generated output, reputational judgment, and high-touch relationships, with fewer supporting specialists beneath each manager.

title: Public relations specialists
rationale: Core deliverables — press releases, speeches, social posts, media lists, sentiment monitoring, message drafting — are almost entirely language and digital-analytics tasks that current LLMs already perform at near-professional quality, so disruption is very high; the remaining human-anchored portions are journalist relationships, crisis judgment, executive counsel, and in-person events. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper content and monitoring lets small organizations, nonprofits, and mid-market firms afford ongoing PR and lets teams cover far more channels and languages, but reputational communication is ultimately gated by the number of organizations, the finite attention of media outlets, and the fact that firms do not want 10x more press releases. That combination points to restructuring rather than pure replacement: routine writing and clip-tracking roles shrink while value concentrates in strategy, relationship-building, crisis judgment, and AI-assisted campaign orchestration.
_dimension_clarification: Disruption >= 7 with elasticity of 6 places this squarely in the restructure band, consistent with BLS's modest 5% growth projection alongside a substantially changed skill mix.

title: Public safety telecommunicators
rationale: The core work — receiving voice/text input, extracting location and incident type, classifying severity against protocol trees, entering data into CAD systems, and relaying structured information — is almost entirely language and information processing, which puts it squarely in AI's path; speech recognition, real-time translation, automated address geolocation, protocol-driven triage, and AI handling of non-emergency and administrative calls are already deployed or piloted in PSAPs. Demand is only moderately elastic: total 911 call volume tracks population, not price, so productivity gains cannot be absorbed by 10x more calls — but chronic 20-30% vacancy rates, unmet needs in text/video/social-media intake, mental-health diversion, and quality assurance mean freed capacity gets reabsorbed rather than immediately cut. Public-sector budgets, union protection, liability exposure, and the irreducible need for a calm empathetic human on life-threatening calls further slow displacement. The result is a role that survives at roughly flat headcount but shifts substantially toward supervising AI triage, handling high-acuity and ambiguous calls, and managing multi-channel incident coordination — a restructuring rather than a wholesale replacement.

title: Purchasing managers, buyers, and purchasing agents
rationale: The core work — analyzing price proposals, comparing supplier bids, monitoring inventory and contract compliance, drafting POs and maintaining records — is largely digital, structured, data-driven cognitive work that procurement automation and AI agents already handle well; supplier relationship management, plant visits, and complex negotiation preserve some human role, especially for purchasing managers. Elasticity is low because procurement volume is derived from the organization's actual need for goods and services, not from the cost of the procurement function itself; cheaper sourcing analysis does not make companies buy dramatically more, though there is modest expansion as smaller firms and more spend categories get professionally managed and tail spend gets optimized. With high task exposure and demand tied to fixed underlying purchasing needs, productivity gains mainly reduce transactional buyer headcount while a smaller cadre of strategic sourcing and supplier-relationship professionals remains.

title: Quality control inspectors
rationale: The core task — detecting defects and deviations from specification via visual, dimensional, and sensor-based inspection, then logging results — is precisely the target of machine vision, 3D scanning, and AI anomaly detection, which are already deployed on production lines; documentation, blueprint interpretation, and root-cause reporting are also increasingly AI-assisted. Physical handling, lifting, fixturing, and inspection in messy or low-volume environments keep the score below 8, since full automation requires capital investment and doesn't fit every plant. Elasticity is low because inspection volume is derived from production volume — no manufacturer wants 10x more inspections of the same output, and cheaper inspection mostly means 100% automated in-line checking rather than more human inspectors. High automatability of the perceptual core plus demand rigidly tied to production output implies gradual headcount contraction, with surviving roles shifting toward monitoring and calibrating automated inspection systems.

title: Radiation therapists
rationale: Core work is physically embodied: positioning and immobilizing patients, operating linear accelerators, verifying setup imaging, monitoring reactions, and providing emotional support over weeks of daily treatment. AI is already reshaping adjacent functions — auto-contouring, adaptive planning, dose calculation, and image verification — which compresses the planning/dosimetry side and adds QA-oversight duties, but it does not remove the need for a licensed human at the machine with the patient. Elasticity is low because demand is set by cancer incidence and prescribed fractions, not price; indeed hypofractionation trends actively reduce visits per patient, so productivity gains do not create new volume. Disruption stays at or below 6 while the physical, regulated, patient-facing core persists, making this occupation resilient with modest skill drift toward technology oversight.

title: Radiologic and MRI technologists
rationale: The core work is hands-on and physical: positioning patients, operating and maintaining large imaging hardware, injecting contrast media, calming anxious or injured people, and lifting or turning patients. AI is transforming image interpretation (the radiologist's job) and adds workflow aids like automated positioning assistance, protocol optimization, scan-time reduction, and dose/quality checks, but these change the periphery rather than replace the technologist at the machine. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster scanning plus AI-accelerated MRI throughput could expand screening volumes and shift some capacity, but demand is capped by scanner capital, referral patterns, and reimbursement, and aging demographics already drive steady growth. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI likely makes each technologist more productive per scan without displacing the role.

title: Railroad workers
rationale: Core work is physical and safety-critical: operating locomotives, coupling cars, inspecting equipment, throwing switches, and managing passengers in unpredictable outdoor conditions. Automation pressure on railroads is real (PTC, remote-control locomotives, automated inspection, yard scheduling optimization), but it stems from long-cycle industrial/robotic automation heavily constrained by FRA rules and union crew-size agreements rather than from generative AI touching the daily tasks; yardmaster scheduling is the most AI-exposed sliver. Demand is derived from freight tonnage and passenger volume, which respond to shipping economics rather than to crew productivity, so elasticity is low. Because disruption over the next decade stays well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient, with slow attrition driven by conventional automation rather than AI displacement.

title: Real estate brokers and sales agents
rationale: Much of the work — listing research, comparative market analysis, marketing copy, lead generation, document and contract prep, client communication — is digital and squarely in AI's path, and portals plus AI valuation tools already erode the informational advantage agents once monopolized. But the core value proposition remains in-person: showing homes, local relationship networks, trust during the largest financial transaction of a client's life, and licensed negotiation and fiduciary duties, which keeps disruption moderate rather than high. Elasticity is low because transaction volume is driven by interest rates, housing supply, and life events, not by the cost or speed of agent services; cheaper brokerage mainly compresses commissions rather than generating more home sales. The bigger threat to headcount comes from commission-structure reform and disintermediation than from AI absorbing the core work, so the occupation scores as resilient with margin pressure and likely consolidation toward productive full-time agents.

title: Receptionists
rationale: Core receptionist tasks — answering phones, scheduling and confirming appointments, routing calls, entering data, handling correspondence — are almost entirely language and information processing, and AI voice agents, self-check-in kiosks, and online scheduling already displace much of this work today; the main residual is the physical greeting/escorting and security presence, which keeps the score below 9. Demand elasticity is very low: an organization needs one front desk regardless of how cheap the function becomes, and nobody schedules 10x more appointments or receives 10x more visitors because check-in got faster. Productivity gains therefore convert almost directly into fewer front-desk positions, especially in multi-site healthcare and professional offices consolidating reception into centralized or automated systems. High disruption plus inelastic demand puts this squarely in the replace category, consistent with BLS's flat-to-declining projection driven by administrative automation.

title: Recreation workers
rationale: Core work is in-person, physical, and social: leading group activities, instructing participants, ensuring safety, and providing first aid — tasks AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral duties like drafting newsletters, scheduling, program planning, and paperwork assistance, a small share of the day. Demand is driven by demographics (aging populations in residential care) and public/institutional budgets rather than by production cost, so productivity gains in the admin sliver would not meaningfully change headcount either way. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient.

title: Recreational therapists
rationale: Core work is in-person, physically active, and relational — leading games, sports, aquatics, and community outings while motivating and physically assisting patients — none of which AI can perform. AI can meaningfully help only with peripheral tasks like documentation, progress tracking, treatment-plan drafting, and activity ideation, which is a modest share of the day. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population and mental health/addiction treatment create real latent demand, but reimbursement and funding constraints (especially in nursing homes) cap expansion regardless of productivity. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient; AI becomes a documentation aid rather than a substitute.

title: Registered nurses
rationale: Nursing is fundamentally hands-on: assessment, medication administration, patient handling, monitoring, and bedside comfort require physical presence and judgment in unpredictable settings, so core tasks remain outside AI's reach. AI will meaningfully reshape the documentation, charting, triage, care-plan drafting, and early-warning/monitoring layers — which consume a large share of a nurse's shift — pushing disruption to a moderate 4-5 rather than low. Demand elasticity is high because nursing care is chronically supply-constrained and rationed by staffing shortages and cost; freeing nurses from paperwork would be absorbed by more patient contact and expanded home/community care rather than headcount cuts. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI removes administrative burden and augments clinical vigilance without displacing the core role.

title: Rehabilitation counselors
rationale: Core work is relational and empathetic — in-person counseling, building trust with clients who have disabilities, coordinating with employers, doctors, and community resources — which AI cannot substitute for. AI does meaningfully touch the substantial documentation, case-note, plan-drafting, resource-matching, and benefits/eligibility research portions of the job, freeing counselor time, so disruption is moderate rather than low. Elasticity is moderate: latent need is large (aging population, veterans, underserved disabled clients) but funding is dominated by constrained state and federal vocational rehabilitation budgets, capping headcount growth regardless of productivity. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes paperwork and referral workflows at the periphery while the human counseling core remains.

title: Respiratory therapists
rationale: Core work is hands-on and physical: intubation support, ventilator setup and titration at bedside, chest physiotherapy, drawing arterial blood gases, and patient/family education in homes and ICUs. AI can improve ventilator weaning protocols, alarm triage, pulmonary function test interpretation, and documentation, but these are decision-support layers around an inherently in-person, licensed clinical role. Demand is highly elastic in the sense that aging demographics, COPD prevalence, and understaffed hospitals mean any efficiency gain gets absorbed by more patient coverage rather than headcount cuts. With disruption well below the threshold, this is clearly resilient — AI touches monitoring and charting but not the physical delivery of respiratory care.

title: Retail sales workers
rationale: Core work is in-person: greeting customers, physically showing and demonstrating merchandise, stocking, and processing payments on the floor — tasks AI cannot perform without embodiment. AI does touch the periphery meaningfully (product lookup, inventory and recommendation systems, self-checkout and clienteling apps), and e-commerce driven by AI recommendation engines diverts some transactions away from stores, but that is a channel-shift pressure rather than automation of the role itself. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: retail sales volume is bounded by consumer spending, so cheaper sales assistance does not create much new demand, though richer service could support more specialty and high-touch formats. With disruption at 4, the occupation lands in the resilient category — flat headcount with gradually shifting skill emphasis toward omnichannel and product expertise rather than large-scale displacement by AI.

title: Roofers
rationale: Roofing is almost entirely physical: climbing, lifting 60-pound bundles, cutting and fastening materials in unpredictable outdoor conditions at height — none of which AI can perform, and robotics for steep-slope roofs remains far from commercial viability. AI touches only peripheral tasks like drone-based roof inspection, measurement/estimating software, and scheduling or lead generation, which marginally speed up bidding but not the labor itself. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: roof replacement demand is driven by building stock, weather damage, and roof lifecycles rather than by service cost, though slightly cheaper estimating could pull some deferred repairs forward. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is clearly resilient — headcount is set by construction activity and labor supply, not AI capability.

title: Sales engineers
rationale: Much of a sales engineer's work is knowledge-based and highly AI-assistable: building technical presentations, answering RFPs and security questionnaires, scoping requirements, configuring demos, and troubleshooting documentation. However, the core value lies in trust-building, in-person/live technical persuasion, and tailoring solutions in ambiguous enterprise negotiations, which keeps disruption at the lower end of 'high.' Elasticity is high because pre-sales technical support is currently rationed by cost — many mid-market and smaller deals never get an SE, and proliferation of increasingly complex technical products (including AI products themselves) expands the need for someone to translate technology into customer value. Productivity gains likely mean each SE covers far more accounts and more deals get technical coverage rather than headcount cuts, so the role is augmented with a shift toward higher-touch relationship and solution-architecture skills.

title: Sales managers
rationale: A large share of sales management work — pipeline and sales data analysis, forecasting, territory and quota design, budgeting, CRM hygiene, lead prioritization, training content, and performance reporting — is digital and language-based, and AI-enabled revenue-intelligence tools already automate much of it, though relationship-building, negotiation, hiring, and motivating human teams keep the role from being fully in AI's path. Demand for revenue generation is genuinely expansive (firms rarely say they want less selling), and cheaper sales capability can unlock more accounts, segments, and geographies being actively covered, but manager headcount is structurally tied to span-of-control over sales reps, and AI-driven self-service/automated selling could shrink the rep base that managers oversee, capping expansion at moderate. The mix of high task disruption and moderate demand elasticity means the occupation persists at roughly stable-to-slightly-growing headcount but with a substantially different skill set — from spreadsheet-driven reporting and coaching mechanics toward AI-tool orchestration, strategic account judgment, and interpreting model-generated forecasts. Managers who cannot move up the value chain from data wrangling to strategy and human leadership will be squeezed out.

title: School and career counselors and advisors
rationale: A meaningful slice of this work is information-heavy and highly automatable — college/financial aid research, aptitude and interest matching, resume and interview coaching, course scheduling, data analysis of attendance and grades — and AI chatbots already handle much of the advising triage in higher education. But the core of school counseling is relational and situational: building trust with adolescents, crisis and behavioral intervention, mandated abuse reporting, family and teacher collaboration, and licensed presence in a physical school building, which caps disruption at the moderate-to-high boundary. Elasticity is high because counselor-to-student ratios are badly underserved (often 350-400:1 versus a recommended 250:1) and career coaching is a service most workers never access due to cost, so cheaper delivery unlocks large latent demand. Because the disruption score sits at 6 and the human, credentialed, in-person core remains intact, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the administrative and informational periphery while headcount continues its slow growth.

title: Secretaries and administrative assistants
rationale: Core tasks — scheduling, drafting memos and reports, managing email and files, transcription, basic bookkeeping, and information lookup — are almost entirely digital, language-based, and highly routinized, placing them squarely in AI's direct path; agentic scheduling and document generation tools already absorb much of this work, though some in-person reception, physical mail, and interpersonal coordination remain. Demand is largely inelastic: administrative support is a fixed overhead function tied to headcount of the professionals being supported, not a service that organizations consume dramatically more of when it gets cheaper — instead, managers and clinicians increasingly self-serve. Medical secretaries are partly insulated by healthcare volume growth and insurance/patient-facing interaction, which is why BLS projects flat rather than steep decline. High disruption combined with low elasticity points to continued erosion of headcount and consolidation of remaining roles into fewer, higher-level coordinator positions.

title: Securities, commodities, and financial services sales agents
rationale: The analytical and information-processing core of this work — market monitoring, security research, comparable-company and valuation analysis, pitch book and prospectus drafting, client prospecting lists, and algorithmic execution — is almost entirely digital and squarely in AI's path, and automation has already hollowed out floor trading and simple order execution. What limits the disruption score is that a large share of the job is relationship-building, persuasion, trust, and regulated fiduciary judgment with clients who want a human accountable for their money. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper advice does unlock some latent demand among mass-affluent and smaller-business clients who currently get no personalized service, but robo-advisory tools capture much of that segment without adding human headcount, and deal flow in IPOs and M&A is capped by capital-market cycles and regulation rather than by advisor cost. The result is restructuring: total employment roughly flat as commodity execution and research roles shrink while the surviving job shifts toward complex advisory, specialized expertise, and client relationship management augmented by AI analytics.

title: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers
rationale: Core work is physical presence, patrol, deterrence, access control, and de-escalation with the public — tasks AI cannot perform, though AI video analytics directly substitutes for the monitoring/surveillance portion of the job (especially the small gambling surveillance segment and remote camera-watching posts), and AI can draft incident reports. That mix puts disruption in the moderate range, weighted down by the fact that the vast majority of the 1.27 million jobs involve on-site human presence. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand for security is driven by crime concern, insurance and liability requirements, and the desire for a visible human deterrent rather than by cost per unit of monitoring, so cheaper AI surveillance tends to substitute for guard-hours rather than expand total guarding. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes how monitoring is done and thins camera-room staffing, but the physical, interpersonal core of guarding remains human.

title: Semiconductor processing technicians
rationale: Core work is physically situated in cleanrooms — gowning up, loading wafers, operating and adjusting photolithography/etch/polish tools, and hands-on inspection — which AI cannot perform directly, though AI-driven defect detection, process control, and predictive maintenance will absorb a meaningful share of the monitoring, data-capture, and quality-inspection tasks. That mix puts disruption in the moderate range: tools change substantially, but human presence at the station remains essential and further automation is capital-intensive and fab-specific rather than software-driven. Elasticity is high because AI itself is driving enormous semiconductor demand, and US fab construction backed by CHIPS-era funding means more capacity, more tools, and more technicians per shift regardless of productivity gains. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient — AI reshapes the instrumentation and analytics around the job while headcount grows with fab buildout.

title: Set and exhibit designers
rationale: Much of the front-end work — script/artifact analysis, concept ideation, mood boards, renderings, CAD drawings, budgeting — is digital and already directly served by generative image tools, text-to-3D, and AI-assisted CAD, and the shift to virtual production (LED volumes, game-engine environments) pushes even more of the craft into software. What resists automation is the physical reality: overseeing fabrication, on-site installation, material and structural constraints, travel with touring shows, and the deeply collaborative negotiation with directors, curators, and craftspeople. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper design could unlock more exhibits, small-venue theater, corporate/trade-show and streaming content sets, but total demand is anchored to the number of productions, venues, and museum budgets rather than to design cost. High digital exposure plus only moderate demand expansion means the occupation persists at roughly flat headcount while the required skill mix shifts sharply toward virtual environment tooling, AI-assisted visualization, and technical/production supervision.

title: Sheet metal workers
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical: measuring, cutting, bending, welding, and installing ductwork in cramped construction sites or standing at fabrication stations. AI touches only peripheral areas — CADD design, layout optimization, and shop scheduling — while factory automation (CNC shears, presses) is a longstanding mechanical trend distinct from AI. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper HVAC fabrication and prefabrication could expand retrofit and energy-efficiency work, but building volume ultimately caps it. With disruption far below the threshold, the occupation is resilient; the main employment headwind is prefabrication and shop automation rather than AI.

title: Skincare specialists
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical touch — facials, waxing, laser hair removal, massage — performed on clients in person, which AI cannot perform; AI touches only peripheral tasks like skin-analysis apps, product recommendation, scheduling, and marketing for self-employed practitioners. Demand is fairly elastic since cheaper, faster grooming services (mini-sessions, mobile facials) unlock latent consumer demand, and social-media-driven appearance concerns keep expanding the market. But because disruption to the core task set is minimal, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity; AI-assisted diagnostics may even enhance the consultative side and raise per-worker value.

title: Small engine mechanics
rationale: The work is overwhelmingly hands-on: disassembling engines, replacing parts, using hand and pneumatic tools in shops, marinas, and cramped boat compartments. AI can help with diagnostic support, service manual lookup, parts ordering, and scheduling/recordkeeping, but these are peripheral to the physical repair itself, and no viable robotics exist for varied small-engine teardown. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because repair demand is tied to the installed base of equipment and seasonal usage rather than to service cost, and electrification may actually reduce maintenance needs. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Social and community service managers
rationale: A meaningful share of the job — grant and proposal writing, program evaluation reports, budget tracking, outcome data analysis, outreach materials — is language and data work squarely in AI's path, and current tools already accelerate these tasks. But the core of the role is human: supervising and coaching frontline social workers, hiring, crisis handling, stakeholder and community relationship building, public speaking, and navigating local political and funding contexts. Elasticity is moderate at best because demand for social services is set by government and philanthropic budgets, statutory mandates, and population need rather than by the cost of managerial labor; freeing manager time mostly shifts effort toward more program oversight rather than eliminating or multiplying positions. With disruption at 6 and administrative burden reduction reinvested in supervisory work, the occupation is resilient — reshaped at the periphery but not at its core.

title: Social and human service assistants
rationale: A meaningful slice of this job is information work AI handles well — researching available benefit programs, filling out and filing paperwork, coordinating referrals, and documenting case notes — so AI will noticeably reshape the administrative half of the role. But the core remains in-person, relational, and trust-based: interviewing clients in crisis, home and shelter visits, judging safety and need, and physically navigating fragmented local service systems, which keeps disruption moderate. Elasticity is high because demand for social services is enormously suppressed by funding and staffing limits, with large unserved populations of elderly, homeless, and substance-use clients, so any productivity gain gets absorbed by higher caseload coverage rather than layoffs. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI removes paperwork burden and expands the share of time spent on human contact, and BLS-projected demographic growth reinforces headcount stability.

title: Social workers
rationale: Core social work depends on in-person assessment, trust-building, crisis intervention, home and school visits, and legally accountable judgment about vulnerable people — tasks AI cannot assume. AI does meaningfully attack the substantial paperwork load (case notes, assessments, benefit eligibility research, resource matching, referral letters), which is a real but peripheral-to-core share of the job, placing disruption in the moderate range. Elasticity is moderate: unmet need for mental health and family services is enormous, so freed capacity would be absorbed by larger served populations, but growth is capped by state and local government budgets and licensure/reimbursement structures rather than by cost of production. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reduces administrative burden and shifts time toward client contact rather than reshaping the core work.

title: Software developers, quality assurance analysts, and testers
rationale: Software development is almost entirely digital cognitive work — writing, reviewing, testing, and documenting code — which is exactly where coding assistants and agentic AI tools are already most capable, so disruption is very high and the trajectory is steep. Demand elasticity is high because software is a classic case of cost-suppressed latent demand: countless internal tools, integrations, custom applications, and modernization projects go unbuilt today purely because engineering capacity is expensive and scarce, and cheaper production expands the total software market rather than merely shrinking teams. The main caveat is a bifurcation: routine manual QA testing and entry-level implementation work is more inelastic and faces contraction, while architecture, systems design, integration, and verification of AI-generated code expand. Net effect is augment, though individual roles restructure substantially toward specification, review, and system-level judgment rather than hand-writing code.

title: Solar photovoltaic installers
rationale: Core work is physical: climbing roofs, mounting racking, lifting 60-pound panels, wiring, sealing, and testing in unpredictable site conditions — tasks far outside AI's direct path. AI touches only peripheral elements like site assessment, system design/layout optimization, permitting paperwork, and remote performance monitoring/predictive maintenance. Demand elasticity is high because solar adoption is strongly cost-suppressed; any reduction in soft costs (design, permitting, sales) unlocks substantial latent residential and utility-scale installation demand, consistent with the projected 42% growth. Low disruption places this firmly in the resilient category, with AI acting as a demand accelerant rather than a substitute for installer labor.

title: Special education teachers
rationale: A large share of the documented workload — IEP drafting and updating, progress documentation, adapting general-education lessons, differentiating materials, and communicating with parents and specialists — is language-based paperwork that AI already handles well, and this is a notorious time sink for special educators. But the core of the job is irreducibly human and physical: in-person behavioral management, one-on-one and small-group instruction with students who have emotional, sensory, and physical disabilities, assistive-technology support, mandated legal presence at IEP meetings, and staffing ratios fixed by IDEA and state law. Elasticity is fairly high in principle because individualized instruction is deeply cost-suppressed and AI could unlock more intensive support per student, but public school budgets and federal maintenance-of-effort funding rules cap actual headcount response. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate range — AI removes paperwork burden rather than the teaching relationship — this is resilient, with the likely effect being more time redirected to direct student contact.

title: Special effects artists and animators
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital creation — modeling, animating, compositing, texturing, and even code — precisely the domain where generative image/video models, AI rotoscoping, motion capture cleanup, and procedural asset tools are already in production pipelines, so disruption is very high. Demand elasticity is high because animation and VFX are notoriously cost-constrained: studios cut shots, indie developers and small advertisers skip animation entirely, and long-form animated content is rationed by budget; if per-shot cost collapses, far more content gets animated across games, streaming, ads, social, and personalized media. Because 62% are self-employed freelancers serving a fragmented market, cheaper tools tend to expand the number of viable projects rather than consolidate headcount, though individual roles shift toward direction, art supervision, and AI-pipeline orchestration. Net effect is augment, with the caveat that mid-level production tasks (in-betweening, cleanup, basic asset creation) will contract sharply while creative-lead and technical-integration roles grow.

title: Speech-language pathologists
rationale: Core work is in-person, relational therapy: eliciting speech, physically assessing swallowing, motivating frustrated clients and coaching families — tasks that require human presence, clinical judgment, and licensure. AI does meaningfully touch the periphery and some middle: documentation, IEP and progress-note drafting, automated speech/voice analysis, and AI-driven home practice apps that extend therapy between sessions, so disruption is moderate rather than low. Elasticity is high because speech therapy access is severely rationed by cost, waitlists, and clinician shortages in schools and rural areas — cheaper delivery would unlock large latent demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6 (the hands-on therapeutic core is not reshaped), the occupation is resilient, with AI mostly relieving paperwork burden and letting each clinician serve more clients.

title: Stationary engineers and boiler operators
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical operation, inspection, and repair of boilers, turbines, and HVAC equipment in dirty, confined, on-site environments — tasks AI cannot perform. AI and IoT sensor automation can improve monitoring, predictive maintenance, and logging, which trims some routine gauge-watching and record-keeping, but licensing requirements and safety regulations mandate a qualified human on premises. Elasticity is low because demand is determined by the fixed stock of buildings and industrial plants needing utilities, not by the cost of the labor. Low disruption places this firmly in the resilient category, consistent with BLS's modest 2 percent growth projection.

title: Substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors
rationale: The work is language-based, which puts intake assessment, treatment-plan drafting, documentation, and even some psychoeducation and between-session support squarely in AI's path — chatbot-based CBT tools already exist. But the therapeutic core depends on trust, empathy, crisis intervention, in-person and residential settings, court-mandated supervision, and licensure requirements, so AI mostly offloads paperwork and augments rather than replaces sessions, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is very high: mental health and addiction treatment demand is massively suppressed by cost, stigma, and provider shortages, so any productivity gain gets absorbed by unmet need rather than headcount cuts. Because disruption stays at or below 6, this is resilient — AI reshapes documentation and triage at the periphery while clinical headcount continues its strong projected growth.

title: Surgical assistants and technologists
rationale: The work is almost entirely hands-on and physical: sterilizing instruments, draping and positioning patients, passing instruments, holding retractors, suturing and suctioning in a sterile operating field. AI touches only peripheral elements like inventory tracking, scheduling, instrument counting, and robotic surgery setup, and surgical robots still require human scrub personnel at the table. Demand is moderately elastic — an aging population and cheaper, faster outpatient surgery could unlock meaningful additional procedure volume — but surgery volume is capped by surgeon supply, OR capacity, and reimbursement. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI changes the surrounding technology stack, not the core role.

title: Survey researchers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — background research, questionnaire drafting and cognitive testing, sampling design, weighting/nonresponse adjustment, statistical analysis, and report/visualization writing — are digital and language- or code-based, and current LLM plus statistical tooling already handles much of it; AI can even simulate respondent panels and pretest wording, making disruption very high despite occasional in-person focus-group facilitation. Elasticity is low because demand for survey-based insight is capped by client research budgets and, more importantly, is being actively substituted away by passive big data, digital trace data, and social media analytics; cheaper surveys do not make organizations commission proportionally more of them, and respondent fatigue limits volume. BLS already projects a 5 percent decline in this small (8,800-job) occupation. High disruption combined with structurally shrinking, inelastic demand fits 'replace' — the surviving roles will concentrate in methodological oversight at a smaller headcount.

title: Surveying and mapping technicians
rationale: The occupation splits between physical fieldwork — visiting sites, setting markers, operating instruments in rugged terrain — and digital processing of GIS/CAD data, where AI-assisted point-cloud classification, automated feature extraction, and drone/LiDAR photogrammetry pipelines already materially reduce manual labor. That mixed profile caps disruption around 6: the office-side mapping and data-processing tasks are squarely in AI's path, but the site-presence and equipment-handling core is not. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster surveying does unlock more frequent as-built scans, digital twins, infrastructure monitoring and higher-resolution municipal GIS layers, though total demand is still tied to construction, land transaction, and utility project volumes and to licensed surveyor sign-off. Because the physical field component keeps disruption at or below 6, the occupation is best classified resilient, with the caveat that the purely desk-based mapping/GIS technician subset faces meaningfully more displacement risk than the field subset.

title: Surveyors
rationale: Surveying blends substantial fieldwork — traveling to sites, setting instruments, walking rugged terrain, physically marking boundaries — with digital tasks like records research, CAD/GIS processing, data reduction, and report preparation. AI plus drones/LiDAR automation meaningfully compresses the office and data-processing half of the job and speeds deed/title research, but licensed professional judgment, legal certification, court testimony, and on-site presence keep the core intact. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper surveys could unlock more frequent boundary verification, as-built and monitoring surveys tied to construction and infrastructure cycles, though it is ultimately capped by the volume of land transactions and building projects and by state licensure. With disruption at 5 the occupation falls in the resilient band — technology raises productivity per surveyor (as BLS notes) without reshaping the fundamental role.

title: Tax examiners and collectors, and revenue agents
rationale: The core work — reviewing returns, matching documentation, applying tax code rules, flagging questionable deductions, and computing penalties and interest — is almost entirely digital, rule-based document analysis that AI and automated matching systems already perform well; field collections and taxpayer negotiation are the main human-anchored residual. Demand is highly inelastic because it is set by the number of filers and by government budget appropriations rather than by the cost of examination; even if audits became 10x cheaper, political and statutory limits, plus fixed headcount budgets, cap expansion (some latent demand exists since audit coverage rates are low, which is why elasticity isn't a 1-2). With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains flow into fewer positions, reinforcing the already-projected employment decline. Remaining roles will concentrate in complex corporate revenue-agent work and in-person collection enforcement.

title: Taxi drivers, shuttle drivers, and chauffeurs
rationale: Although the work is physical rather than digital, driving is the single physical task AI is most directly and aggressively automating: robotaxi fleets are already commercially deployed and scaling in multiple US metros, and the core task set (navigate, pick up, transport, collect fare) is almost fully addressable by autonomous systems, with only luggage handling, wheelchair assistance, and concierge/executive-assistant duties resisting. This justifies a high disruption score even though the peripheral customer-service and paratransit segments remain human for the next decade. Elasticity is low from the worker's perspective: cheaper rides do unlock substantial latent trip demand, but that expansion is served by driverless vehicles rather than by each human driver completing 10x more trips — a driver's output is capped by hours in a car, so productivity gains accrue to the platform and vehicle, not to human headcount. High disruption plus structurally capped per-worker output points to replacement, with residual demand concentrated in assisted-transport, luxury chauffeur, and paratransit niches.

title: Teacher assistants
rationale: The core of this job is physical, in-person presence: supervising students at recess and lunch, managing behavior, lifting and assisting special-needs students with feeding and hygiene, and providing the human attention a lead teacher cannot. AI can absorb some peripheral tasks (attendance, grade calculation, preparing materials) and adaptive tutoring software may substitute for a portion of one-on-one lesson reinforcement, but these are a minority of daily duties and cannot replace custodial supervision or caregiving. Demand elasticity is moderate: there is genuine latent demand for more individualized student support, but headcount is set almost entirely by school district budgets and state aide-to-student ratios rather than by productivity or price, so cheaper AI tools would not translate into more aides being hired. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — its trajectory will continue to be driven by school funding and enrollment rather than by AI.

title: Technical writers
rationale: Technical writing is almost entirely digital language work — drafting manuals, editing, standardizing terminology, restructuring content for different audiences and formats — which is squarely in the path of current LLMs, and AI tools already draft and localize documentation from code, specs, and SME interviews. Demand has some latent expansion (more products documented, more languages, richer multimedia, always-current docs), but documentation is a cost center tied to the number of products shipped rather than a service consumers buy more of when cheaper, so volume growth is structurally capped. With very high disruption and only low elasticity, productivity gains mostly convert into smaller documentation teams where a few senior writers curate AI output and manage information architecture, matching BLS's own note that AI productivity will slow employment growth.

title: Telecommunications technicians
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical installation and repair — climbing towers, splicing fiber, crawling in attics, working in customer premises — which AI cannot perform without robotics that is far from deployment. AI touches only peripheral elements: remote network monitoring, automated fault diagnostics and self-healing networks, scheduling optimization, and AR-assisted troubleshooting guides, which can modestly reduce truck rolls and diagnostic labor per job. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because telecom buildout is driven by capital investment cycles, spectrum policy, and broadband funding rather than technician labor cost, and newer fiber infrastructure inherently needs less maintenance. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient to AI even though BLS projects mild decline for structural (infrastructure cycle) reasons rather than AI substitution.

title: Tellers
rationale: Teller work is routine transaction processing, identity verification, account Q&A, and light product referral — nearly all of which is already being absorbed by mobile banking, enhanced ATMs, video kiosks, and AI chat/voice agents; the only genuinely physical component is cash handling, which machines already do well. Demand elasticity is very low: cheaper transaction processing does not make people deposit checks or exchange currency 10x more often, and branch traffic is structurally declining as customers self-serve. Productivity gains therefore flow directly into fewer tellers per branch and fewer branches, consistent with the BLS -13% projection. High disruption plus near-fixed demand puts this squarely in the replace category, with surviving roles skewing toward complex problem resolution and sales referral.

title: Top executives
rationale: Much of the executive information-processing layer — analyzing financial statements, sales reports, drafting policies, preparing board materials, scheduling and coordinating operations — is squarely in AI's path, and general/operations managers will see reporting and planning workflows substantially automated. But the irreducible core is accountability, legal and fiduciary authority, negotiation, motivating and appointing people, and bearing responsibility for outcomes; organizations require a human decision-maker regardless of how cheap analysis becomes, and much of the role involves in-person presence and political/relational capital. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper management overhead could let more small ventures and units exist (and self-employed executives are 26% of chief executives), but headcount is fundamentally tied to the number of organizations and units rather than to output volume, so gains partly compress middle-layer management. With disruption at 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes how executives get information and possibly thins the ranks of coordination-heavy operations managers, but does not displace the core authority function.

title: Tour and travel guides
rationale: The core of the job is in-person: physically leading groups, reading the room, managing logistics on the ground, and providing a human hospitality experience that tourists explicitly pay for. AI meaningfully helps with the peripheral knowledge work — researching site history, drafting scripts, planning routes, handling bookings and translation — and audio/AR self-guided apps offer some substitution at the low end, but they mostly compete with free/cheap alternatives rather than replace guided experiences. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper trip planning and translation could expand tour offerings and niche/multilingual tours, but the service is inherently time-bound and labor-intensive, capping expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient; AI becomes a prep and marketing tool for guides rather than a substitute for their presence.

title: Training and development managers
rationale: Core work — designing curricula, producing training content, assessing needs, evaluating program effectiveness — is predominantly digital and language-based, and generative AI already produces course materials, assessments, simulations, and personalized learning paths at a fraction of prior cost, so disruption is high; the leadership, budget, and stakeholder-alignment portions remain human. Elasticity is high because corporate learning is chronically underfunded and rationed by content-production cost, and AI-driven workforce change is itself creating enormous reskilling demand — cheaper, personalized training means far more of it gets delivered, not less.
