The likely path is each manager overseeing dramatically more content and more AI-assisted personalization rather than headcount shrinking, though the skill mix shifts toward learning-technology and AI-tool orchestration.

title: Training and development specialists
rationale: Core tasks — needs assessment surveys, writing training manuals, building e-learning modules, quizzes and evaluation reports — are language- and content-generation work squarely in AI's path; authoring tools with generative AI already compress instructional design cycles from weeks to hours. The counterweight is live facilitation, stakeholder consultation, and organization-specific credibility, which keeps a human presence requirement and holds disruption at the lower end of 'high.' Elasticity is high because corporate training is chronically under-supplied and cost-rationed: personalized, role-specific, continuously updated curricula were previously unaffordable, and the AI transition itself is generating enormous new upskilling and compliance-training demand. Cheaper content production therefore expands the volume and granularity of training rather than shrinking headcount, though the skill mix shifts toward AI-assisted design, curation, quality control, and facilitation.

title: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers
rationale: A substantial share of this role — route and network optimization, demand and inventory forecasting, load planning, compliance log review, budgeting and reporting — is exactly the kind of data-heavy analytic work AI and optimization software are already absorbing, which pushes disruption toward the high end. But the core of the job remains physically situated supervision of warehouse and driver workforces, on-the-ground crisis response to disruptions, facility safety, and negotiation with carriers, suppliers, and clients, which caps disruption at moderate-high. Elasticity is moderate: goods volume is bounded by real physical throughput and facility count, so cheaper planning does not create proportionally more freight, though smaller firms could afford more sophisticated logistics management and e-commerce keeps expanding node counts. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient — AI reshapes the analytical toolkit and raises expectations for data fluency, but the supervisory and physical-coordination core endures.

title: Travel agents
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — searching fares and schedules, comparing options, building itineraries, calculating costs, booking reservations, and answering destination questions — are digital information-retrieval and language tasks squarely in AI's path, and this occupation was already hollowed out by online booking platforms. Consumer-facing AI travel planners disintermediate the agent directly rather than making agents more productive, so productivity gains accrue to travelers and platforms, not to agent headcount. Latent demand for trip planning does exist (people would plan more elaborate trips if expert advice were free), but that demand will be captured by AI tools and OTAs; total travel spending is capped by household budgets and time off, not by planning cost. A residual high-touch niche (luxury, complex group, corporate duty-of-care, crisis rebooking, first-hand destination knowledge) will persist, but overall the combination of very high disruption and inelastic, disintermediated demand points to headcount contraction.

title: Tutors
rationale: Tutoring is almost entirely language- and cognition-based work — explaining concepts, generating practice problems, giving feedback, drilling vocabulary — which sits directly in generative AI's core competence, and BLS itself notes AI software can already perform many routine tutoring activities. Elasticity is very high because personalized one-on-one instruction has historically been rationed by cost: most students who need academic support never get it, and cheap adaptive instruction unlocks enormous latent demand across K-12 remediation, ESL, test prep, and adult reskilling. The likely equilibrium is that AI handles content delivery and drilling while human tutors shift toward motivation, accountability, diagnosis, special-needs support, and supervising AI-driven learning plans — a large expansion of the total tutoring market that keeps human headcount roughly stable to growing even as productivity per tutor rises. The main downside risk is that much of the expanded demand is captured by software vendors rather than human tutors, which would push this toward restructure; but the sheer scale of unmet demand and the irreplaceable relational/engagement component support augment.

title: Umpires, referees, and other sports officials
rationale: The core work is physical presence at live events, positioning, split-second judgment, and managing human disputes with players and coaches — almost none of which AI can replace. Automated ball-strike systems, goal-line technology, and video review do encroach on specific calls at elite levels, but these affect a tiny fraction of the 19,300 jobs (the vast majority officiate youth, high school, and recreational sports where cameras and tracking systems are cost-prohibitive), and even in pro leagues humans remain on the field to administer the game. Elasticity is moderate: demand is driven by the number of games played and youth sports participation, not by officiating cost, though officiating shortages suggest some latent unmet demand. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI becomes a decision-support tool at the top of the pyramid rather than a substitute for the workforce.

title: Urban and regional planners
rationale: Planning work is predominantly knowledge work — data gathering and analysis, GIS mapping, scenario modeling, drafting comprehensive plans, reviewing site plans against zoning codes, and writing reports — all directly in AI's path, and generative AI plus automated GIS/zoning-compliance tools already materially accelerate these tasks. However, the occupation retains substantial non-automatable components: public hearings, stakeholder negotiation, political judgment, site visits, and legally accountable recommendations, which caps disruption below the very-high tier. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could unlock more frequent plan updates, faster permitting review, and planning capacity for small and rural jurisdictions that currently go without, but headcount is fundamentally gated by government budgets, fixed numbers of jurisdictions, and statutory processes rather than by analytical throughput. High disruption with moderate, budget-constrained demand expansion means the role persists but shifts toward facilitation, political navigation, and oversight of AI-generated analysis — a restructuring of the skill set rather than wholesale replacement.

title: Veterinarians
rationale: Veterinary work is fundamentally hands-on: physical examination, surgery, dressing wounds, restraining frightened animals, and traveling to farms cannot be delegated to AI. AI meaningfully assists the diagnostic, imaging-interpretation, recordkeeping, and client-communication portions of the job, so disruption is moderate but not core-reshaping. Elasticity is high because veterinary care is heavily cost-suppressed — many owners forgo diagnostics and advanced procedures on price, and cheaper workups would unlock substantial latent demand, alongside chronic vet shortages especially in rural and food-animal practice. With disruption at 5, the occupation falls into the resilient category: AI improves throughput and diagnostic quality at the periphery while the physical, licensed core remains human.

title: Veterinary assistants and laboratory animal caretakers
rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: feeding, bathing, restraining animals, cleaning cages, sterilizing instruments, and post-surgical monitoring. AI touches only peripheral elements such as scheduling, recordkeeping, and possibly automated monitoring sensors, none of which displace the need for a human physically present with animals. Demand for veterinary services has meaningful latent expansion as pet spending rises and lower-cost care reaches more owners, but this is driven by pet ownership trends rather than AI productivity. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI may modestly assist documentation and monitoring while headcount continues to grow.

title: Veterinary technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on animal handling: restraining, bathing, drawing blood, positioning for x-rays, administering anesthesia and monitoring patients, and prepping surgical instruments — tasks requiring physical presence, dexterity, and strength that AI cannot perform. AI touches only the periphery: records and case histories, lab image/sample interpretation, client education materials, scheduling, and diagnostic decision support, which may modestly speed documentation and testing workflows. Elasticity is high because veterinary care is significantly cost-suppressed — cheaper diagnostics and streamlined workflows would expand treatment volume and increase the number of pets receiving advanced care — but this expands demand for technicians rather than shrinking it. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient; growing pet ownership and treatment options reinforce the BLS projection of above-average growth.

title: Waiters and waitresses
rationale: The core work is physical and interpersonal: carrying trays, setting tables, reading customers, and handling in-person service — tasks AI language models cannot perform. Disruption comes mainly from adjacent automation (ordering kiosks, QR-code menus, payment apps) which trims order-taking and payment tasks but doesn't touch food delivery, table maintenance, or hospitality; this is digitization rather than AI per se. Elasticity is moderate because dining out demand responds somewhat to price and convenience, but restaurant capacity, real estate, and consumer appetite cap expansion. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient — headcount pressures come from self-service kiosks and takeout trends, not from AI absorbing the core role.

title: Water and wastewater treatment plant and system operators
rationale: Core work blends physical plant tasks — inspecting equipment, adding chemicals, collecting samples, maintenance, emergency manual operation — with SCADA monitoring and regulatory reporting that AI/automation can meaningfully optimize, so disruption is moderate rather than low. Demand is highly inelastic: water volumes treated are driven by population and infrastructure capacity, not by the cost of operator labor, and licensing plus regulatory staffing rules cap any expansion. The real headcount pressure here comes from process automation and remote monitoring (already reflected in BLS's -7% projection) rather than from generative AI absorbing the job. Because a majority of tasks still require on-site physical presence, hands-on troubleshooting, and licensed accountability, the occupation scores as resilient despite its declining trend.

title: Water transportation workers
rationale: Core work is physical and presence-based: standing watch, handling lines, maintaining engines and pumps, maneuvering vessels in confined waters, and assisting passengers. AI aids navigation planning, weather routing, predictive maintenance, and logs/paperwork, and autonomous vessel pilots exist, but Coast Guard credentialing, STCW rules, safety liability, and slow fleet turnover mean crewed operation remains the norm well beyond ten years. Elasticity is low because shipping volume is driven by commodity trade and port infrastructure, not by the cost of crew labor — cheaper crewing would not multiply cargo tonnage or ferry trips. Low disruption places this squarely in the resilient category, with gradual crew-size reduction on the most automated vessels as the main long-run risk.

title: Web developers and digital designers
rationale: Web development and digital design are almost entirely digital, language- and code-based tasks — HTML/CSS/JS coding, layout mockups, asset generation, testing, and content creation are precisely what current generative AI and no-code/AI site builders already do well, giving a very high disruption score. Elasticity is high because web presence and interface work are cost-suppressed at the low end: millions of small businesses, nonprofits, and individuals currently forgo custom sites or app interfaces, and cheaper production means more frequent redesigns, more personalized and localized experiences, and more digital surfaces (mobile, wearables, kiosks) getting bespoke design. However, the commoditized template end of the market is genuinely vulnerable, so expansion is strong but not unlimited. Net effect is augment: individual productivity rises sharply while total demand for digital experiences expands enough to keep headcount roughly stable to growing, with the work shifting toward orchestration, UX judgment, brand strategy, accessibility, and client consultation rather than hand-coding.

title: Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers
rationale: Welding is overwhelmingly physical, hands-on work requiring manual dexterity, positioning in awkward or confined spaces, and real-time judgment about molten metal behavior — tasks far outside AI's direct path. AI touches only peripheral elements like blueprint interpretation, weld inspection imaging, job scheduling, and robotic welding cells (which mainly affect high-volume repetitive shop work already counted as machine operation, not field welding). Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper fabrication could unlock more infrastructure and custom metalwork, but growth is bounded by capital project cycles and material costs, and the binding constraint is a shortage of skilled welders rather than cost of their output. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — automation pressure comes from physical robotics, not generative AI, and remains slow-moving for non-repetitive field and repair work.

title: Wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives
rationale: Much of the work — prospecting, lead qualification, cold outreach, product Q&A, quote and contract preparation, CRM logging, sales reporting, and follow-up — is language and data work squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven lead scoring, automated outreach and e-commerce ordering already reshape B2B selling; the residual core is relationship-building, in-person negotiation, and trade-show presence, which keeps disruption below the very high band. Elasticity is moderate: total B2B transaction volume is bounded by underlying goods demand rather than by sales-rep cost, so cheaper selling mostly means fewer reps per dollar of revenue, though longer-tail accounts and smaller customers that were previously uneconomic to cover can be served, and reps can carry larger territories. The result is an occupation that persists at roughly flat headcount but with a substantially shifted skill mix — transactional order-taking and inside-sales cold-calling erode toward automation while consultative, technical, and negotiation-heavy roles gain weight. That combination of high task disruption with only partial demand expansion fits restructure.

title: Wind turbine technicians
rationale: The core work is intensely physical — climbing 200+ foot towers, rappelling down blades, working in confined nacelles with hand and power tools — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only the periphery: predictive maintenance analytics from SCADA and sensor data may reorder maintenance schedules and improve diagnostics, plus drone-based inspection reduces some manual inspection time, but the repair itself still requires a human on site. Elasticity is high because demand is driven by electricity demand growth and the installed turbine fleet, not by technician cost; better diagnostics that raise turbine uptime increase the value of maintenance rather than eliminating it, and BLS projects 50% growth. With disruption well under 6, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Woodworkers
rationale: Woodworking is predominantly physical: lifting bulky lumber, setting up and tending machines, hand assembly, sanding, staining, and finishing. AI touches only peripheral elements — CAD/design generation, CNC toolpath optimization, nesting/yield software, and quality inspection — while the ongoing automation pressure comes from CNC machinery rather than AI per se. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because furniture and cabinetry demand is tied to housing, renovation cycles, and material costs, not to the cost of design or programming labor; cheaper custom design could unlock some latent demand for bespoke cabinetry, but material and installation costs dominate. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient in AI terms, though it continues its slow secular decline from conventional automation and import competition.

title: Writers and authors
rationale: Writing is the single most directly automatable knowledge task by current LLMs — drafting copy, blog posts, content marketing, summaries, and even fiction outlines are already produced at near-zero marginal cost, so disruption is very high. Elasticity is mixed: total content volume expands enormously and cheap generation unlocks more marketing, localization, and self-publishing, but human attention is a hard cap, commodity content pay collapses, and demand for prestige human-authored work (novels, screenplays, speeches, brand voice) is bounded by audience time and gatekeeping. The result is a bifurcated occupation: high-volume commodity copywriting contracts sharply while roles shift toward prompting, editing, curating, fact-checking, and supplying distinctive voice and credibility. That skill-set migration with only moderate demand absorption fits 'restructure' rather than outright replacement or headcount growth.

title: Zoologists and wildlife biologists
rationale: A substantial share of the work is fieldwork — capturing, handling, and observing animals in remote terrain, collecting specimens, and running lab tests — which AI cannot perform, though AI-assisted camera-trap/bioacoustic identification, GIS modeling, population estimation, and literature/report writing already materially speed the analytical and documentation half of the job. That mix puts disruption in the moderate range: the core scientific judgment and field presence remain human, but data processing is being transformed. Elasticity is low because roughly 69% of employment is government-funded and demand is capped by appropriations and conservation budgets rather than by the cost of analysis; cheaper monitoring yields more data per biologist, not many more biologist positions. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes tools and workflows at the periphery while headcount stays roughly flat, as BLS projections suggest.

title: Sociologists
rationale: Sociologists' core workflow — literature synthesis, survey and interview instrument design, statistical analysis, coding qualitative data, and writing reports and articles — is almost entirely digital, language- and analysis-based, and squarely in the path of current LLM and data-analysis tools; even fieldwork interviews are increasingly transcribed and coded automatically. Demand elasticity is only moderate: social research output is gated by grant funding, university budgets, government contracts, and publication/policy channels rather than by production cost, though cheaper research could let more advocacy groups, agencies, and small institutions commission studies they cannot currently afford. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation persists (institutionally embedded in academia and government) but the skill mix shifts sharply toward AI-assisted mixed-methods design, causal inference, ethical framing, and interpretation for policymakers. Workers who remain manual-analysis specialists are displaced; those who orchestrate AI tools and own the theory and credibility layer will handle far more projects each.
